- **C-385** telling added · 10.7 *Dedicating* (recorded, 2026-10-24)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Dedicating  To dedicate, *qādash*, is to give something to the Lord and set it apart for him. In most of these verses the one who gives is a person, and what is given is his own.  A man can dedicate his house or his field, and the law then sets its worth. - *"When a man dedicates his house as a holy gift to the Lord, the priest shall value it as either good or bad; as the priest values it, so it shall stand"* (Leviticus 27:14). - He can buy it back at a cost: *"if the donor wishes to redeem his house, he shall add a fifth to the valuation price, and it shall be his"* (27:15). - A field can be lost for good: *"if he does not wish to redeem the field, or if he has sold the field to another man, it shall not be redeemed anymore"* (27:20).  The worth of the gift is set by the priest, not by the one who gives it.  Some things cannot be given, because they are already the Lord's: *"a firstborn of animals, which as a firstborn belongs to the Lord, no man may dedicate; whether ox or sheep, it is the Lord's"* (Leviticus 27:26). Where the firstborn is commanded, the command comes with a memory. - *"Consecrate to me all the firstborn. Whatever is the first to open the womb among the people of Israel, both of man and of beast, is mine"* (Exodus 13:2), and straight after it, *"Remember this day in which you came out from Egypt"* (13:3). - *"All the firstborn males that are born of your herd and flock you shall dedicate to the Lord your God"* (Deuteronomy 15:19), a few verses after *"You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the Lord your God redeemed you"* (15:15).  Kings and leaders dedicate what they have won. - *"These also King David dedicated to the Lord, together with the silver and gold that he dedicated from all the nations he subdued"* (2 Samuel 8:11; 1 Chronicles 18:11). The passage ends, *"And the Lord gave victory to David wherever he went"* (2 Samuel 8:14). - *"From spoil won in battles they dedicated gifts for the maintenance of the house of the Lord"* (1 Chronicles 26:27). The givers named include *"Samuel the seer and Saul the son of Kish and Abner the son of Ner and Joab the son of Zeruiah"* (26:28).  Solomon dedicates the house inside a plan, and with a question. *"Now Solomon purposed to build a temple for the name of the Lord"* (2 Chronicles 2:1). *"Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of the Lord my God and dedicate it to him"* (2:4). Then: *"But who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him? Who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to make offerings before him?"* (2:6).  The giving is done in abundance, and with joy. - Under Hezekiah *"the people of Israel gave in abundance"* (2 Chronicles 31:5), and brought *"the tithe of the dedicated things that had been dedicated to the Lord their God, and laid them in heaps"* (31:6). *"When Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the Lord and his people Israel"* (31:8). - In the days of Nehemiah *"they set apart that which was for the Levites"* (Nehemiah 12:47), on the day when *"God had made them rejoice with great joy"* (12:43).  A dedication can be taken back. When Hazael *"set his face to go up against Jerusalem"* (2 Kings 12:17), *"Jehoash king of Judah took all the sacred gifts that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah his fathers, the kings of Judah, had dedicated, and his own sacred gifts … and sent these to Hazael king of Syria. Then Hazael went away from Jerusalem"* (12:18). The verse does not say what moved him.  The same giving can go to an idol. - Micah's mother: *"I dedicate the silver to the Lord from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image"* (Judges 17:3). The chapter ends, *"Everyone did what was right in his own eyes"* (17:6). - Israel *"came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the thing of shame, and became detestable like the thing they loved"* (Hosea 9:10). The verse opens with God: *"Like grapes in the wilderness, I found Israel"*. The word there is *nāzar*, "to separate, set apart". - Ezekiel names *"any one of the house of Israel"* *"who separates himself from me, taking his idols into his heart"* (Ezekiel 14:7), the same word. Chapter 12 (*Idols taken inside*) follows the heart.  The same *nāzar* is used of abstaining, and God asks what it was for. *"Should I weep and abstain in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?"* (Zechariah 7:3). The answer is a question: *"When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and in the seventh, for these seventy years, was it for me that you fasted?"* (7:5).  God also dedicates a person, before the person is born. *"Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations"* (Jeremiah 1:5). Jeremiah answers, *"Ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth"* (1:6), and is told, *"Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you"* (1:8).
  - note: in full

The givers named include *"Samuel the seer and Saul the son of Kish and Abner the son of Ner and Joab the son of Zeruiah"* (26:28).  Solomon dedicates the house inside a plan, and with a question. *"Now Solomon purposed to build a temple for the name of the Lord"* (2 Chronicles 2:1). *"Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of the Lord my God and dedicate it to him"* (2:4). Then: *"But who is able to build him a house, since heaven, even highest heaven, cannot contain him? Who am I to build a house for him, except as a place to make offerings before him?"* (2:6).  The giving is done in abundance, and with joy. - Under Hezekiah *"the people of Israel gave in abundance"* (2 Chronicles 31:5), and brought *"the tithe of the dedicated things that had been dedicated to the Lord their God, and laid them in heaps"* (31:6). *"When Hezekiah and the princes came and saw the heaps, they blessed the Lord and his people Israel"* (31:8). - In the days of Nehemiah *"they set apart that which was for the Levites"* (Nehemiah 12:47), on the day when *"God had made them rejoice with great joy"* (12:43).  A dedication can be taken back. When Hazael *"set his face to go up against Jerusalem"* (2 Kings 12:17), *"Jehoash king of Judah took all the sacred gifts that Jehoshaphat and Jehoram and Ahaziah his fathers, the kings of Judah, had dedicated, and his own sacred gifts … and sent these to Hazael king of Syria. Then Hazael went away from Jerusalem"* (12:18). The verse does not say what moved him.  The same giving can go to an idol. - Micah's mother: *"I dedicate the silver to the Lord from my hand for my son, to make a carved image and a metal image"* (Judges 17:3). The chapter ends, *"Everyone did what was right in his own eyes"* (17:6). - Israel *"came to Baal-peor and consecrated themselves to the thing of shame, and became detestable like the thing they loved"* (Hosea 9:10). The verse opens with God: *"Like grapes in the wilderness, I found Israel"*. The word there is *nāzar*, "to separate, set apart". - Ezekiel names *"any one of the house of Israel"* *"who separates himself from me, taking his idols into his heart"* (Ezekiel 14:7), the same word. Chapter 12 (*Idols taken inside*) follows the heart.  The same *nāzar* is used of abstaining, and God asks what it was for. *"Should I weep and abstain in the fifth month, as I have done for so many years?"* (Zechariah 7:3). The answer is a question: *"When you fasted and mourned in the fifth month and in the seventh, for these seventy years, was it for me that you fasted?"* (7:5).  God also dedicates a person, before the person is born. *"Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you were born I consecrated you; I appointed you a prophet to the nations"* (Jeremiah 1:5). Jeremiah answers, *"Ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth"* (1:6), and is told, *"Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you"* (1:8).

## 2026-10-19 — OT-05.16: self-glory (Rev 18:7, Php 3:19), read outward and woven (#2160 group C)

**Strand:** open threads on completed clusters (#2160), OT-05.16 (M25 -> M08)

**Researcher:** "proceed with C" (2026-10-19), on the proposal in ot-05-16-self-glory-reading-v1-20261019.md

**Method:** Group C of #2160 had proposed re-pointing OT-05.16 to M22 because the self-glory words (doxazo G1392, doxa G1391) are M22-tagged. Read outward by guide v2 (#2168), with the passages Rev 18:2-10 and Php 3:17-21: both verses were uncited and carry the inner being now. Rev 18:7 takes up Isa 47:7-9 (no widow; one day). Original checked in verse_lexical: G1392 reflexive in Rev 18:7 (the Mat 5:16 verb), G2836 koilia (Rom 16:18 'appetites'), G5426 phroneo in Php 3:19 and Col 3:2, G1391 in Php 3:19 and 3:21. Woven: 10.15 v3 (It gives itself the glory; It tells itself that loss will not come; The boast: In shame; Where it ends: A like measure), Ch 4 v22 (About myself), 10.6 v28 (served as a god), 10.7 v34 (the set mind, beside Rom 8:6; moved from the proposal's 10.4, which has no account of the set mind), Ch 11 v39 (section 4 Glory), 10.10 v35 (another's pride wept over). Rule 77 reconciliation for pride in the touched 10.15 sections: C-214 to C-221, C-228 to C-232, C-235 to C-237, C-182, C-243, C-244 read; none rests on these verses and none needs restating.

- **C-324** telling added · 10.15 *The heart that says what God says* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: **It tells itself that loss will not come.** Babylon in Isaiah says more than "I am". She says, "I shall not sit as a widow or know the loss of children" (Isaiah 47:8). Before it: "You said, 'I shall be mistress forever,' so that you did not lay these things to heart or remember their end" (47:7). The answer: "These two things shall come to you in a moment, in one day" (47:9). Revelation gives the great city the same voice: "in her heart she says, 'I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see'" (Revelation 18:7). And the same answer: "For this reason her plagues will come in a single day, death and mourning and famine" (18:8). I read Revelation as taking up Isaiah's words. Pride's heart says that it will not be moved from where it sits, and that nothing will be taken from it. The verse in Isaiah names what goes with it: the end is not laid to heart.
  - note: in full
- **C-324** telling added · 04 *The heart speaks to itself* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: - **About myself.** "I shall not be moved; throughout all generations I shall not meet adversity" (Psalm 10:6). "I will ascend to heaven" (Isaiah 14:13). "Who will bring me down to the ground?" (Obadiah 3). "I sit as a queen, I am no widow, and mourning I shall never see" (Revelation 18:7; 10.15).
  - note: in part: Revelation 18:7
- **C-325** telling added · 10.15 *Given, then held as one's own* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: **It gives itself the glory.** The great city "glorified herself and lived in luxury" (Revelation 18:7). The Greek verb is the one used where people give glory to God: "so that they may see your good works and give glory to your Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 5:16). Here she is the one who gives the glory and the one who receives it. What it brings her is in *Where it ends*, below.
  - note: in full
- **C-325** telling added · 11 *4. One word, opposite values* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: - **Glory.** The verb that gives glory to God (Matthew 5:16) is the great city's own: she "glorified herself" (Revelation 18:7). The noun is the glory some take "in their shame" (Philippians 3:19), and two verses later the glory of the body to come, "like his glorious body" (3:21). The same word names glory taken where it does not belong and glory given (10.15).
  - note: in part: Revelation 18:7
- **C-326** telling added · 10.15 *Where it ends* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: **A like measure.** "As she glorified herself and lived in luxury, so give her a like measure of torment and mourning" (Revelation 18:7). The measure of what comes to the city is the measure of the glory she gave herself and the luxury she lived in. The mourning she said she would never see is what she is given. The verse before says the same of her deeds: "Pay her back as she herself has paid back others … mix a double portion for her in the cup she mixed" (18:6). Those who shared her luxury "will stand far off, in fear of her torment" (18:9–10). And before it all comes a call: "Come out of her, my people, lest you take part in her sins, lest you share in her plagues" (18:4).
  - note: in full
- **C-327** telling added · 10.15 *The boast* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: **In shame.** Paul names many who "walk as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things" (Philippians 3:18–19). The word is "glory" (*doxa*), not the boast word. I read it as doing the boast's work, saying what a person stands on, and as turned upside down: it rests on what should shame. Paul tells it "even with tears" (3:18; 10.10). Against it he sets, "But our citizenship is in heaven", and a Savior who "will transform our lowly body to be like his glorious body" (3:20–21). "Glorious" is the same word. Their glory is in their shame, and the glory awaited is his.
  - note: in full

  - passage before: —
  - passage after: - **Glory.** The verb that gives glory to God (Matthew 5:16) is the great city's own: she "glorified herself" (Revelation 18:7). The noun is the glory some take "in their shame" (Philippians 3:19), and two verses later the glory of the body to come, "like his glorious body" (3:21). The same word names glory taken where it does not belong and glory given (10.15).
  - note: in part: Philippians 3:19, 21
- **C-328** telling added · 10.6 *Wanting that owns the one who wants* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: The verses give desire the verbs of a person acting on the one who wants. It is obeyed under sin as king: *"Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions"* (Romans 6:12). It is followed: *"grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires"* (Jude 16); *"scoffers will come in the last days with scoffing, following their own sinful desires. They will say, 'Where is the promise of his coming?'"* (2 Peter 3:3–4). It picks what is heard: *"having itching ears they will accumulate for themselves teachers to suit their own passions, and will turn away from listening to the truth and wander off into myths"* (2 Timothy 4:3–4). The itch is a want to be scratched, and the teachers are gathered to scratch it. It keeps learning from arriving: *"led astray by various passions, always learning and never able to arrive at a knowledge of the truth"* (3:6–7). It deceives: *"your old self … is corrupt through deceitful desires"* (Ephesians 4:22). It baits: *"each person is tempted when he is lured and enticed by his own desire"* (James 1:14). That is the fisherman's or hunter's picture, and it comes before the conceiving of 1:15. It takes captive: *"the treacherous are taken captive by their lust"* (Proverbs 11:6). It crouches like an animal at the threshold: *"sin is crouching at the door. Its desire is for you, and you must rule over it"* (Genesis 4:7). And it can be inherited: *"You are of your father the devil, and your will is to do your father's desires"* (John 8:44). It is served as a god. Some "walk as enemies of the cross of Christ … their god is their belly" (Philippians 3:18–19). The same Greek word is "appetites" where Paul writes of those who "do not serve our Lord Christ, but their own appetites" (Romans 16:18). I read the belly as the appetite, set in the place of God and served. I read these as one act seen from different sides: the want leads, and the one who wants follows.
  - note: in part: served as a god
- **C-329** telling added · 10.7 *Planning* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: **A purpose held.** Some plans are aimed at one's own life. *"You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress"* (Psalm 17:3). The psalmist has set a course for his own speech ahead of time, and he states it under God's testing. He goes on: *"My steps have held fast to your paths"* (17:5). - Barnabas, at Antioch, *"exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose"* (Acts 11:23). The verse says what moved him: he *"saw the grace of God"* and *"was glad"*. - Paul lists his *"aim in life"* among what Timothy had followed, beside *"my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness"* (2 Timothy 3:10). - David prays that God will keep what the people have set: *"keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you"* (1 Chronicles 29:18). He asks God to hold the purpose in place. - Paul uses a purpose word for where the mind is set: *"to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace"* (Romans 8:6). *"For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"* (8:7). Chapter 7 gives the flesh. - The verb of the same word names a mind set downward: *"their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things"* (Philippians 3:19). The next verse turns it: *"But our citizenship is in heaven"* (3:20). And the call uses the same verb: *"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth"* (Colossians 3:2). - *"You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you"* (Isaiah 26:3).
  - note: in part: minds set on earthly things
- **C-330** telling added · 10.10 *Pride over another* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: Another's pride can also be wept over. "But if you will not listen, my soul will weep in secret for your pride" (Jeremiah 13:17). Paul writes of many "of whom I have often told you and now tell you even with tears, walk as enemies of the cross of Christ" (Philippians 3:18), who "glory in their shame" (3:19). He tells it with tears, and he still tells it: "keep your eyes on those who walk according to the example you have in us" (3:17).
  - note: in full

## 2026-10-19 — 10.13: 2Ki 3:18 citation written in full (#2170)

**Strand:** open threads on completed clusters (#2160), OT-07.3 (M02)

**Method:** Update 157 left one unresolved reference (#2170): in 10.13 How it is spoken of, '(3:18)' followed a 2 Chronicles reference and was read as 2Ch 3:18. The citation is 2 Kings 3:18; written in full in 10.13 v14. No other text changed.

**Refs:** escalation 2160, escalation 2170

**Quote check:** 0 parts, 0 failures. no quote changed

- **C-293** telling changed · 10.13 *How it is spoken of* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: The verses describe God's anger in pictures, and they keep the pictures. - **Fire, smoke and breath:** "By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed" (Job 4:9). "Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture?" (Psalm 74:1). - **A poured liquid:** "he has poured out his fury like fire" (Lamentations 2:4). - **A cup.** "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it" (Jeremiah 25:15). It is drunk to the dregs and then taken away: "Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering … and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors" (Isaiah 51:22–23). A man's wrath is also poured as a drink: "Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink—you pour out your wrath and make them drunk" (Habakkuk 2:15), and "The cup in the Lord's right hand will come around to you" (2:16). - **A storm:** "Behold, the storm of the Lord! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked" (Jeremiah 23:19). - **Weight:** "Your wrath lies heavy upon me" (Psalm 88:7). - **In the New Testament,** it is revealed (Romans 1:18), stored up (Romans 2:5), it remains (John 3:36), and it is finished (Revelation 15:1). - **Once, with no bearer named.** At the siege, when the king of Moab "saw that the battle was going against him", he "took his oldest son who was to reign in his place and offered him for a burnt offering on the wall. And there came great wrath against Israel. And they withdrew from him and returned to their own land" (2 Kings 3:26–27). Elsewhere the same words, wrath coming upon a people, follow a breach, and once the wrath is then named "the wrath of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 32:25–26). Here no breach is named, and Elisha had said, "He will also give the Moabites into your hand" (3:18). I read the verse as leaving open whose wrath it was. The king gave up his own heir at the point of defeat, and the campaign ended short of the word.
  - passage after: The verses describe God's anger in pictures, and they keep the pictures. - **Fire, smoke and breath:** "By the breath of God they perish, and by the blast of his anger they are consumed" (Job 4:9). "Why does your anger smoke against the sheep of your pasture?" (Psalm 74:1). - **A poured liquid:** "he has poured out his fury like fire" (Lamentations 2:4). - **A cup.** "Take from my hand this cup of the wine of wrath, and make all the nations to whom I send you drink it" (Jeremiah 25:15). It is drunk to the dregs and then taken away: "Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of staggering … and I will put it into the hand of your tormentors" (Isaiah 51:22–23). A man's wrath is also poured as a drink: "Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink—you pour out your wrath and make them drunk" (Habakkuk 2:15), and "The cup in the Lord's right hand will come around to you" (2:16). - **A storm:** "Behold, the storm of the Lord! Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked" (Jeremiah 23:19). - **Weight:** "Your wrath lies heavy upon me" (Psalm 88:7). - **In the New Testament,** it is revealed (Romans 1:18), stored up (Romans 2:5), it remains (John 3:36), and it is finished (Revelation 15:1). - **Once, with no bearer named.** At the siege, when the king of Moab "saw that the battle was going against him", he "took his oldest son who was to reign in his place and offered him for a burnt offering on the wall. And there came great wrath against Israel. And they withdrew from him and returned to their own land" (2 Kings 3:26–27). Elsewhere the same words, wrath coming upon a people, follow a breach, and once the wrath is then named "the wrath of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 32:25–26). Here no breach is named, and Elisha had said, "He will also give the Moabites into your hand" (2 Kings 3:18). I read the verse as leaving open whose wrath it was. The king gave up his own heir at the point of defeat, and the campaign ended short of the word.

- **C-258** telling changed · 10.13 *Other parties* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: Each party that comes into anger's verses does so in its own way. - **The Spirit of God** comes with anger. "And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled" (1 Samuel 11:6). The Spirit rushed upon Samson, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men; after it, "In hot anger he went back to his father's house" (Judges 14:19). Ezekiel, lifted by the Spirit, went "in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the Lord being strong upon me" (Ezekiel 3:14). The anger list in Ephesians is set beside the Spirit grieved (Ephesians 4:30–31). - **The prophet is filled with God's wrath:** "Therefore I am full of the wrath of the Lord; I am weary of holding it in" (Jeremiah 6:11). "I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation" (Jeremiah 15:17). - **Angels.** The angel of the Lord stood in Balaam's way, seen by the donkey and not by the man: "God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the Lord took his stand in the way as his adversary" (Numbers 22:22). Balaam's own anger fell on the donkey (22:27). God "let loose on them his burning anger … a company of destroying angels" (Psalm 78:49). An angel asked how long: "O Lord of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem … against which you have been angry these seventy years?", and "the Lord answered gracious and comforting words" (Zechariah 1:12–13). - **The devil:** "Woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!" (Revelation 12:12). - **The master in Jesus' parables,** a figure standing for God. "In anger his master delivered him to the jailers" (Matthew 18:34), after "should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" (18:33). The applied lesson places the requirement in the hearer's heart: "So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart" (18:35). In another parable the anger turns into a wider invitation. Those invited "all alike began to make excuses": a field to see, oxen to examine, a wife just married (Luke 14:18–20). "So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, 'Go out quickly … and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame'" (14:21). The anger has its ground in the refusals, and its end is stated: "none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet" (14:24). - **Onlookers:** "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls … lest the Lord see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him" (Proverbs 24:17–18). - **The physical world** bears it. "My anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground" (Jeremiah 7:20). "The foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked, because he was angry" (Psalm 18:7). - **Enemies' anger,** as the one attacked bears it: "then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us" (Psalm 124:3). Answered by God's hand: "you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me" (Psalm 138:7). And by "do not fear": "Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin" (Isaiah 7:4). "By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king" (Hebrews 11:27). - **A ruler's anger,** as those beneath it bear it: "A king's wrath is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it" (Proverbs 16:14). "The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life" (20:2). The next verse says what to do instead: "It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling" (20:3). - **Those who pursue another.** Job's friends say, "How we will pursue him!" and "The root of the matter is found in him" (Job 19:28). He answers them: "be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment" (19:29). He says it straight after "I know that my Redeemer lives" (19:25). I read the one accused as turning the fear of wrath back on those who pursue him, from the confidence he has just spoken. - **The nations.** In worship the elders say, "The nations raged, but your wrath came" (Revelation 11:18). Two angers stand in one sentence, and the second answers the first. The same verse names the reward of "those who fear your name, both small and great" (10.12; 13.1).

- **C-290** telling added · 10.13 *What it rises at* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: Human anger in the verses is often set off by something perceived. Sometimes the verse names hearing or seeing; sometimes the setting gives the cause. - **A report:** Potiphar's anger rose on his wife's words (Genesis 39:19). It was not tested, and it was false. - **A sight:** "when Haman saw Mordecai in the king's gate, that he neither rose nor trembled before him, he was filled with wrath" (Esther 5:9). - **A demand, an expectation or a slight.** Rachel demanded children, and "Jacob's anger was kindled against Rachel, and he said, 'Am I in the place of God?'" (Genesis 30:2). Naaman: "Behold, I thought that he would surely come out to me" (2 Kings 5:11). Queen Vashti refused to come, and the king's "anger burned within him" (Esther 1:12). - **A rival's honour:** the women sang of David's ten thousands, and "Saul was very angry" (1 Samuel 18:8). The elder brother heard the music for his returned brother, "was angry and refused to go in" (Luke 15:28). - **A wrong done to another.** Jacob's sons were indignant "because he had done an outrageous thing in Israel" (Genesis 34:7). David burned at the rich man in Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12:5). Nehemiah: "I was very angry when I heard their outcry" (Nehemiah 5:6). Paul's "spirit was provoked within him as he saw that the city was full of idols" (Acts 17:16). - **Good done,** where it breaks a rule: the ruler of the synagogue was "indignant because Jesus had healed on the Sabbath" (Luke 13:14). - **A word that exposes.** At Nazareth, "When they heard these things, all in the synagogue were filled with wrath" (Luke 4:28). At Stephen's speech, "they cried out with a loud voice and stopped their ears and rushed together at him" (Acts 7:57). - **Being outwitted through someone close.** Samson's riddle was got out of him through his wife's tears (Judges 14:15–17; 10.10). When the men of the city answered it, he said, "If you had not plowed with my heifer, you would not have found out my riddle" (14:18). The Spirit rushed upon him for the striking at Ashkelon, and then, "In hot anger he went back to his father's house" (14:19). "And Samson's wife was given to his companion, who had been his best man" (14:20). - **Something within.** "What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?" (James 4:1).
  - note: in part: Being outwitted through someone close

- **C-291** telling added · 10.13 *Anger in the body* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: Anger shows, and the verses see it in the teeth. - "The wicked man sees it and is angry; he gnashes his teeth and melts away" (Psalm 112:10). - "The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him" (Psalm 37:12). - At Stephen's speech, "they were enraged, and they ground their teeth at him" (Acts 7:54). (Lamentations 2:16). It is how the anger looks to the one under it (*Living under God's anger*, below).
  - note: in part: the teeth

Wrath has gone forth, a whirling tempest; it will burst upon the head of the wicked" (Jeremiah 23:19). - **Weight:** "Your wrath lies heavy upon me" (Psalm 88:7). - **In the New Testament,** it is revealed (Romans 1:18), stored up (Romans 2:5), it remains (John 3:36), and it is finished (Revelation 15:1). - **Once, with no bearer named.** At the siege, when the king of Moab "saw that the battle was going against him", he "took his oldest son who was to reign in his place and offered him for a burnt offering on the wall. And there came great wrath against Israel. And they withdrew from him and returned to their own land" (2 Kings 3:26–27). Elsewhere the same words, wrath coming upon a people, follow a breach, and once the wrath is then named "the wrath of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 32:25–26). Here no breach is named, and Elisha had said, "He will also give the Moabites into your hand" (3:18). I read the verse as leaving open whose wrath it was. The king gave up his own heir at the point of defeat, and the campaign ended short of the word.
  - note: in part: Once, with no bearer named

The verses say what it led to. - "The fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth" (Genesis 9:2). - "a terror from God fell upon the cities that were around them, so that they did not pursue the sons of Jacob" (Genesis 35:5). - "Put them in fear, O Lord! Let the nations know that they are but men!" (Psalm 9:20). - "that their hearts may melt, and many stumble. At all their gates I have given the glittering sword" (Ezekiel 21:15). The melting heart is what the sword is given for (*Fear in the body*, above).
  - note: in part: Ezekiel 21:15

  - passage after: Fear can be passed on as pressure. At Samson's wedding the guests threatened his wife: "Entice your husband to tell us what the riddle is, lest we burn you and your father's house with fire" (Judges 14:15). She pressed him with tears and with a charge against his love: "You only hate me; you do not love me" (14:16). "She wept before him the seven days that their feast lasted, and on the seventh day he told her, because she pressed him hard" (14:17). I read the fear laid on her as becoming the weeping she laid on him. His anger at the end is in 10.13.

  - passage before: —
  - passage after: Jesus speaks of what the shut-out feel. "In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God but you yourselves cast out" (Luke 13:28). The saying comes seven times (Matthew 8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30; Luke 13:28). In Luke the weeping and gnashing come at a sight: others inside, oneself outside. I read the gnashing as standing with the weeping. The verses do not say whether it is anguish or rage (10.13, *Anger in the body*).

- **C-282** telling added · 10.12 *Fear in the body* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: Fear is not only felt. It is seen, and the verses see it first in the hands. - **The hands fall when the report comes.** The people's hands fall helpless at the report (Jeremiah 6:24, above). The same is said of an enemy king: "The king of Babylon heard the report of them, and his hands fell helpless; anguish seized him, pain as of a woman in labor" (Jeremiah 50:43). - **The hands go with the heart.** "Therefore all hands will be feeble, and every human heart will melt. They will be dismayed: pangs and agony will seize them; they will be in anguish like a woman in labor. They will look aghast at one another; their faces will be aflame" (Isaiah 13:7–8). Ezekiel names the inner and the outer in one breath: "Every heart will melt, and all hands will be feeble; every spirit will faint, and all knees will be weak as water" (Ezekiel 21:7). "All hands are feeble, and all knees turn to water" (7:17). - **The body takes up the posture of labour.** "Why then do I see every man with his hands on his stomach like a woman in labor? Why has every face turned pale?" (Jeremiah 30:6). - **Fear is aimed at the hands.** Nehemiah's enemies "all wanted to frighten us, thinking, 'Their hands will drop from the work, and it will not be done.' But now, O God, strengthen my hands" (Nehemiah 6:9). God speaks to the same place: "Fear not, O Zion; let not your hands grow weak" (Zephaniah 3:16). - **And the answer is given to the hands.** "Strengthen the weak hands, and make firm the feeble knees" (Isaiah 35:3). "Therefore lift your drooping hands and strengthen your weak knees" (Hebrews 12:12). Eliphaz says to Job, "you have instructed many, and you have strengthened the weak hands" (Job 4:3).

  - passage before: —
  - passage after: The Hebrew verb behind much of this anguish is *ḥûl*, "to twist, writhe". It is the writhing of a woman in labour, and the heart's anguish: "My heart is in anguish within me" (Psalm 55:4). In Lamentations it is said of hands. The ESV reads, "For the chastisement of the daughter of my people has been greater than the punishment of Sodom, which was overthrown in a moment, and no hands were wrung for her" (Lamentations 4:6). The English chooses the first. Either way the writhing of hands is the body's anguish, and the root carries it; "wrung" is the translator's word for it. Chapter 11 sets out the root's other faces.

- **C-288** telling added · 02 *Life weighed* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: A death can be weighed against a death. In the siege of Jerusalem, "Happier were the victims of the sword than the victims of hunger, who wasted away, pierced by lack of the fruits of the field" (Lamentations 4:9). The verse before says what the wasting was: "their skin has shriveled on their bones; it has become as dry as wood" (4:8). The same lament sets Zion's long punishment above Sodom's, "which was overthrown in a moment" (4:6). The quick death is called the happier one. The lingering is what makes it worse.

- **C-289** telling added · 10.10 *Friends, company and care* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: Thirst can be left unmet by those who should meet it. In the siege, *"Even jackals offer the breast; they nurse their young; but the daughter of my people has become cruel … The tongue of the nursing infant sticks to the roof of its mouth for thirst; the children beg for food, but no one gives to them"* (Lamentations 4:3–4). The animals are set above the people. The same lament goes further: "The hands of compassionate women have boiled their own children; they became their food during the destruction of the daughter of my people" (Lamentations 4:10). The women are called compassionate, and the verse names when it happened: "during the destruction". I read the siege as what turned the hands of compassion. The verse does not explain it, and I do not try to. And the worker thirsts among what he makes for another: *"they tread the winepresses, but suffer thirst … yet God charges no one with wrong"* (Job 24:11–12; 10.9).

The body's raising is still to come. But Paul also speaks of believers as raised already: they were "raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God" (Colossians 2:12), and God "raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places" (Ephesians 2:6). He draws from it at once where the mind is to be: "If then you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth" (Colossians 3:1–2). He prays that they may know "the immeasurable greatness of his power toward us who believe", the power "that he worked in Christ when he raised him from the dead" (Ephesians 1:19–20). Peter says the same of new birth. God "has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead" (1 Peter 1:3), "not of perishable seed but of imperishable" (1:23), "so that your faith and hope are in God" (1:21). Chapter 14 follows that.

- **C-272** telling added · 02 *Sown and raised* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: The word for "natural" is *psychikos* ("natural, of the soul"), from *psychē* ("soul"). Said of the body, it carries no blame: "it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual" (1 Corinthians 15:46). Said of a person, the same word does carry blame: "The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God" (1 Corinthians 2:14). James uses it of a wisdom that "is earthly, unspiritual, demonic" (James 3:15), and Jude of "worldly people, devoid of the Spirit" (Jude 19). Paul does not say what a spiritual body is made of, and I do not try to.
  - note: in full
- **C-273** telling added · 02 *Christ first* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: The Gospels show his risen body. They do not define it. - **He could be touched, and he ate.** When the disciples "thought they saw a spirit", he said, "See my hands and my feet, that it is I myself. Touch me, and see. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have" (Luke 24:37, 39). They gave him broiled fish, "and he took it and ate before them" (24:42–43). The apostles "ate and drank with him after he rose from the dead" (Acts 10:41). To Thomas he said, "put out your hand, and place it in my side" (John 20:27). - **He came and went.** With "the doors being locked … Jesus came and stood among them" (John 20:19). At Emmaus "their eyes were opened, and they recognized him. And he vanished from their sight" (Luke 24:31). - **He was not known at once.** On the road, "their eyes were kept from recognizing him" (Luke 24:16). Mary "saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus" (John 20:14). At the lake, "the disciples did not know that it was Jesus" (21:4).
  - note: in full
- **C-274** telling added · 02 *Believed, questioned, denied* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: The raising of the dead is not only told. It is met, and the verses show how people met it. - **Denied.** Luke notes that "the Sadducees say that there is no resurrection, nor angel, nor spirit" (Acts 23:8). They brought Jesus a woman who had been married to seven brothers: "In the resurrection, therefore, of the seven, whose wife will she be?" (Matthew 22:28). He named the cause of their error: "You are wrong, because you know neither the Scriptures nor the power of God" (22:29). He answered from God's own words to Moses, "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob" (Mark 12:26), and Luke adds, "Now he is not God of the dead, but of the living, for all live to him" (Luke 20:38). - **Questioned, and understood later.** Coming down the mountain, the disciples "kept the matter to themselves, questioning what this rising from the dead might mean" (Mark 9:10). At the empty tomb, "as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead" (John 20:9). The understanding came afterwards. "When therefore he was raised from the dead, his disciples remembered that he had said this, and they believed the Scripture and the word that Jesus had spoken" (John 2:22). "Then he opened their minds to understand the Scriptures" (Luke 24:45). Paul still writes, "Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead" (2 Timothy 2:8). - **Known, and believed.** Martha knew the teaching: "I know that he will rise again in the resurrection on the last day" (John 11:24). Jesus turned it to himself, "I am the resurrection and the life", and asked her, "Do you believe this?" She answered, "Yes, Lord; I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world" (11:25–27). - **Mocked, put off, thought incredible.** At Athens, "when they heard of the resurrection of the dead, some mocked. But others said, 'We will hear you again about this'" (Acts 17:32). Paul asks, "Why is it thought incredible by any of you that God raises the dead?" (Acts 26:8). He says he is on trial "with respect to the hope and the resurrection of the dead" (23:6). - **Faith resting on it.** Paul puts the question to believers: "how can some of you say that there is no resurrection of the dead?" (1 Corinthians 15:12). He lets everything rest on it: "if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile and you are still in your sins" (15:17); "If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied" (15:19). Teaching that "the resurrection has already happened" is "upsetting the faith of some" (2 Timothy 2:18). - **Feared.** The chief priests had the tomb sealed, "lest his disciples go and steal him away and tell the people, 'He has risen from the dead'" (Matthew 27:64). When Herod heard of Jesus he said, "John, whom I beheaded, has been raised" (Mark 6:16), and "he was perplexed" (Luke 9:7). I read Herod's word as his conscience speaking, because it names the beheading. - **A sign that moves people.** When John asked from prison, "Are you the one who is to come, or shall we look for another?", part of the answer was that "the dead are raised up" (Matthew 11:3, 5). After Lazarus was raised, "the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus" (John 12:10–11).
  - note: in part: Denied

- **C-278** telling added · 02 *Waited for* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: The hope is given as a reason for how a person lives now. Jesus tells a host to invite those who cannot repay: "and you will be blessed, because they cannot repay you. For you will be repaid at the resurrection of the just" (Luke 14:14). Some who were tortured refused release, "so that they might rise again to a better life" (Hebrews 11:35). Athletes exercise self-control "to receive a perishable wreath, but we an imperishable" (1 Corinthians 9:25). God gives eternal life "to those who by patience in well-doing seek for glory and honor and immortality" (Romans 2:7). Paul ends his chapter on the resurrection with the present: "Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labor is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58).
  - note: in full
- **C-279** telling added · 02 *Changed* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: The word for the imperishable is not kept for the body. Paul blesses "all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible" (Ephesians 6:24). Peter speaks of new birth "not of perishable seed but of imperishable" (1 Peter 1:23), of "an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading" (1:4), and of "the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (3:4). Chapter 11 sets the word beside its other uses. The immortality that "this mortal body must put on" (1 Corinthians 15:53) is said of God as his own: he "alone has immortality" (1 Timothy 6:16; 13.1).
  - note: in full
- **C-279** telling added · 11 *4. One word, opposite values* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: - **Imperishable.** The Greek *aphthartos* and its noun name what the dead are raised: "the dead will be raised imperishable" (1 Corinthians 15:52). The same words name love, "love incorruptible" (Ephesians 6:24), the seed of new birth (1 Peter 1:23), an inheritance (1:4), "the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit" (3:4), the wreath that self-control runs for (1 Corinthians 9:25), and God himself, "immortal, invisible" (1 Timothy 1:17). (Chapter 2, *Changed*; 13.1, *Immortal*.)
  - note: in full
- **C-280** telling added · 02 *Waited for* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: The raised body is waited for, and the waiting is felt within. Paul sets the creation's waiting first. "For the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God", because "the creation itself will be set free from its bondage to corruption", and "the whole creation has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until now" (Romans 8:19, 21–22). Then: "we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies" (8:23). Paul calls the present body a tent: "if the tent that is our earthly home is destroyed, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens. For in this tent we groan, longing to put on our heavenly dwelling" (2 Corinthians 5:1–2). He does not long to be without a body: "not that we would be unclothed, but that we would be further clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life" (5:4). Sections 10.1 and 10.6 follow the groaning and the longing.
  - note: in part: Rom 8:19-23
- **C-281** telling added · 13.1 *Immortal* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: Paul's praise names God as the one whose life has no end: "To the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen" (1 Timothy 1:17). He is the one "who alone has immortality, who dwells in unapproachable light, whom no one has ever seen or can see" (6:16). The same word is what "this mortal body must put on" (1 Corinthians 15:53; Chapter 2, *Changed*). - **He raises the dead.** Paul learned to rely "not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). - **By his Spirit.** "If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you" (Romans 8:11). - **In the Son.** "I am the resurrection and the life" (John 11:25). "I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades" (Revelation 1:18). - **It is his pledge of judgment.** "He has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness by a man whom he has appointed; and of this he has given assurance to all by raising him from the dead" (Acts 17:31).
  - note: in full

Chapter 11 sets the word beside its other uses. The immortality that "this mortal body must put on" (1 Corinthians 15:53) is said of God as his own: he "alone has immortality" (1 Timothy 6:16; 13.1).

- **C-92** telling added · 02 *Life, and judgment* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: The rising is not to life for all. "An hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out, those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment" (John 5:28–29). Daniel had been told it: "many of those who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt" (Daniel 12:2). Paul states his hope "that there will be a resurrection of both the just and the unjust" (Acts 24:15).
  - note: in full
- **C-139** telling added · 02 *Life, and judgment* (recorded, 2026-10-19)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: Revelation names a second death beyond the first. "The one who conquers will not be hurt by the second death" (Revelation 2:11). "Blessed and holy is the one who shares in the first resurrection! Over such the second death has no power" (20:6). Its list opens with the cowardly and the faithless: "But as for the cowardly, the faithless, the detestable, as for murderers, the sexually immoral, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake that burns with fire and sulfur, which is the second death" (Revelation 21:8). Death itself goes there: "Then Death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire. This is the second death, the lake of fire" (Revelation 20:14). Chapter 13 follows God's anger.
  - note: in part: a death beyond death

## 2026-10-18 — OT-106.3: the poor person's own side, woven (#2160)

**Strand:** open threads on completed clusters (#2160), OT-106.3 (M47)

**Researcher:** "Weave all five OT-106.3 placements as proposed with their claims, close OT-106.3, commit and push, then read OT-05.11 (M47)." (2026-10-18)

**Method:** OT-106.3 (poverty joined to the spirit or heart: Mat 5:3, Pro 16:19, Psa 109:22, with the five other S-coded M09 verses that carry an M47 word) read in their passages for OT-106's question (the researcher's three dimensions of poor/needy, #2148). Woven: Pro 13:7-8 and 2Sa 12:3-4 (10.6 Possessions), Mat 5:3-4 (Ch 6), Psa 109:22-26 (Ch 4), Psa 34:4-6 and 69:29, 33 (10.9 Waiting, and pleading). Pro 13:7: both verbs are the reflexive (hithpael) stem of 'be rich' (H6238) and 'be poor' (H7326), checked in iba.db span. Rule 77: 2-2 (Ch 6) and C-189 (Ch 4) told in touched passages; both stand; C-189 gains Psa 109:23-26 as sources.

**Sources:** _analytics/Clusters/M47 - inner-seat/ot-106-3-m47-poor-own-side-reading-v1-20261018.md

**Original claims changed:** Six new claims; C-189 gains sources Psa 109:23-26.

**Refs:** escalation 2160, thread OT-106, thread item OT-106.3, escalation 2148

**Quote check:** 14 parts, 0 failures. checked against iba.db verse (ESV)

- **2-2** telling changed · 06 *The human spirit* (recorded, 2026-10-18)
  - passage before: **It is lowly or proud, and it is judged.** "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (Proverbs 16:18). The next verse chooses the company: "It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud" (16:19). "One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor" (Proverbs 29:23). "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Matthew 5:3). God dwells "with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (Isaiah 57:15). God looks to "he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word" (Isaiah 66:2). Israel was "a generation whose heart was not steadfast, whose spirit was not faithful to God" (Psalm 78:8). The psalm's blessed man is "the one whose transgression is forgiven" (Psalm 32:1), the man "against whom the Lord counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit" (32:2). The no-deceit stands beside his confession: "I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity" (32:5). David prays for "a right spirit" (Psalm 51:10). Paul calls for cleansing "from every defilement of body and spirit" (2 Corinthians 7:1). And "the Lord weighs the spirit" (Proverbs 16:2).
  - passage after: **It is lowly or proud, and it is judged.** "Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall" (Proverbs 16:18). The next verse chooses the company: "It is better to be of a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud" (16:19). "One's pride will bring him low, but he who is lowly in spirit will obtain honor" (Proverbs 29:23). "Blessed are the poor in spirit" (Matthew 5:3). The verse places the poverty in the spirit, not in what a person has, and the next blessing is on "those who mourn, for they shall be comforted" (5:4). God dwells "with him who is of a contrite and lowly spirit" (Isaiah 57:15). God looks to "he who is humble and contrite in spirit and trembles at my word" (Isaiah 66:2). Israel was "a generation whose heart was not steadfast, whose spirit was not faithful to God" (Psalm 78:8). The psalm's blessed man is "the one whose transgression is forgiven" (Psalm 32:1), the man "against whom the Lord counts no iniquity, and in whose spirit there is no deceit" (32:2). The no-deceit stands beside his confession: "I acknowledged my sin to you, and I did not cover my iniquity" (32:5). David prays for "a right spirit" (Psalm 51:10). Paul calls for cleansing "from every defilement of body and spirit" (2 Corinthians 7:1). And "the Lord weighs the spirit" (Proverbs 16:2).
- **C-189** telling changed · 04 *The heart humbled* (recorded, 2026-10-18)
  - passage before: The heart can be broken. "Reproaches have broken my heart, so that I am in despair" (Psalm 69:20). "I am poor and needy, and my heart is stricken within me" (Psalm 109:22). - **C-258** claim created (recorded, 2026-10-18)
  - claim before: —
  - claim after: In the parable of the banquet the master's anger rests on the invited guests' refusals, turns into a wider invitation to the poor, and ends with the refusers shut out
  - verdict before: —
  - verdict after: New
- **C-258** telling added · 10.13 *Other parties* (recorded, 2026-10-18)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: Each party that comes into anger's verses does so in its own way. - **The Spirit of God** comes with anger. "And the Spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger was greatly kindled" (1 Samuel 11:6). The Spirit rushed upon Samson, and he went down to Ashkelon and struck down thirty men; after it, "In hot anger he went back to his father's house" (Judges 14:19). Ezekiel, lifted by the Spirit, went "in the heat of my spirit, the hand of the Lord being strong upon me" (Ezekiel 3:14). The anger list in Ephesians is set beside the Spirit grieved (Ephesians 4:30–31). - **The prophet is filled with God's wrath:** "Therefore I am full of the wrath of the Lord; I am weary of holding it in" (Jeremiah 6:11). "I sat alone, because your hand was upon me, for you had filled me with indignation" (Jeremiah 15:17). - **Angels.** The angel of the Lord stood in Balaam's way, seen by the donkey and not by the man: "God's anger was kindled because he went, and the angel of the Lord took his stand in the way as his adversary" (Numbers 22:22). Balaam's own anger fell on the donkey (22:27). God "let loose on them his burning anger … a company of destroying angels" (Psalm 78:49). An angel asked how long: "O Lord of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem … against which you have been angry these seventy years?", and "the Lord answered gracious and comforting words" (Zechariah 1:12–13). - **The devil:** "Woe to you, O earth and sea, for the devil has come down to you in great wrath, because he knows that his time is short!" (Revelation 12:12). - **The master in Jesus' parables,** a figure standing for God. "In anger his master delivered him to the jailers" (Matthew 18:34), after "should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" (18:33). The applied lesson places the requirement in the hearer's heart: "So also my heavenly Father will do to every one of you, if you do not forgive your brother from your heart" (18:35). In another parable the anger turns into a wider invitation. Those invited "all alike began to make excuses": a field to see, oxen to examine, a wife just married (Luke 14:18–20). "So the servant came and reported these things to his master. Then the master of the house became angry and said to his servant, 'Go out quickly … and bring in the poor and crippled and blind and lame'" (14:21). The anger has its ground in the refusals, and its end is stated: "none of those men who were invited shall taste my banquet" (14:24). - **Onlookers:** "Do not rejoice when your enemy falls … lest the Lord see it and be displeased, and turn away his anger from him" (Proverbs 24:17–18). - **The physical world** bears it. "My anger and my wrath will be poured out on this place, upon man and beast, upon the trees of the field and the fruit of the ground" (Jeremiah 7:20). "The foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked, because he was angry" (Psalm 18:7). - **Enemies' anger,** as the one attacked bears it: "then they would have swallowed us up alive, when their anger was kindled against us" (Psalm 124:3). Answered by God's hand: "you stretch out your hand against the wrath of my enemies, and your right hand delivers me" (Psalm 138:7). And by "do not fear": "Be careful, be quiet, do not fear, and do not let your heart be faint because of these two smoldering stumps of firebrands, at the fierce anger of Rezin" (Isaiah 7:4). "By faith he left Egypt, not being afraid of the anger of the king" (Hebrews 11:27). - **A ruler's anger,** as those beneath it bear it: "A king's wrath is a messenger of death, and a wise man will appease it" (Proverbs 16:14). "The terror of a king is like the growling of a lion; whoever provokes him to anger forfeits his life" (20:2). The next verse says what to do instead: "It is an honor for a man to keep aloof from strife, but every fool will be quarreling" (20:3). - **Those who pursue another.** Job's friends say, "How we will pursue him!" and "The root of the matter is found in him" (Job 19:28). He answers them: "be afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword, that you may know there is a judgment" (19:29). He says it straight after "I know that my Redeemer lives" (19:25). I read the one accused as turning the fear of wrath back on those who pursue him, from the confidence he has just spoken. - **The nations.** In worship the elders say, "The nations raged, but your wrath came" (Revelation 11:18). Two angers stand in one sentence, and the second answers the first. The same verse names the reward of "those who fear your name, both small and great" (10.12; 13.1).
  - note: in part: The master in Jesus' parables (Luke 14:18-24)

He cannot. "Not from the east or from the west … comes lifting up, but it is God who executes judgment, putting down one and lifting up another" (Psalm 75:6–7). Ezekiel gives it in a figure, with what it is for: "And all the trees of the field shall know that I am the Lord; I bring low the high tree, and make high the low tree, dry up the green tree, and make the dry tree flourish. I am the Lord; I have spoken, and I will do it" (Ezekiel 17:24). The reversal is done so that he is known, and it is as sure as his word.

Hide not your face from me" (Psalm 27:8–9). The plea comes from a heart that is already turned toward his face. - **A penitent heart.** David asks God to hide his face from the sin, and in the next breath not to send him away: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me. Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me" (Psalm 51:10–11). - **A heart that takes it as permission.** The wicked "says in his heart, 'God has forgotten, he has hidden his face, he will never see it'" (Psalm 10:11; Chapter 12). - **A heart that does not notice.** "I hid my face and was angry, but he went on backsliding in the way of his own heart" (Isaiah 57:17). Here the hidden face is not felt at all. Peace, peace, to the far and to the near," says the Lord, "and I will heal him" (57:18–19). The heart's own way is seen, and healing is promised anyway. - **A heart that waits.** "I will wait for the Lord, who is hiding his face from the house of Jacob, and I will hope in him" (Isaiah 8:17). "Truly, you are a God who hides himself, O God of Israel, the Savior" (Isaiah 45:15). Isaiah calls the God who hides himself the Savior in the same breath.

The false prophets say it to a whole people: "It shall be well with you" (Jeremiah 23:17). The guilty say it of God: "surely his anger has turned from me" (Jeremiah 2:35). God's word is the opposite: "But the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt. There is no peace," says my God, "for the wicked" (Isaiah 57:20–21). I read the sea as the picture of the inner state: it cannot be still, and what it throws up is mire. The same oracle gives peace "to the far and to the near" whom God heals (57:19; 10.9). The arrogant man is likewise "never at rest" (Habakkuk 2:5; 10.15). Chapter 13 follows how the human heart meets God's anger: provoking it, bearing it, and turning under it.
  - note: in part: the tossing sea (Isaiah 57:20-21)
- **C-256** telling added · 04 *The heart is hidden, and God sees it* (recorded, 2026-10-18)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9). "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy" (Proverbs 14:10). Other people cannot fully see into it, and often its owner cannot either. But "man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). The word corrects a prophet. Samuel had looked on Eliab and "thought, 'Surely the Lord's anointed is before him'" (16:6). The one sent to choose formed his thought from what he saw. God is the one who "knows the secrets of the heart" (Psalm 44:21). "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2). He knows the heart's leaning before it acts: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). He tests it and weighs it: "the Lord weighs the heart" (Proverbs 21:2). People try to hide what the heart holds, and Isaiah answers them: "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?' You turn things upside down!" (Isaiah 29:15–16). Section 10.11 follows hiding and disclosing.
  - note: in part: Samuel's thought (1 Samuel 16:6-7)

  - passage after: The verses also give greed's reasons and its roots. A root: *"For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils. It is through this craving that some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many pangs"* (1 Timothy 6:10). Refuge in the wrong place: *"See the man who would not make God his refuge, but trusted in the abundance of his riches and sought refuge in his own destruction!"* (Psalm 52:7). The picture is a bird nesting out of reach. The same taunt says what that safety comes to. Of the one "who heaps up what is not his own" it asks, "Will not your debtors suddenly arise, and those awake who will make you tremble? Then you will be spoil for them" (2:6–7). I read the two woes together: the safety gathered by taking from others is answered by fear of those it took from. Forgetting God: *"you … make gain of your neighbors by extortion; but me you have forgotten"* (Ezekiel 22:12). No contentment: *"Because he knew no contentment in his belly, he will not let anything in which he delights escape him"* (Job 20:20). And it can sit in the leaders, with a false peace: *"everyone is greedy for unjust gain; and from prophet to priest, everyone deals falsely. They have healed the wound of my people lightly, saying, 'Peace, peace,' when there is no peace"* (Jeremiah 6:13–14).

- **C-247** telling added · 10.7 *Setting the heart* (recorded, 2026-10-18)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: Scripture speaks of the heart being set, inclined and directed, and of the state it is in: - **Inclined, and asked for.** *"Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to selfish gain!"* (Psalm 119:36). The one who prays this has just chosen (119:30), and asks God to do the inclining. - **Whole or divided.** *"unite my heart to fear your name"* (Psalm 86:11), against *"a double heart"* (Psalm 12:2). Solomon's *"heart was not wholly true to the Lord his God"* (1 Kings 11:4). - **Stubborn.** *"the stubbornness of their evil hearts"* runs through Jeremiah (Jeremiah 7:24). - **Moved from within.** *"everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him"* (Exodus 35:21) puts heart and spirit side by side in setting out to give. - **Set, beside a wrong love.** Jehoshaphat was told, *"Should you help the wicked and love those who hate the Lord? Because of this, wrath has gone out against you from the Lord. Nevertheless, some good is found in you, for you destroyed the Asheroth out of the land, and have set your heart to seek God"* (2 Chronicles 19:2–3). A love wrongly given and a heart set to seek God stand in one king, and the prophet's verdict holds both. - **Set to study, to do and to teach.** *"For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the Lord, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel"* (Ezra 7:10). The setting has three steps, and the doing stands between the study and the teaching. The verse before ends *"for the good hand of his God was on him"* (7:9), and this one opens with *"For"*. I read the second *"For"* as giving the good hand its ground in Ezra's heart. Its opposite is Rehoboam, who *"did evil, for he did not set his heart to seek the Lord"* (2 Chronicles 12:14; 10.14). - **Set as an aim.** The word for ambition is used three times by Paul, and its aims are not what ambition usually seeks: *"I make it my ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named"* (Romans 15:20); *"whether we are at home or away, we make it our aim to please him. For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ"* (2 Corinthians 5:9–10); *"aspire to live quietly, and to mind your own affairs, and to work with your hands"* (1 Thessalonians 4:11). Also: *"If anyone aspires to the office of overseer, he desires a noble task"* (1 Timothy 3:1). I read the aims as going where no one has gone, pleasing him wherever one is, and quietness.
  - note: in part: Set to study, to do and to teach (Ezra 7:10)
- **C-248** telling added · 10.12 *What changes it* (recorded, 2026-10-18)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: The verses show fear changing character, and they point to what changes it. - **What it is turned toward.** At the sea Israel "feared greatly" as Egypt marched, and after the crossing "the people feared the Lord, and they believed in the Lord" (Exodus 14:10, 31). In between, fear spoke as a preference: "it would have been better for us to serve the Egyptians than to die in the wilderness" (14:12; 10.6, *Shaped by fear*). In the boat, fear of the storm became fear of the one who stilled it (Mark 4:41). In these cases the change came after God acted. - **One fear set in place of another, by the same speaker.** "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you" (Exodus 20:20). "do not fear what they fear … Let him be your fear" (Isaiah 8:12–13). "Rather fear him who can destroy both soul and body in hell", and then, "Fear not, therefore; you are of more value than many sparrows" (Matthew 10:28, 31). - **Who speaks to it, and why.** God's "for I am with you" (Isaiah 41:10), and Jael's "do not be afraid" (Judges 4:18). - **Knowing whose hand is on one.** Ezra: "I took courage, for the hand of the Lord my God was on me, and I gathered leading men from Israel to go up with me" (Ezra 7:28). The verse names the ground of the courage, and the courage turns at once into a deed. Ezra then would not ask the king for soldiers, "since we had told the king, 'The hand of our God is for good on all who seek him'" (8:22; 10.14). What he told others did the same for them (Nehemiah 2:18; 10.10). - **Who meets it.** "When justice is done, it is a joy to the righteous but terror to evildoers" (Proverbs 21:15). One scroll was read aloud: the officials "turned one to another in fear", and "neither the king nor any of his servants who heard all these words was afraid" (Jeremiah 36:16, 24). At the signs of the end, "people fainting with fear", and to the disciples, "straighten up and raise your heads, because your redemption is drawing near" (Luke 21:26, 28). - **One's own conduct.** "rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to bad" (Romans 13:3). "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered" (Isaiah 66:4). The same passage opens with the one God looks to, who "trembles at my word" (66:2). I read the passage as setting that trembling beside "their fears". - **Pride.** "So do not become proud, but fear" (Romans 11:20). "The horror you inspire has deceived you, and the pride of your heart" (Jeremiah 49:16). - **Where the heart is.** Fear "taught by men" while "their hearts are far from me", against fear put "in their hearts" (Isaiah 29:13; Jeremiah 32:40). - **Faith, trust and love** (the section above). - **Joy or silence.** The women left the tomb "with fear and great joy, and ran to tell his disciples" (Matthew 28:8). In Mark's account "they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid" (Mark 16:8). The two accounts stand side by side. - **The same root, rendered as another movement.** *Rāgaz*, "to tremble", is also anger and grief (Psalm 4:4; 2 Samuel 18:33). *Paḥad*, "dread", is also "thrill" (Isaiah 60:5). *Phobos*, "fear", is also "respect" (Romans 13:7).
  - note: in part: Knowing whose hand is on one (Ezra 7:28)
- **C-249** telling added · 10.10 *Care, discouragement and hiding between people* (recorded, 2026-10-18)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: What one person carries inside can be for another, or done to another. - **Care for another is a good anxiety.** Paul's "daily pressure on me of my anxiety for all the churches" is to be weak with the weak (2 Corinthians 11:28–29). Members of one body are to "have the same care for one another" (1 Corinthians 12:25). Section 10.1 sets out the difference between this care and anxiety for oneself. - **Losing heart is done by another.** "Fathers, do not provoke your children, lest they become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). Every use of the words for losing heart has another party behind it (10.1). - **Resolve is given by another, too.** Nehemiah, at the ruined walls, said, "You see the trouble we are in" (Nehemiah 2:17). Then: "I told them of the hand of my God that had been upon me for good, and also of the words that the king had spoken to me. And they said, 'Let us rise up and build.' So they strengthened their hands for the good work" (2:18). What he told was what had been done for him; the resolve was theirs. I read the strengthened hands as resolve taken, the verse's own figure. Ezra took courage on the same ground (Ezra 7:28; 10.12). - **A whisperer separates friends.** "A whisperer separates close friends" (Proverbs 16:28), and "where there is no whisperer, quarreling ceases" (26:20) (10.5). - **People hide from people, and hide one another.** The weaker side hides: "When the wicked rise, people hide themselves" (Proverbs 28:28). Rahab and Obadiah hid others to keep them alive (Joshua 2:4; 1 Kings 18:4). And no one can hide from a friend who turns: "it is not an adversary who deals insolently with me — then I could hide from him. But it is you, a man, my equal" (Psalm 55:12–13). Section 10.11 follows all of this.
  - note: in part: Resolve is given by another, too (Nehemiah 2:18)

- **C-250** telling added · 13.1 *Ruling* (recorded, 2026-10-18)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: **He gives authority and takes it away.** "the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, and the might, and the glory" (Daniel 2:37). Of a steward removed: "will commit your authority to his hand. And he shall be a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem" (Isaiah 22:21). When Saul seized the skirt of Samuel's robe and it tore, the tear became the word: "The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you this day and has given it to a neighbor of yours, who is better than you" (15:27–28). The rejection answers a rejection, in the same word.

The watchmen "lift up their voice; together they sing for joy", "for the Lord has comforted his people" (52:8–9).
