## 2026-09-30 — Reset: what the latest findings add that the original never had (digest §4)

**Strand:** inner seat (M47)

**Sources:** _analytics/essay/spirit_soul_body/wa-essay-spirit-soul-body-digest-v1-20260930.md

**Notes:** ## 4. What the latest findings add that the original never had

These areas are absent from the original, or are listed there only as gaps. [Claude reading]

1. **Flesh as a full component** (original gap 1–2): kin, "all flesh", frailty, response to the inner seat, the "heart of flesh", and Paul's flesh as an orientation. Depiction §2.4; C §11.5; D §11.8; G §7.
2. **The heart as the centre**: inner speech ("said in his heart"), attention as "setting the heart", the heart as store, surface and soil, its opacity to all but God. Depiction §2.1; B §9.1; C §11.2.
3. **Conscience and bosom** (original gap 4): conscience as the NT's name for what the OT does with the heart ("David's heart struck him"); the bosom as the holding place. Depiction §2.5–2.6; D §11.6.
4. **The inner seat between persons**: souls knit, hearts stolen, spirit passed on, states spreading from one person to another. Depiction §3.8; F §14.
5. **The seat acted upon**: God turns, stirs, hardens and fills; the king's heart. H §7.1; G §11.
6. **The seat in motion** (the twelve threads, framework overview §5): thresholds of eating and drinking, components giving way in sequence, one word with opposite values, voices to the soul, the governed seat, hearing as the way in, spirits that arrive, wind and breath as emptiness, God's own heart and soul.
7. **Beyond the seat**: only about 10% of inner-being verses name a seat at all; twelve other ways the text carries an inner operation. Framework overview §6.

- **C-387** telling added · 12 *Idols taken inside* (recorded, 2026-10-24)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Idols taken inside  Idolatry is not only a matter of statues. God says to Ezekiel of Israel's elders, "these men have taken their idols into their hearts" (Ezekiel 14:3). Their hearts "went after their idols" (Ezekiel 20:16). And Hosea: "a spirit of whoredom has led them astray" (Hosea 4:12). "The spirit of whoredom is within them, and they know not the Lord" (Hosea 5:4).  It also starts in the power to imagine and design. Paul says, "we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man" (Acts 17:29). Habakkuk sees the maker turned upside down: "its maker trusts in his own creation when he makes speechless idols!" (Habakkuk 2:18). The word for "creation" there is the word for the heart's inclination (Chapter 10.4).  Isaiah first says what the delight comes to: *"All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit. Their witnesses neither see nor know, that they may be put to shame"* (Isaiah 44:9).  Isaiah shows the man who makes one: "He takes a part of it and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it" (Isaiah 44:15). "Also he warms himself and says, 'Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire!' And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it" (44:16–17). The same log gives him comfort and a god. The prophet says what is inside: "No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment" (44:19); "a deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, 'Is there not a lie in my right hand?'" (44:20). A body satisfied and a heart deceived stand in one man. He is pleased with the warmth and does not see what he has done with the rest. Babylon's counsellors are the same kind of fire: "No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!" (47:14). 
  - note: in part: idols taken into their hearts

- **C-331** telling added · 13.1 *Choosing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Choosing  The verses on a person's choosing keep speaking of God. They speak of him in his own right, not only as the one a person chooses.  **He chooses.** The verb used of a person's choosing is also used of his: - **a place:** "the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there" (Deuteronomy 12:5) - **people, for a purpose:** "God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe" (Acts 15:7) - **an answer to people's choosing:** "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen" (Isaiah 66:4). The verse gives the reason for his choice.  **He chooses before anything is in the one chosen.** "he chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses those whom others pass over: "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). He chooses witnesses who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8), "that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he" (43:10). His choosing is spoken of with his own love and pleasure: - "In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will" (Ephesians 1:4–5) - "among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel" (1 Chronicles 28:4) - "who chose me above your father and above all his house" (2 Samuel 6:21) - Not for what they were: *"It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the Lord set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the Lord loves you"* (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). *"Yet the Lord set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them … Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart"* (10:15–16). His set heart is answered by a call on theirs.  **He chooses his servant with delight, and puts his Spirit on him.** Matthew applies Isaiah's words to Jesus: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles" (Matthew 12:18, quoting Isaiah 42:1). The one verse holds the one who chooses, whose soul is well pleased; the servant he has chosen, whom Matthew sees fulfilled in Jesus; and his Spirit, put upon him. Matthew gives the setting. The Pharisees "conspired against him, how to destroy him" (Matthew 12:14). Jesus, "aware of this, withdrew", healed them all, and "ordered them not to make him known" (12:15–16). "This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah" (12:17), and the words go on: "He will not quarrel or cry aloud … a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory" (12:19–20).  **He has eyes and delight, and they are the measure of a choice.** The same verse goes on: "but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight" (Isaiah 66:4). Its opposite is those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4).  **He acts first.** At Shechem he speaks of what he has done before anyone chooses: "I took your father Abraham from beyond the River" (Joshua 24:3); "I gave you a land on which you had not labored" (24:13). In Isaiah he offers himself to people who did not look for him: - "I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me" (Isaiah 65:1) - "I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name" (65:1) - "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (65:2)  **He is good, upright and holy.** His instructing comes from his goodness: "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way" (Psalm 25:8). "The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him" (25:14). Joshua tells the people who have just chosen him what he is: "he is a holy God. He is a jealous God" (Joshua 24:19).  His goodness is named toward those who wait: *"The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him"* (Lamentations 3:25). It is said straight after the soul's own word, *"'The Lord is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in him'"* (3:24). And it is asked for the upright under pressure: *"Do good, O Lord, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts!"* (Psalm 125:4; 10.8).  **He knows the heart, and gives.** - "God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us" (Acts 15:8). - "thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you" (2 Corinthians 8:16). - The church's decision is spoken as one with the Spirit's: "it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28).  **He searches hearts, and acts on them.** "the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9). He acts on the hearts of people who are not his chosen, and the verses give his purpose: - of those who "refused to love the truth": "Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false" (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11) - of the kings who give their power to the beast: "for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind" (Revelation 17:17) - of the rest of Israel, who sought and did not obtain: "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear" (Romans 11:8). Paul at once refuses to make it the end: "did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!" (11:11). The remnant is "chosen by grace" (11:5). - of those who do not believe: "They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do" (1 Peter 2:8). The verse gives the disobedience as the cause, and does not explain the rest.  Solomon prays to him as the one who alone knows hearts: "for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1 Kings 8:39). He also asks him to do the turning: "that he may incline our hearts to him" (8:58).  **He answers those who set themselves against his choosing.** The verses show others resenting the one he chose, and they show him answering. - **He counts it as against himself, and makes his choice plain.** "What is Aaron that you grumble against him?" (Numbers 16:11). "And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you" (17:5). The staff is kept "that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die" (17:10). - **He turns contempt round by his faithfulness.** To the one "deeply despised, abhorred by the nation": "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the Lord, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you" (Isaiah 49:7). - **He sets his choosing beside the fixed order of creation.** When people say "The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose" (Jeremiah 33:24), he answers: "If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant … For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them" (33:25–26). - **He is hated first.** "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you" (John 15:18). "I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you" (15:19).  **He calls those who do not know him, for the sake of his chosen.** "For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me. … I equip you, though you do not know me, that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me" (Isaiah 45:4–6).  **He blesses at the place he chose, so that his people rejoice.** "because the Lord your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful" (Deuteronomy 16:15). Those who return to him he gathers there: "I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there" (Nehemiah 1:9).  **His eyes and his heart are at the place he chose.** At night he says to Solomon: "I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice" (2 Chronicles 7:12). "Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place. For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (7:15–16). His choosing of the place goes with his hearing of the prayer made there. In the same speech he says what he will do if he is forsaken: "this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight" (7:20).  **What he chooses is turned toward others.** "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?" (Isaiah 58:6). The self-humbling offered beside oppression is not what he chooses (58:3–5).  **His wrath is turned away when his chosen one stands before him.** "Therefore he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them" (Psalm 106:23). His anger is taken up in 10.13.  **He remembers, and he does not remember.** "He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations" (Psalm 105:8). "For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant" (105:42). When his chosen people had forgotten him, "For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love" (106:45). Of their sins he says the opposite: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins" (Isaiah 43:25). To the one he has chosen: "you will not be forgotten by me" (44:21).  **He reasons, answers and judges.** - He invites a people to reason with him: "Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord" (Isaiah 1:18). - He answers a person's verdict on himself. The eunuch said "Behold, I am a dry tree" (56:3), and the Lord says "I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off" (56:5). - He gives the last word on those who weighed Job's choices: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7).  "he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve … so that they might be with him" (Mark 3:13–14). The calling follows his desire, and the purpose is that they be with him. 
  - note: in part: his eyes and heart at the place he chose; he blesses and gathers there
- **C-331** telling added · 10.7 *Others around a choice* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Others around a choice  A choice does not stay between the one who chooses and the one chosen. Others stand near it: at the place God chose, turned toward it from far away, set against the person chosen, standing with them, or knowing that a choice was made. The verses seldom say what these others feel about the choosing itself. They say what they are to do and be around it, and what moves them.  **At the place God chose.** When God chooses a place, the people are not told to admire it. They are told what to be there. They are to rejoice: *"you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake"* (Deuteronomy 12:18). The joy rests on the blessing, not on the place: *"in which the Lord your God has blessed you"* (12:7). At the Feast of Booths the joy is what the blessing is for: *"because the Lord your God will bless you … so that you will be altogether joyful"* (16:15). The joy is never had alone. The servants, the Levite, *"the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow"* are named in it (16:11), and the one rejoicing is told in the next breath, *"You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt"* (16:12).  Fear is learned there too, at a meal: *"that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always"* (Deuteronomy 14:23). In the same passage the people spend their money *"for whatever you desire … whatever your appetite craves"*, and *"eat there before the Lord your God and rejoice"* (14:26). Fear of the Lord, a satisfied appetite and joy belong to the one meal, and the passage does not set them against each other. When a case is *"too difficult for you"*, the decision is sought at the place, and what is asked is *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (17:8, 10). Presumption is the opposite, and its end is that *"all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (17:13). I read this as a person's own judgement reaching its limit and being asked to yield. The passage names the limit and the carefulness, not the struggle.  **Desire, near and far.** The soul's desire comes in twice, turned two ways. Away from the place it is given room. If the place is too far, *"you may eat within your towns whenever you desire"* (Deuteronomy 12:21). In the same words, desire draws a man to the place: a Levite *"may come when he desires"*, literally with all the desire of his soul, *"to the place that the Lord will choose"* (18:6). His coming is left to that desire. It is the account of wanting (10.6) seen from beside a choice.  **Turned toward it from far off.** For people far from the chosen city, the city is the direction of their prayer. Solomon's prayer takes the hardest case: the people in captivity because they sinned, *"for there is no one who does not sin"* (1 Kings 8:46). The turning happens in the enemy's land, in steps. First *"if they turn their heart"*, then words, *"We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly"* (8:47), then *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul … and pray to you toward … the city that you have chosen"* (8:48). "Turn" and "repent" are the one verb. Solomon prays it to the one who alone knows hearts (8:39), and he asks God himself to *"incline our hearts to him"* (8:58). Nehemiah prays from exile in the same verb, holding God to his word: *"if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, … I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen"* (Nehemiah 1:9). The return is to God, and the place is where he brings those who return.  **Set against the one chosen.** Several passages show others turning on someone chosen, and each names what moves them. - **Grumbling, and seeking more.** When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also? … What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (Numbers 16:10–11). Psalm 106 calls it jealousy (106:16). God counts the grumbling as against himself, and makes his choice plain *"to cease from me the grumblings"* (Numbers 17:5). Once it was plain, the grumbling turned to terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (17:13). - **Anger at what a choice costs.** Saul's anger is kindled against Jonathan: *"do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame"* (1 Samuel 20:30). He gives his reason: *"neither you nor your kingdom shall be established"* (20:31). The anger is for his house, and it ends in a spear thrown at his own son (20:33). Jonathan chose in love, *"for he loved him as he loved his own soul"* (20:17). His anger in reply is grief for the one he chose: *"he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him"* (20:34). He keeps the choice, and seals it with an oath in the name of the Lord (20:42). - **Contempt in the heart.** Michal *"saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart"* (2 Samuel 6:16). It was inward before it was spoken, and when it came out its measure was the servants' eyes (6:20). - **Despised and abhorred.** The servant is addressed as *"one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation"* (Isaiah 49:7), in the same verb as Michal's. The same verse turns it round, not by anything the servant does: *"Kings shall see and arise … because of the Lord, who is faithful, … who has chosen you"*. - **A verdict drawn from ruin.** People looked at the chosen in their ruin and said *"The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose"*, and so *"despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight"* (Jeremiah 33:24). - **Hatred.** *"because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you"* (John 15:19). The world loves *"its own"*. The verse names the choosing as the cause. The passage says the hatred fell first on Jesus (15:18), and puts under it *"because they do not know him who sent me"* (15:21). - **Rejection after testing.** *"a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious"* (1 Peter 2:4).  **With the chosen, and for them.** Others stand with the chosen too. The psalmist asks to be let in: *"Remember me, O Lord, … that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:4–5). He asks God, not the chosen, and he asks it confessing his sin (106:6). Paul writes in chains: *"I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation"* (2 Timothy 2:10). The elder loves the elect lady *"in truth"*, *"because of the truth that abides in us"* (2 John 1–2): the love rests on the truth, not on her being chosen. And whoever believes in the stone God chose *"will not be put to shame"* (1 Peter 2:6). For those who do not believe, the same stone is *"a stone of stumbling"* (2:8).  **Knowing that a choice was made, and not knowing.** Knowing of a choice can settle a quarrel. In the dispute at Jerusalem, Peter appeals to what they all know: *"you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (Acts 15:7). The purpose of God's choosing one man lay in others, that they would hear and believe, and their hearts were *"cleansed … by faith"* (15:9). The debate falls silent (15:12). Paul knows that the Thessalonians are chosen from what he saw happen: *"because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5).  Not knowing does not stop God from using a man for the sake of the chosen. To Cyrus: *"For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me"* (Isaiah 45:4). Knowing is still held out to him: *"that you may know that it is I"* (45:3). Of those outside the chosen, Paul says *"Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"* (Romans 11:7). They were seeking, and did not see. He refuses at once to make it the end: *"did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!"* (11:11).  **An inner act weighed by what God chooses.** In one passage what the others offer from within is set against God's own choosing. The people fast and complain, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"*, while *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (Isaiah 58:3). God answers, *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). What he chooses is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7). The humbling stood beside oppression in the same people, and it was not what he chooses. The same people *"delight to know my ways"* (58:2), in the same delight word as Isaiah 66:4 in *Whose measure*.  The same passage opens on what they appear to be doing: "Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness and did not forsake the judgment of their God; they ask of me righteous judgments; they delight to draw near to God" (Isaiah 58:2). The act is seeking and drawing near. Their delight measures how eager it is, and "as if" says what it lacks. I read that eagerness to draw near can sit beside oppressing workers (58:3) without the person seeing the two together.  Malachi has the same pairing of seeking and delight, and God answers it. The people had said, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he delights in them", and asked, "Where is the God of justice?" (Malachi 2:17). The answer takes their own words: "And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming" (3:1). Then: "But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire" (3:2). Their seeking and their delight are taken at their word, and the question turns back on them. I read a delight in what is asked for that has not yet faced what it asks. The comparison with Isaiah 58:2 is mine; each passage says its own part. His coming as refiner is in 13.1 (*Delight*).  **Rule offered, refused, and sought.** "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon refused: "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the Lord will rule over you" (Judges 8:22–23). Daniel, offered a place as third ruler for reading the writing, refused the reward and did the task: "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king and make known to him the interpretation" (Daniel 5:17). Gideon's son sought what his father refused, and won it by kinship. "Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you? Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." And "their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'" (Judges 9:2–3). He then killed his seventy brothers (9:5). The verses set refusing and seeking side by side in one family, and say no more about why. 
  - note: in part: the people at the place God chose, and turned toward it in prayer
- **C-332** telling added · 13.1 *Choosing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Choosing  The verses on a person's choosing keep speaking of God. They speak of him in his own right, not only as the one a person chooses.  **He chooses.** The verb used of a person's choosing is also used of his: - **a place:** "the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there" (Deuteronomy 12:5) - **people, for a purpose:** "God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe" (Acts 15:7) - **an answer to people's choosing:** "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen" (Isaiah 66:4). The verse gives the reason for his choice.  **He chooses before anything is in the one chosen.** "he chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses those whom others pass over: "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). He chooses witnesses who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8), "that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he" (43:10). His choosing is spoken of with his own love and pleasure: - "In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will" (Ephesians 1:4–5) - "among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel" (1 Chronicles 28:4) - "who chose me above your father and above all his house" (2 Samuel 6:21) - Not for what they were: *"It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the Lord set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the Lord loves you"* (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). *"Yet the Lord set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them … Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart"* (10:15–16). His set heart is answered by a call on theirs.  **He chooses his servant with delight, and puts his Spirit on him.** Matthew applies Isaiah's words to Jesus: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles" (Matthew 12:18, quoting Isaiah 42:1). The one verse holds the one who chooses, whose soul is well pleased; the servant he has chosen, whom Matthew sees fulfilled in Jesus; and his Spirit, put upon him. Matthew gives the setting. The Pharisees "conspired against him, how to destroy him" (Matthew 12:14). Jesus, "aware of this, withdrew", healed them all, and "ordered them not to make him known" (12:15–16). "This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah" (12:17), and the words go on: "He will not quarrel or cry aloud … a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory" (12:19–20).  **He has eyes and delight, and they are the measure of a choice.** The same verse goes on: "but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight" (Isaiah 66:4). Its opposite is those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4).  **He acts first.** At Shechem he speaks of what he has done before anyone chooses: "I took your father Abraham from beyond the River" (Joshua 24:3); "I gave you a land on which you had not labored" (24:13). In Isaiah he offers himself to people who did not look for him: - "I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me" (Isaiah 65:1) - "I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name" (65:1) - "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (65:2)  **He is good, upright and holy.** His instructing comes from his goodness: "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way" (Psalm 25:8). "The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him" (25:14). Joshua tells the people who have just chosen him what he is: "he is a holy God. He is a jealous God" (Joshua 24:19).  His goodness is named toward those who wait: *"The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him"* (Lamentations 3:25). It is said straight after the soul's own word, *"'The Lord is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in him'"* (3:24). And it is asked for the upright under pressure: *"Do good, O Lord, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts!"* (Psalm 125:4; 10.8).  **He knows the heart, and gives.** - "God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us" (Acts 15:8). - "thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you" (2 Corinthians 8:16). - The church's decision is spoken as one with the Spirit's: "it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28).  **He searches hearts, and acts on them.** "the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9). He acts on the hearts of people who are not his chosen, and the verses give his purpose: - of those who "refused to love the truth": "Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false" (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11) - of the kings who give their power to the beast: "for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind" (Revelation 17:17) - of the rest of Israel, who sought and did not obtain: "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear" (Romans 11:8). Paul at once refuses to make it the end: "did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!" (11:11). The remnant is "chosen by grace" (11:5). - of those who do not believe: "They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do" (1 Peter 2:8). The verse gives the disobedience as the cause, and does not explain the rest.  Solomon prays to him as the one who alone knows hearts: "for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1 Kings 8:39). He also asks him to do the turning: "that he may incline our hearts to him" (8:58).  **He answers those who set themselves against his choosing.** The verses show others resenting the one he chose, and they show him answering. - **He counts it as against himself, and makes his choice plain.** "What is Aaron that you grumble against him?" (Numbers 16:11). "And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you" (17:5). The staff is kept "that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die" (17:10). - **He turns contempt round by his faithfulness.** To the one "deeply despised, abhorred by the nation": "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the Lord, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you" (Isaiah 49:7). - **He sets his choosing beside the fixed order of creation.** When people say "The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose" (Jeremiah 33:24), he answers: "If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant … For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them" (33:25–26). - **He is hated first.** "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you" (John 15:18). "I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you" (15:19).  **He calls those who do not know him, for the sake of his chosen.** "For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me. … I equip you, though you do not know me, that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me" (Isaiah 45:4–6).  **He blesses at the place he chose, so that his people rejoice.** "because the Lord your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful" (Deuteronomy 16:15). Those who return to him he gathers there: "I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there" (Nehemiah 1:9).  **His eyes and his heart are at the place he chose.** At night he says to Solomon: "I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice" (2 Chronicles 7:12). "Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place. For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (7:15–16). His choosing of the place goes with his hearing of the prayer made there. In the same speech he says what he will do if he is forsaken: "this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight" (7:20).  **What he chooses is turned toward others.** "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?" (Isaiah 58:6). The self-humbling offered beside oppression is not what he chooses (58:3–5).  **His wrath is turned away when his chosen one stands before him.** "Therefore he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them" (Psalm 106:23). His anger is taken up in 10.13.  **He remembers, and he does not remember.** "He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations" (Psalm 105:8). "For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant" (105:42). When his chosen people had forgotten him, "For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love" (106:45). Of their sins he says the opposite: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins" (Isaiah 43:25). To the one he has chosen: "you will not be forgotten by me" (44:21).  **He reasons, answers and judges.** - He invites a people to reason with him: "Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord" (Isaiah 1:18). - He answers a person's verdict on himself. The eunuch said "Behold, I am a dry tree" (56:3), and the Lord says "I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off" (56:5). - He gives the last word on those who weighed Job's choices: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7).  "he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve … so that they might be with him" (Mark 3:13–14). The calling follows his desire, and the purpose is that they be with him. 
  - note: in part: not for what they were: his set heart and love
- **C-332** telling added · 10.7 *Being chosen* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Being chosen  The verb a person uses to choose is also used when God chooses a person. Then the one who chooses is God. In these verses the inner life of the one chosen is not what made them chosen. It is what the choosing is for, and what follows from it.  **The choosing comes first.** When God chooses, the verses put the inner life of the chosen after the choosing, as its purpose: - *"my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he"* (Isaiah 43:10). The witnesses he chose are *"the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears"* (43:8). - *"he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him"* (Ephesians 1:4). - *"has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith"* (James 2:5). - *"Blessed is the one you choose and bring near"* (Psalm 65:4) comes straight after *"When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions"* (65:3).  One verse names God's choosing and a person's belief together: *"God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth"* (2 Thessalonians 2:13). It does not say how the two fit.  When people choose a person, the order is the other way. The gathering in Jerusalem was told to *"pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom"* (Acts 6:3), and they chose Stephen, *"a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit"* (6:5). They chose by what was already seen in him. It was seen in him to the end: *"full of the Holy Spirit"*, he prayed for those who stoned him, *"Lord, do not hold this sin against them"* (7:55, 60).  **What the chosen are moved to.** The verses set an inner response beside being chosen. Twice they name the choosing as its ground. - **Celebrating.** David, rebuked by Michal for dancing before the ark: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house … and I will celebrate before the Lord"* (2 Samuel 6:21). Her measure was the eyes of the servants (6:20). His was the Lord. Being chosen had not kept him from being angry, afraid and unwilling when Uzzah died (6:8–10). - **Not fearing.** *"Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen"* (Isaiah 44:2). The ground is who chose him: *"the Lord who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you"*. - **Satisfaction.** *"We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!"* (Psalm 65:4). - **Joy and singing.** *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (Psalm 105:43). - **Gladness that another asks to share.** *"that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:5). He asks it while confessing *"Both we and our fathers have sinned"* (106:6).  **What the chosen are called to.** Being chosen is given as the ground of commands: - **Be strong and do it.** *"the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it"* (1 Chronicles 28:10), with *"serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts"* (28:9). - **Put on.** *"Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience"* (Colossians 3:12). What is put on is turned toward others: *"as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive"* (3:13); *"above all these put on love"* (3:14). - **Stand firm.** *"stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us"* (2 Thessalonians 2:15). - **Confirm it.** *"be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall"* (2 Peter 1:10). The qualities are added one to another, from faith to love (1:5–7). The effort follows what was given first: *"His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness"* (1:3). - **Remember.** *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (Psalm 105:5–6); *"Remember these things, O Jacob … you will not be forgotten by me"* (Isaiah 44:21).  **Standing for others.** The chosen can stand between God and people who have turned from him. After the calf, *"he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them"* (Psalm 106:23). The psalm calls Moses chosen at the very point where he stands for people who *"forgot God, their Savior"* (106:21). It also says what those people did to him. They *"were jealous of Moses"* (106:16), and later *"they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips"* (106:33). Standing for them did not keep him from being embittered by them. The anger he turned away is taken up in 10.13.  **Faith, and the truth.** Several verses name faith, and knowing the truth, for the chosen: - *"the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness"* (Titus 1:1) - *"rich in faith"* (James 2:5) - *"belief in the truth"* (2 Thessalonians 2:13)  For people already chosen, Paul prays for *"the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you"* (Ephesians 1:18). Faith is shown in what it does: *"faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead"* (James 2:17).  **Being chosen is not a guarantee.** The verses say plainly that the chosen can fail: - **A condition.** *"if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever"* (1 Chronicles 28:9). - **Forgetting and despising.** The chosen people *"soon forgot his works"* and *"despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise"* (Psalm 106:13, 24). "Despised" is the refusing verb of Isaiah 7:15. - **Not calling.** *"Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel!"* (Isaiah 43:22). - **Blindness.** Whoever lacks the qualities is *"so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins"* (2 Peter 1:9).  The way back is the Lord's remembering: *"For their sake he remembered his covenant"* (Psalm 106:45); *"I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins"* (Isaiah 43:25).  **Set against others.** In each passage the chosen stand beside others who choose otherwise, or cannot see: - the idol-maker, whose heart is shut *"so that they cannot understand"* (Isaiah 44:18) - those who *"refused to love the truth"* and *"had pleasure in unrighteousness"* (2 Thessalonians 2:10, 12) - those who *"profess to know God, but they deny him by their works"* (Titus 1:16) - an assembly that seats the rich and sends the poor to stand, having *"become judges with evil thoughts"* (James 2:4). God chose the poor: *"But you have dishonored the poor man"* (2:6). - kings who *"are of one mind"* with the beast, against *"those with him"*, who *"are called and chosen and faithful"* (Revelation 17:13–14) 
  - note: in part: the choosing comes first; knowing is what it is for
- **C-333** telling added · 10.7 *Being chosen* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Being chosen  The verb a person uses to choose is also used when God chooses a person. Then the one who chooses is God. In these verses the inner life of the one chosen is not what made them chosen. It is what the choosing is for, and what follows from it.  **The choosing comes first.** When God chooses, the verses put the inner life of the chosen after the choosing, as its purpose: - *"my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he"* (Isaiah 43:10). The witnesses he chose are *"the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears"* (43:8). - *"he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him"* (Ephesians 1:4). - *"has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith"* (James 2:5). - *"Blessed is the one you choose and bring near"* (Psalm 65:4) comes straight after *"When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions"* (65:3).  One verse names God's choosing and a person's belief together: *"God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved, through sanctification by the Spirit and belief in the truth"* (2 Thessalonians 2:13). It does not say how the two fit.  When people choose a person, the order is the other way. The gathering in Jerusalem was told to *"pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom"* (Acts 6:3), and they chose Stephen, *"a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit"* (6:5). They chose by what was already seen in him. It was seen in him to the end: *"full of the Holy Spirit"*, he prayed for those who stoned him, *"Lord, do not hold this sin against them"* (7:55, 60).  **What the chosen are moved to.** The verses set an inner response beside being chosen. Twice they name the choosing as its ground. - **Celebrating.** David, rebuked by Michal for dancing before the ark: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house … and I will celebrate before the Lord"* (2 Samuel 6:21). Her measure was the eyes of the servants (6:20). His was the Lord. Being chosen had not kept him from being angry, afraid and unwilling when Uzzah died (6:8–10). - **Not fearing.** *"Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen"* (Isaiah 44:2). The ground is who chose him: *"the Lord who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you"*. - **Satisfaction.** *"We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!"* (Psalm 65:4). - **Joy and singing.** *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (Psalm 105:43). - **Gladness that another asks to share.** *"that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:5). He asks it while confessing *"Both we and our fathers have sinned"* (106:6).  **What the chosen are called to.** Being chosen is given as the ground of commands: - **Be strong and do it.** *"the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it"* (1 Chronicles 28:10), with *"serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts"* (28:9). - **Put on.** *"Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience"* (Colossians 3:12). What is put on is turned toward others: *"as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive"* (3:13); *"above all these put on love"* (3:14). - **Stand firm.** *"stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us"* (2 Thessalonians 2:15). - **Confirm it.** *"be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall"* (2 Peter 1:10). The qualities are added one to another, from faith to love (1:5–7). The effort follows what was given first: *"His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness"* (1:3). - **Remember.** *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (Psalm 105:5–6); *"Remember these things, O Jacob … you will not be forgotten by me"* (Isaiah 44:21).  **Standing for others.** The chosen can stand between God and people who have turned from him. After the calf, *"he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them"* (Psalm 106:23). The psalm calls Moses chosen at the very point where he stands for people who *"forgot God, their Savior"* (106:21). It also says what those people did to him. They *"were jealous of Moses"* (106:16), and later *"they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips"* (106:33). Standing for them did not keep him from being embittered by them. The anger he turned away is taken up in 10.13.  **Faith, and the truth.** Several verses name faith, and knowing the truth, for the chosen: - *"the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness"* (Titus 1:1) - *"rich in faith"* (James 2:5) - *"belief in the truth"* (2 Thessalonians 2:13)  For people already chosen, Paul prays for *"the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you"* (Ephesians 1:18). Faith is shown in what it does: *"faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead"* (James 2:17).  **Being chosen is not a guarantee.** The verses say plainly that the chosen can fail: - **A condition.** *"if you forsake him, he will cast you off forever"* (1 Chronicles 28:9). - **Forgetting and despising.** The chosen people *"soon forgot his works"* and *"despised the pleasant land, having no faith in his promise"* (Psalm 106:13, 24). "Despised" is the refusing verb of Isaiah 7:15. - **Not calling.** *"Yet you did not call upon me, O Jacob; but you have been weary of me, O Israel!"* (Isaiah 43:22). - **Blindness.** Whoever lacks the qualities is *"so nearsighted that he is blind, having forgotten that he was cleansed from his former sins"* (2 Peter 1:9).  The way back is the Lord's remembering: *"For their sake he remembered his covenant"* (Psalm 106:45); *"I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins"* (Isaiah 43:25).  **Set against others.** In each passage the chosen stand beside others who choose otherwise, or cannot see: - the idol-maker, whose heart is shut *"so that they cannot understand"* (Isaiah 44:18) - those who *"refused to love the truth"* and *"had pleasure in unrighteousness"* (2 Thessalonians 2:10, 12) - those who *"profess to know God, but they deny him by their works"* (Titus 1:16) - an assembly that seats the rich and sends the poor to stand, having *"become judges with evil thoughts"* (James 2:4). God chose the poor: *"But you have dishonored the poor man"* (2:6). - kings who *"are of one mind"* with the beast, against *"those with him"*, who *"are called and chosen and faithful"* (Revelation 17:13–14) 
  - note: in part: brought near; called to be strong and do it
- **C-333** telling added · 13.1 *Choosing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Choosing  The verses on a person's choosing keep speaking of God. They speak of him in his own right, not only as the one a person chooses.  **He chooses.** The verb used of a person's choosing is also used of his: - **a place:** "the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there" (Deuteronomy 12:5) - **people, for a purpose:** "God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe" (Acts 15:7) - **an answer to people's choosing:** "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen" (Isaiah 66:4). The verse gives the reason for his choice.  **He chooses before anything is in the one chosen.** "he chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses those whom others pass over: "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). He chooses witnesses who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8), "that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he" (43:10). His choosing is spoken of with his own love and pleasure: - "In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will" (Ephesians 1:4–5) - "among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel" (1 Chronicles 28:4) - "who chose me above your father and above all his house" (2 Samuel 6:21) - Not for what they were: *"It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the Lord set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the Lord loves you"* (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). *"Yet the Lord set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them … Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart"* (10:15–16). His set heart is answered by a call on theirs.  **He chooses his servant with delight, and puts his Spirit on him.** Matthew applies Isaiah's words to Jesus: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles" (Matthew 12:18, quoting Isaiah 42:1). The one verse holds the one who chooses, whose soul is well pleased; the servant he has chosen, whom Matthew sees fulfilled in Jesus; and his Spirit, put upon him. Matthew gives the setting. The Pharisees "conspired against him, how to destroy him" (Matthew 12:14). Jesus, "aware of this, withdrew", healed them all, and "ordered them not to make him known" (12:15–16). "This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah" (12:17), and the words go on: "He will not quarrel or cry aloud … a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory" (12:19–20).  **He has eyes and delight, and they are the measure of a choice.** The same verse goes on: "but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight" (Isaiah 66:4). Its opposite is those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4).  **He acts first.** At Shechem he speaks of what he has done before anyone chooses: "I took your father Abraham from beyond the River" (Joshua 24:3); "I gave you a land on which you had not labored" (24:13). In Isaiah he offers himself to people who did not look for him: - "I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me" (Isaiah 65:1) - "I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name" (65:1) - "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (65:2)  **He is good, upright and holy.** His instructing comes from his goodness: "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way" (Psalm 25:8). "The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him" (25:14). Joshua tells the people who have just chosen him what he is: "he is a holy God. He is a jealous God" (Joshua 24:19).  His goodness is named toward those who wait: *"The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him"* (Lamentations 3:25). It is said straight after the soul's own word, *"'The Lord is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in him'"* (3:24). And it is asked for the upright under pressure: *"Do good, O Lord, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts!"* (Psalm 125:4; 10.8).  **He knows the heart, and gives.** - "God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us" (Acts 15:8). - "thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you" (2 Corinthians 8:16). - The church's decision is spoken as one with the Spirit's: "it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28).  **He searches hearts, and acts on them.** "the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9). He acts on the hearts of people who are not his chosen, and the verses give his purpose: - of those who "refused to love the truth": "Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false" (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11) - of the kings who give their power to the beast: "for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind" (Revelation 17:17) - of the rest of Israel, who sought and did not obtain: "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear" (Romans 11:8). Paul at once refuses to make it the end: "did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!" (11:11). The remnant is "chosen by grace" (11:5). - of those who do not believe: "They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do" (1 Peter 2:8). The verse gives the disobedience as the cause, and does not explain the rest.  Solomon prays to him as the one who alone knows hearts: "for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1 Kings 8:39). He also asks him to do the turning: "that he may incline our hearts to him" (8:58).  **He answers those who set themselves against his choosing.** The verses show others resenting the one he chose, and they show him answering. - **He counts it as against himself, and makes his choice plain.** "What is Aaron that you grumble against him?" (Numbers 16:11). "And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you" (17:5). The staff is kept "that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die" (17:10). - **He turns contempt round by his faithfulness.** To the one "deeply despised, abhorred by the nation": "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the Lord, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you" (Isaiah 49:7). - **He sets his choosing beside the fixed order of creation.** When people say "The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose" (Jeremiah 33:24), he answers: "If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant … For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them" (33:25–26). - **He is hated first.** "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you" (John 15:18). "I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you" (15:19).  **He calls those who do not know him, for the sake of his chosen.** "For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me. … I equip you, though you do not know me, that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me" (Isaiah 45:4–6).  **He blesses at the place he chose, so that his people rejoice.** "because the Lord your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful" (Deuteronomy 16:15). Those who return to him he gathers there: "I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there" (Nehemiah 1:9).  **His eyes and his heart are at the place he chose.** At night he says to Solomon: "I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice" (2 Chronicles 7:12). "Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place. For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (7:15–16). His choosing of the place goes with his hearing of the prayer made there. In the same speech he says what he will do if he is forsaken: "this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight" (7:20).  **What he chooses is turned toward others.** "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?" (Isaiah 58:6). The self-humbling offered beside oppression is not what he chooses (58:3–5).  **His wrath is turned away when his chosen one stands before him.** "Therefore he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them" (Psalm 106:23). His anger is taken up in 10.13.  **He remembers, and he does not remember.** "He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations" (Psalm 105:8). "For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant" (105:42). When his chosen people had forgotten him, "For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love" (106:45). Of their sins he says the opposite: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins" (Isaiah 43:25). To the one he has chosen: "you will not be forgotten by me" (44:21).  **He reasons, answers and judges.** - He invites a people to reason with him: "Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord" (Isaiah 1:18). - He answers a person's verdict on himself. The eunuch said "Behold, I am a dry tree" (56:3), and the Lord says "I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off" (56:5). - He gives the last word on those who weighed Job's choices: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7).  "he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve … so that they might be with him" (Mark 3:13–14). The calling follows his desire, and the purpose is that they be with him. 
  - note: in part: the servant chosen with delight; the staff that makes the choice plain
- **C-334** telling added · 10.7 *Being chosen* (recorded, 2026-10-23)

  - passage after: ## Being chosen  The verb a person uses to choose is also used when God chooses a person. Then the one who chooses is God. In these verses the inner life of the one chosen is not what made them chosen. It is what the choosing is for, and what follows from it.  **The choosing comes first.** When God chooses, the verses put the inner life of the chosen after the choosing, as its purpose: - *"my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he"* (Isaiah 43:10). The witnesses he chose are *"the people who are blind, yet have eyes, who are deaf, yet have ears"* (43:8). - *"he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him"* (Ephesians 1:4). - *"has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith"* (James 2:5). - *"Blessed is the one you choose and bring near"* (Psalm 65:4) comes straight after *"When iniquities prevail against me, you atone for our transgressions"* (65:3). It does not say how the two fit.  When people choose a person, the order is the other way. The gathering in Jerusalem was told to *"pick out from among you seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and of wisdom"* (Acts 6:3), and they chose Stephen, *"a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit"* (6:5). They chose by what was already seen in him. It was seen in him to the end: *"full of the Holy Spirit"*, he prayed for those who stoned him, *"Lord, do not hold this sin against them"* (7:55, 60).  **What the chosen are moved to.** The verses set an inner response beside being chosen. Twice they name the choosing as its ground. - **Celebrating.** David, rebuked by Michal for dancing before the ark: *"It was before the Lord, who chose me above your father and above all his house … and I will celebrate before the Lord"* (2 Samuel 6:21). Her measure was the eyes of the servants (6:20). His was the Lord. Being chosen had not kept him from being angry, afraid and unwilling when Uzzah died (6:8–10). - **Not fearing.** *"Fear not, O Jacob my servant, Jeshurun whom I have chosen"* (Isaiah 44:2). The ground is who chose him: *"the Lord who made you, who formed you from the womb and will help you"*. - **Satisfaction.** *"We shall be satisfied with the goodness of your house, the holiness of your temple!"* (Psalm 65:4). - **Joy and singing.** *"So he brought his people out with joy, his chosen ones with singing"* (Psalm 105:43). - **Gladness that another asks to share.** *"that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:5). He asks it while confessing *"Both we and our fathers have sinned"* (106:6).  **What the chosen are called to.** Being chosen is given as the ground of commands: - **Be strong and do it.** *"the Lord has chosen you to build a house for the sanctuary; be strong and do it"* (1 Chronicles 28:10), with *"serve him with a whole heart and with a willing mind, for the Lord searches all hearts"* (28:9). - **Put on.** *"Put on then, as God's chosen ones, holy and beloved, compassionate hearts, kindness, humility, meekness, and patience"* (Colossians 3:12). What is put on is turned toward others: *"as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive"* (3:13); *"above all these put on love"* (3:14). - **Stand firm.** *"stand firm and hold to the traditions that you were taught by us"* (2 Thessalonians 2:15). - **Confirm it.** *"be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election, for if you practice these qualities you will never fall"* (2 Peter 1:10). The qualities are added one to another, from faith to love (1:5–7). The effort follows what was given first: *"His divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness"* (1:3). - **Remember.** *"Remember the wondrous works that he has done … children of Jacob, his chosen ones!"* (Psalm 105:5–6); *"Remember these things, O Jacob … you will not be forgotten by me"* (Isaiah 44:21).  **Standing for others.** The chosen can stand between God and people who have turned from him. After the calf, *"he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them"* (Psalm 106:23). The psalm calls Moses chosen at the very point where he stands for people who *"forgot God, their Savior"* (106:21). It also says what those people did to him. They *"were jealous of Moses"* (106:16), and later *"they made his spirit bitter, and he spoke rashly with his lips"* (106:33). Standing for them did not keep him from being embittered by them. The anger he turned away is taken up in 10.13.  **Faith, and the truth.** Several verses name faith, and knowing the truth, for the chosen: - *"the faith of God's elect and their knowledge of the truth, which accords with godliness"* (Titus 1:1) - *"rich in faith"* (James 2:5) - *"belief in the truth"* (2 Thessalonians 2:13)  For people already chosen, Paul prays for *"the eyes of your hearts enlightened, that you may know what is the hope to which he has called you"* (Ephesians 1:18).
