- **C-335** telling added · 10.7 *What draws it* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## What draws it  What a person wants is named beside what they choose. The account of wanting is in 10.6. Here the verses set it next to the choice. - **Desire.** *"For they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isaiah 1:29). - **The soul's delight.** *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isaiah 66:3). - **Envy.** The pull is named before the choice, and the command reaches it: *"Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways"* (Proverbs 3:31). - **Being pleased.** *"what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen"* (Acts 6:5). - **Earnestness.** Titus, *"being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (2 Corinthians 8:17). - **Preferring.** To choose can be to weigh one good above another: *"How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Proverbs 16:16). Proverbs 3 sets wisdom above all desire: *"nothing you desire can compare with her"* (3:15).  What is seen as pleasant can draw a person under a yoke. "Issachar is a strong donkey, crouching between the sheepfolds. He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant, so he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant at forced labor" (Genesis 49:14–15). The act is bowing the shoulder. What draws it is the rest and the land, seen as good and pleasant. I read a strong animal choosing to lie down, and the rest costing it its freedom.  Folly draws by what is hidden. "The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing", and she calls, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" and "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." "But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol" (Proverbs 9:13, 16–18). The act is her call and the turning in. The sweetness is what she claims for stolen water. The one who turns in knows the claim and not the end. 
  - note: in part: what is seen as pleasant draws the choice
- **C-336** telling added · 10.7 *What a choice rests on* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## What a choice rests on  In these verses a choice does not come from nowhere. Each verse names something that stands under the choice.  **Knowing how.** The child chooses *"when he knows how"* (Isaiah 7:15). The oracle of Isaiah 1 opens with that knowing missing: *"Israel does not know, my people do not understand"* (1:3). For the person God chooses, the order runs the other way, and knowing is what the choosing is for (*Being chosen*, below).  **Being taught.** The way to choose is taught, and the teaching comes from who the Lord is: - *"Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way"* (Psalm 25:8) - *"Who is the man who fears the Lord? Him will he instruct in the way that he should choose"* (25:12) - The one who chooses asks for it: *"Make me to know your ways, O Lord; teach me your paths"* (25:4); *"graciously teach me your law"* (119:29) - Teaching and the heart are asked for together: *"Teach me your way, O Lord, that I may walk in your truth; unite my heart to fear your name"* (86:11)  In Psalm 119 the one choosing also asks God to do the refusing with him: *"Put false ways far from me"* (119:29).  **The fear of the Lord.** In Psalm 25 it is the one who fears the Lord whom the Lord instructs (25:12). Joshua puts fear before the choice in the same order: *"fear the Lord and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness"* (Joshua 24:14), and then *"choose this day"* (24:15). What fear does to a choice is taken up below, in *Fear and choosing*.  **What has been seen and remembered.** - The people at Shechem choose from memory: *"it is the Lord our God who brought us and our fathers up from the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and who did those great signs in our sight"* (Joshua 24:17). - Job's turning is made when he sees: *"now my eye sees you"* (Job 42:5). - The psalmist keeps his eyes on what he chose: *"My eyes are ever toward the Lord"* (Psalm 25:15).  **What is good to the chooser.** Two verses make the chooser's own good the ground, and honour it: *"wherever it suits him"* (Deuteronomy 23:16), and *"whatever seems good to you"* (2 Samuel 19:38). In Hebrew both say "the good" to him, or in his eyes.  **Convinced that I ought.** A choice can rest on a conviction that is wrong, held with authority from others. "I myself was convinced that I ought to do many things in opposing the name of Jesus of Nazareth. And I did so in Jerusalem. I not only locked up many of the saints in prison after receiving authority from the chief priests, but when they were put to death I cast my vote against them" (Acts 26:9–10). The voice that stopped him named it: "It is hard for you to kick against the goads" (26:14). 
  - note: in part: knowing how, and being taught the way to choose
- **C-336** telling added · 10.7 *Holding a choice* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Holding a choice  A choice spoken is not yet a choice carried out, and the verses say so in several ways. - **It binds the one who made it.** *"You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the Lord"* (Joshua 24:22). - **Choosing is not the same as being able.** *"You are not able to serve the Lord, for he is a holy God"* (Joshua 24:19). Joshua says this to people who have just chosen, and they answer *"No, but we will serve the Lord"* (24:21). - **It is held by keeping it in view, and by clinging.** *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me. I cling to your testimonies, O Lord"* (Psalm 119:30–31). The verb for "cling" is the one used a few verses earlier: *"My soul clings to the dust"* (119:25). The one verb is used of the soul clinging to the dust and of the one who chose clinging to God's testimonies. - **It is held by keeping and holding fast.** *"who keep my Sabbaths, who choose the things that please me and hold fast my covenant"* (Isaiah 56:4). The choice stands between a keeping and a holding on. - **It is held while waiting.** *"May integrity and uprightness preserve me, for I wait for you"* (Psalm 25:21). The psalm ends still waiting and in trouble. The right choice has not ended the trouble. - **Readiness has to be completed.** *"so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it"* (2 Corinthians 8:11). - **Those God has chosen are told to make it firm.** *"be all the more diligent to confirm your calling and election"* (2 Peter 1:10). See *Being chosen*. - **It is held as a purpose set ahead.** *"I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress"* (Psalm 17:3). See *Planning*. - **It can be guarded by another.** Mary *"sat at the Lord's feet and listened to his teaching"* (Luke 10:39). Martha asked Jesus to send her to help (10:40). He named what Mary was doing a choice, and kept it for her: *"Mary has chosen the good portion, which will not be taken away from her"* (10:42).  The choice at Shechem held for a time: *"Israel served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and had known all the work that the Lord did for Israel"* (Joshua 24:31). The verse ties those years to people who had known the work the choice was made from. It gives the timing; it does not give the cause. 
  - note: in part: the choice binds the chooser and is held by holding fast
- **C-337** telling added · 10.7 *What draws it* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## What draws it  What a person wants is named beside what they choose. The account of wanting is in 10.6. Here the verses set it next to the choice. - **Desire.** *"For they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isaiah 1:29). - **The soul's delight.** *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isaiah 66:3). - **Envy.** The pull is named before the choice, and the command reaches it: *"Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways"* (Proverbs 3:31). - **Being pleased.** *"what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen"* (Acts 6:5). - **Earnestness.** Titus, *"being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (2 Corinthians 8:17). - **Preferring.** To choose can be to weigh one good above another: *"How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Proverbs 16:16). Proverbs 3 sets wisdom above all desire: *"nothing you desire can compare with her"* (3:15).  What is seen as pleasant can draw a person under a yoke. "Issachar is a strong donkey, crouching between the sheepfolds. He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant, so he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant at forced labor" (Genesis 49:14–15). The act is bowing the shoulder. What draws it is the rest and the land, seen as good and pleasant. I read a strong animal choosing to lie down, and the rest costing it its freedom.  Folly draws by what is hidden. "The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing", and she calls, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" and "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." "But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol" (Proverbs 9:13, 16–18). The act is her call and the turning in. The sweetness is what she claims for stolen water. The one who turns in knows the claim and not the end. 
  - note: in part: desire, the soul's delight and envy named beside the choice
- **C-337** telling added · 10.7 *What follows a choice* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## What follows a choice  In these verses the outcome of a choice reaches the inner being, whether the choice was right or wrong.  **When the choice is right:** - *"His soul shall abide in well-being, and his offspring shall inherit the land"* (Psalm 25:13). "Well-being" is the same word as "the good" in *"choose the good"* (Isaiah 7:15). - *"The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him, and he makes known to them his covenant"* (Psalm 25:14). The upright are *"in his confidence"* (Proverbs 3:32), which is the same word as "friendship", in the verse after *"do not choose any of his ways"*. - *"these I will bring to my holy mountain, and make them joyful in my house of prayer"* (Isaiah 56:7), with *"a name better than sons and daughters"* (56:5). - At Antioch *"they rejoiced because of its encouragement"*, and the men chosen were *"sent off in peace"* (Acts 15:31, 33). - Barzillai: *"the king kissed Barzillai and blessed him"* (2 Samuel 19:39). - The child who refuses the evil and chooses the good eats *"curds and honey"* (Isaiah 7:15), the food of *"everyone who is left in the land"* (7:22).  **When the choice is wrong:** - **Shame at the thing chosen.** *"you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isaiah 1:29); *"you shall be put to shame"* (65:13); *"it is they who shall be put to shame"* (66:5). - **The heart and the spirit.** *"you shall cry out for pain of heart and shall wail for breaking of spirit"* (Isaiah 65:14). - **Their own fears.** *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them"* (Isaiah 66:4). - **Filled with one's own ways.** *"The backslider in heart will be filled with the fruit of his ways, and a good man will be filled with the fruit of his ways"* (Proverbs 14:14). It is the same filling as *"have their fill of their own devices"* (Proverbs 1:31). The verse before it: *"Even in laughter the heart may ache"* (14:13). - **Too late.** Esau "sold his birthright for a single meal. For you know that afterward, when he desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no chance to repent, though he sought it with tears" (Hebrews 12:16–17).  **In three of Isaiah's oracles the outcome answers the choice in its own terms.** Each verse says it in its own figure: - They set *"cups of mixed wine for Destiny"*, and the Lord says *"I will destine you to the sword"* (Isaiah 65:11–12). "Destiny" and "destine" share a root. - They chose gardens and desired oaks, and *"you shall be like an oak whose leaf withers, and like a garden without water"* (1:30). - They chose what he did not delight in, and *"I also will choose harsh treatment for them"* (66:4).  **The way back stays open.** In the same oracles the offer stands: *"Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord: though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow"* (Isaiah 1:18); *"those in her who repent"* (1:27). 
  - note: in part: shame at the thing chosen
- **C-337** telling added · 10.7 *Choices weighed by another* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Choices weighed by another  Another person can weigh someone's choices. In the book of Job the friends do this, and the verses show how far it reaches. - **They read the choice from the words.** Eliphaz: *"For your iniquity teaches your mouth, and you choose the tongue of the crafty. Your own mouth condemns you, and not I"* (Job 15:5–6). He goes from the mouth to the heart: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash"* (15:12). - **They weigh it as tasting.** Elihu: *"the ear tests words as the palate tastes food. Let us choose what is right"* (34:3–4). - **They read it in suffering.** Elihu: *"this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (36:21). - **They cannot make the choice for the other.** *"For you must choose, and not I"* (34:33).  The book does not let these verdicts have the last word. The Lord calls Job *"a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil"* (Job 1:8). To Eliphaz he says *"you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has"* (42:7). Elihu is not named in that verdict.  The refusing Elihu pressed is made in the end, in Elihu's own verb, when Job sees the Lord: *"but now my eye sees you; therefore I despise myself, and repent in dust and ashes"* (Job 42:5–6).  A king's choice can be questioned and still stand. Joab: "May the Lord your God add to the people a hundred times as many as they are … but why does my lord the king delight in this thing?" (2 Samuel 24:3). "But the king's word prevailed against Joab and the commanders of the army" (24:4). Afterwards "David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people" (24:10; Chapter 8). The act is a decision made over counsel. Joab names the king's delight as what he cannot understand, and the king's own heart judges it after. 
  - note: in part: the friends read the choice from the words and from suffering
- **C-338** telling added · 10.7 *A choice that is honoured* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## A choice that is honoured  Choosing is a freedom a person can lose, and the law gives it back. The escaped slave *"shall dwell with you, in your midst, in the place that he shall choose within one of your towns, wherever it suits him. You shall not wrong him"* (Deuteronomy 23:16).  The king hands the choice to the man who fed him in the wilderness: *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2 Samuel 19:38). Barzillai had already weighed his own age: *"Can I discern what is pleasant and what is not?"* (19:35). His choice is still honoured.  A choice can be given back after a wrong. Warned by God in a dream, Abimelech returned Sarah, gave sheep, oxen and servants, and said, "Behold, my land is before you; dwell where it pleases you" (Genesis 20:15). To Sarah: "It is a sign of your innocence in the eyes of all who are with you, and before everyone you are vindicated" (20:16). The wrong is answered by giving the other the choice of where to live, and by clearing her before others. 
  - note: in part: the escaped slave and Barzillai given the choice
- **C-338** telling added · 10.7 *Choosing before God* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Choosing before God  In these verses a person's choice is not the first move. It is made in front of a God who has already acted. - At Shechem the choice comes after eleven verses of what the Lord did, beginning *"I took your father Abraham from beyond the River"* (Joshua 24:3). - In Isaiah 65 the wrong choice is made in front of a God who says *"Here I am, here I am"* and *"I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people"* (65:1–2). - At the council in Jerusalem the church's choosing follows Peter's word that *"God made a choice among you"* (Acts 15:7), in the same verb.  The verses also name God at work in a person's choosing, and set it beside the person's own accord without setting the two against each other: - *"thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you"*, and *"being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (2 Corinthians 8:16–17) - the Macedonians gave *"of their own accord"*, and *"they gave themselves first to the Lord and then by the will of God to us"* (8:3, 5) - the church's choice is joined to the Spirit's: *"it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us"* (Acts 15:28) - the psalmist chooses, and asks God for the room to carry it out: *"I will run in the way of your commandments when you enlarge my heart!"* (Psalm 119:32)  In 2 Corinthians 8, I read the earnest care God put into Titus's heart as becoming Titus's own: the same passage calls it both. The verses name both and do not explain how they fit.  A choice can be left wholly to God. David, fleeing Absalom, sends the ark back: "If I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, he will bring me back and let me see both it and his dwelling place. But if he says, 'I have no pleasure in you,' behold, here I am, let him do to me what seems good to him" (2 Samuel 15:25–26). The act is yielding. He does not presume God's pleasure, and he does not keep the ark to secure it (13.1).  Eli yields after the word has been spoken. He made Samuel tell him all of it, "Do not hide it from me" (1 Samuel 3:17), and when he had heard the judgment on his house, "he said, 'It is the Lord. Let him do what seems good to him'" (3:18). David yields before he knows what God will do. Eli yields once he knows.  A course can change when God's pleasure is seen. "When Balaam saw that it pleased the Lord to bless Israel, he did not go, as at other times, to look for omens, but set his face toward the wilderness" (Numbers 24:1). He had gone aside before, "as at other times". Now that he sees what pleases the Lord, he does not go, and he sets his face. The next verse: "And the Spirit of God came upon him" (24:2). The Lord's pleasure itself is in 13.1. 
  - note: in part: giving and going of their own accord
- **C-338** telling added · 10.7 *Choices weighed by another* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Choices weighed by another  Another person can weigh someone's choices. Your own mouth condemns you, and not I"* (Job 15:5–6). He goes from the mouth to the heart: *"Why does your heart carry you away, and why do your eyes flash"* (15:12). - **They weigh it as tasting.** Elihu: *"the ear tests words as the palate tastes food. Let us choose what is right"* (34:3–4). - **They read it in suffering.** Elihu: *"this you have chosen rather than affliction"* (36:21). - **They cannot make the choice for the other.** *"For you must choose, and not I"* (34:33).  The book does not let these verdicts have the last word. The Lord calls Job *"a blameless and upright man, who fears God and turns away from evil"* (Job 1:8). To Eliphaz he says *"you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has"* (42:7). Elihu is not named in that verdict. (2 Samuel 24:3). "But the king's word prevailed against Joab and the commanders of the army" (24:4). Afterwards "David's heart struck him after he had numbered the people" (24:10; Chapter 8). The act is a decision made over counsel. Joab names the king's delight as what he cannot understand, and the king's own heart judges it after.

- **C-339** telling added · 10.7 *What draws it* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## What draws it  What a person wants is named beside what they choose. The account of wanting is in 10.6. Here the verses set it next to the choice. - **Desire.** *"For they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isaiah 1:29). - **The soul's delight.** *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isaiah 66:3). - **Envy.** The pull is named before the choice, and the command reaches it: *"Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways"* (Proverbs 3:31). - **Being pleased.** *"what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen"* (Acts 6:5). - **Earnestness.** Titus, *"being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (2 Corinthians 8:17). - **Preferring.** To choose can be to weigh one good above another: *"How much better to get wisdom than gold! "But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol" (Proverbs 9:13, 16–18). The act is her call and the turning in. - **C-339** telling added · 10.7 *The words* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## The words  The English "choose" stands for a few words, and the verses keep each one's own range. - ***Bāḥar*, "to choose".** It is the ordinary Hebrew verb. The ESV renders it in more than one way:   - "choose": *"choose this day"* (Joshua 24:15)   - "desire": *"all that you desire of me I will do for you"* (2 Samuel 19:38)   - "to be chosen", in the sense of preferred: *"To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Proverbs 16:16) - ***Bāḥîr*, "chosen one".** It is a noun from the same root, for a person or a people God chose: *"Moses, his chosen one"* (Psalm 106:23); *"Israel my chosen"* (Isaiah 45:4). - ***Māʾas*, "to refuse, reject, despise".** It is the other side of the same act:   - *"refuse the evil"* (Isaiah 7:15)   - *"this people has refused the waters of Shiloah"* (8:6)   - Job's last word: *"therefore I despise myself, and repent"* (Job 42:6) - ***Eklegomai*, "to choose".** It is the Greek verb used for the gathering in Jerusalem choosing the seven (Acts 6:5) and the church choosing men to send (15:22, 25). - ***Authairetos*, "of one's own accord".** One Greek word: Titus goes *"of his own accord"* (2 Corinthians 8:17).  The verbs for setting a direction are words of the heart: - **inclining:** *"incline your heart to the Lord"* (Joshua 24:23) - **directing:** *"direct your heart to the Lord"* (1 Samuel 7:3) - **setting before oneself:** *"I have chosen the way of faithfulness; I set your rules before me"* (Psalm 119:30). In this verse the choosing and the setting are one sentence.  The same choosing verb is used for God. When he chooses, a person is the one chosen, and what that means for the person is set out below, in *Being chosen*. God's own choosing, in his own right, is taken up with the other beings (13.1). 
  - note: in part: to be chosen, in the sense of preferred
- **C-340** telling added · 13.1 *Choosing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Choosing  The verses on a person's choosing keep speaking of God. They speak of him in his own right, not only as the one a person chooses.  **He chooses.** The verb used of a person's choosing is also used of his: - **a place:** "the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there" (Deuteronomy 12:5) - **people, for a purpose:** "God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe" (Acts 15:7) - **an answer to people's choosing:** "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen" (Isaiah 66:4). The verse gives the reason for his choice.  **He chooses before anything is in the one chosen.** "he chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses those whom others pass over: "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). He chooses witnesses who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8), "that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he" (43:10). His choosing is spoken of with his own love and pleasure: - "In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will" (Ephesians 1:4–5) - "among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel" (1 Chronicles 28:4) - "who chose me above your father and above all his house" (2 Samuel 6:21) - Not for what they were: *"It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the Lord set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the Lord loves you"* (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). *"Yet the Lord set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them … Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart"* (10:15–16). His set heart is answered by a call on theirs.  **He chooses his servant with delight, and puts his Spirit on him.** Matthew applies Isaiah's words to Jesus: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles" (Matthew 12:18, quoting Isaiah 42:1). The one verse holds the one who chooses, whose soul is well pleased; the servant he has chosen, whom Matthew sees fulfilled in Jesus; and his Spirit, put upon him. Matthew gives the setting. The Pharisees "conspired against him, how to destroy him" (Matthew 12:14). Jesus, "aware of this, withdrew", healed them all, and "ordered them not to make him known" (12:15–16). "This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah" (12:17), and the words go on: "He will not quarrel or cry aloud … a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory" (12:19–20).  **He has eyes and delight, and they are the measure of a choice.** The same verse goes on: "but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight" (Isaiah 66:4). Its opposite is those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4).  **He acts first.** At Shechem he speaks of what he has done before anyone chooses: "I took your father Abraham from beyond the River" (Joshua 24:3); "I gave you a land on which you had not labored" (24:13). In Isaiah he offers himself to people who did not look for him: - "I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me" (Isaiah 65:1) - "I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name" (65:1) - "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (65:2)  **He is good, upright and holy.** His instructing comes from his goodness: "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way" (Psalm 25:8). "The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him" (25:14). Joshua tells the people who have just chosen him what he is: "he is a holy God. He is a jealous God" (Joshua 24:19).  His goodness is named toward those who wait: *"The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him"* (Lamentations 3:25). It is said straight after the soul's own word, *"'The Lord is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in him'"* (3:24). And it is asked for the upright under pressure: *"Do good, O Lord, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts!"* (Psalm 125:4; 10.8).  **He knows the heart, and gives.** - "God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us" (Acts 15:8). - "thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you" (2 Corinthians 8:16). - The church's decision is spoken as one with the Spirit's: "it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28).  **He searches hearts, and acts on them.** "the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9). He acts on the hearts of people who are not his chosen, and the verses give his purpose: - of those who "refused to love the truth": "Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false" (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11) - of the kings who give their power to the beast: "for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind" (Revelation 17:17) - of the rest of Israel, who sought and did not obtain: "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear" (Romans 11:8). Paul at once refuses to make it the end: "did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!" (11:11). The remnant is "chosen by grace" (11:5). - of those who do not believe: "They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do" (1 Peter 2:8). The verse gives the disobedience as the cause, and does not explain the rest.  Solomon prays to him as the one who alone knows hearts: "for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1 Kings 8:39). He also asks him to do the turning: "that he may incline our hearts to him" (8:58).  **He answers those who set themselves against his choosing.** The verses show others resenting the one he chose, and they show him answering. - **He counts it as against himself, and makes his choice plain.** "What is Aaron that you grumble against him?" (Numbers 16:11). "And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you" (17:5). The staff is kept "that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die" (17:10). - **He turns contempt round by his faithfulness.** To the one "deeply despised, abhorred by the nation": "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the Lord, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you" (Isaiah 49:7). - **He sets his choosing beside the fixed order of creation.** When people say "The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose" (Jeremiah 33:24), he answers: "If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant … For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them" (33:25–26). - **He is hated first.** "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you" (John 15:18). "I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you" (15:19).  **He calls those who do not know him, for the sake of his chosen.** "For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me. … I equip you, though you do not know me, that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me" (Isaiah 45:4–6).  **He blesses at the place he chose, so that his people rejoice.** "because the Lord your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful" (Deuteronomy 16:15). Those who return to him he gathers there: "I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there" (Nehemiah 1:9).  **His eyes and his heart are at the place he chose.** At night he says to Solomon: "I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice" (2 Chronicles 7:12). "Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place. For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (7:15–16). His choosing of the place goes with his hearing of the prayer made there. In the same speech he says what he will do if he is forsaken: "this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight" (7:20).  **What he chooses is turned toward others.** "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?" (Isaiah 58:6). The self-humbling offered beside oppression is not what he chooses (58:3–5).  **His wrath is turned away when his chosen one stands before him.** "Therefore he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them" (Psalm 106:23). His anger is taken up in 10.13.  **He remembers, and he does not remember.** "He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations" (Psalm 105:8). "For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant" (105:42). When his chosen people had forgotten him, "For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love" (106:45). Of their sins he says the opposite: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins" (Isaiah 43:25). To the one he has chosen: "you will not be forgotten by me" (44:21).  **He reasons, answers and judges.** - He invites a people to reason with him: "Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord" (Isaiah 1:18). - He answers a person's verdict on himself. The eunuch said "Behold, I am a dry tree" (56:3), and the Lord says "I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off" (56:5). - He gives the last word on those who weighed Job's choices: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7).  "he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve … so that they might be with him" (Mark 3:13–14). The calling follows his desire, and the purpose is that they be with him. 
  - note: in part: what he chooses is turned toward others
- **C-340** telling added · 10.7 *Others around a choice* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Others around a choice  A choice does not stay between the one who chooses and the one chosen. Others stand near it: at the place God chose, turned toward it from far away, set against the person chosen, standing with them, or knowing that a choice was made. The verses seldom say what these others feel about the choosing itself. They say what they are to do and be around it, and what moves them.  **At the place God chose.** When God chooses a place, the people are not told to admire it. They are told what to be there. They are to rejoice: *"you shall rejoice before the Lord your God in all that you undertake"* (Deuteronomy 12:18). The joy rests on the blessing, not on the place: *"in which the Lord your God has blessed you"* (12:7). At the Feast of Booths the joy is what the blessing is for: *"because the Lord your God will bless you … so that you will be altogether joyful"* (16:15). The joy is never had alone. The servants, the Levite, *"the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow"* are named in it (16:11), and the one rejoicing is told in the next breath, *"You shall remember that you were a slave in Egypt"* (16:12).  Fear is learned there too, at a meal: *"that you may learn to fear the Lord your God always"* (Deuteronomy 14:23). In the same passage the people spend their money *"for whatever you desire … whatever your appetite craves"*, and *"eat there before the Lord your God and rejoice"* (14:26). Fear of the Lord, a satisfied appetite and joy belong to the one meal, and the passage does not set them against each other. When a case is *"too difficult for you"*, the decision is sought at the place, and what is asked is *"you shall be careful to do according to all that they direct you"* (17:8, 10). Presumption is the opposite, and its end is that *"all the people shall hear and fear and not act presumptuously again"* (17:13). I read this as a person's own judgement reaching its limit and being asked to yield. The passage names the limit and the carefulness, not the struggle.  **Desire, near and far.** The soul's desire comes in twice, turned two ways. Away from the place it is given room. If the place is too far, *"you may eat within your towns whenever you desire"* (Deuteronomy 12:21). In the same words, desire draws a man to the place: a Levite *"may come when he desires"*, literally with all the desire of his soul, *"to the place that the Lord will choose"* (18:6). His coming is left to that desire. It is the account of wanting (10.6) seen from beside a choice.  **Turned toward it from far off.** For people far from the chosen city, the city is the direction of their prayer. Solomon's prayer takes the hardest case: the people in captivity because they sinned, *"for there is no one who does not sin"* (1 Kings 8:46). The turning happens in the enemy's land, in steps. First *"if they turn their heart"*, then words, *"We have sinned and have acted perversely and wickedly"* (8:47), then *"if they repent with all their heart and with all their soul … and pray to you toward … the city that you have chosen"* (8:48). "Turn" and "repent" are the one verb. Solomon prays it to the one who alone knows hearts (8:39), and he asks God himself to *"incline our hearts to him"* (8:58). Nehemiah prays from exile in the same verb, holding God to his word: *"if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, … I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen"* (Nehemiah 1:9). The return is to God, and the place is where he brings those who return.  **Set against the one chosen.** Several passages show others turning on someone chosen, and each names what moves them. - **Grumbling, and seeking more.** When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also? … What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (Numbers 16:10–11). Psalm 106 calls it jealousy (106:16). God counts the grumbling as against himself, and makes his choice plain *"to cease from me the grumblings"* (Numbers 17:5). Once it was plain, the grumbling turned to terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (17:13). - **Anger at what a choice costs.** Saul's anger is kindled against Jonathan: *"do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame"* (1 Samuel 20:30). He gives his reason: *"neither you nor your kingdom shall be established"* (20:31). The anger is for his house, and it ends in a spear thrown at his own son (20:33). Jonathan chose in love, *"for he loved him as he loved his own soul"* (20:17). His anger in reply is grief for the one he chose: *"he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him"* (20:34). He keeps the choice, and seals it with an oath in the name of the Lord (20:42). - **Contempt in the heart.** Michal *"saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart"* (2 Samuel 6:16). It was inward before it was spoken, and when it came out its measure was the servants' eyes (6:20). - **Despised and abhorred.** The servant is addressed as *"one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation"* (Isaiah 49:7), in the same verb as Michal's. The same verse turns it round, not by anything the servant does: *"Kings shall see and arise … because of the Lord, who is faithful, … who has chosen you"*. - **A verdict drawn from ruin.** People looked at the chosen in their ruin and said *"The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose"*, and so *"despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight"* (Jeremiah 33:24). - **Hatred.** *"because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you"* (John 15:19). The world loves *"its own"*. The verse names the choosing as the cause. The passage says the hatred fell first on Jesus (15:18), and puts under it *"because they do not know him who sent me"* (15:21). - **Rejection after testing.** *"a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious"* (1 Peter 2:4).  **With the chosen, and for them.** Others stand with the chosen too. The psalmist asks to be let in: *"Remember me, O Lord, … that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:4–5). He asks God, not the chosen, and he asks it confessing his sin (106:6). Paul writes in chains: *"I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation"* (2 Timothy 2:10). The elder loves the elect lady *"in truth"*, *"because of the truth that abides in us"* (2 John 1–2): the love rests on the truth, not on her being chosen. And whoever believes in the stone God chose *"will not be put to shame"* (1 Peter 2:6). For those who do not believe, the same stone is *"a stone of stumbling"* (2:8).  **Knowing that a choice was made, and not knowing.** Knowing of a choice can settle a quarrel. In the dispute at Jerusalem, Peter appeals to what they all know: *"you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (Acts 15:7). The purpose of God's choosing one man lay in others, that they would hear and believe, and their hearts were *"cleansed … by faith"* (15:9). The debate falls silent (15:12). Paul knows that the Thessalonians are chosen from what he saw happen: *"because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5).  Not knowing does not stop God from using a man for the sake of the chosen. To Cyrus: *"For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me"* (Isaiah 45:4). Knowing is still held out to him: *"that you may know that it is I"* (45:3). Of those outside the chosen, Paul says *"Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"* (Romans 11:7). They were seeking, and did not see. He refuses at once to make it the end: *"did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!"* (11:11).  **An inner act weighed by what God chooses.** In one passage what the others offer from within is set against God's own choosing. The people fast and complain, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"*, while *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (Isaiah 58:3). God answers, *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). What he chooses is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7). The humbling stood beside oppression in the same people, and it was not what he chooses. The same people *"delight to know my ways"* (58:2), in the same delight word as Isaiah 66:4 in *Whose measure*.  The same passage opens on what they appear to be doing: "Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness and did not forsake the judgment of their God; they ask of me righteous judgments; they delight to draw near to God" (Isaiah 58:2). The act is seeking and drawing near. Their delight measures how eager it is, and "as if" says what it lacks. I read that eagerness to draw near can sit beside oppressing workers (58:3) without the person seeing the two together.  Malachi has the same pairing of seeking and delight, and God answers it. The people had said, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he delights in them", and asked, "Where is the God of justice?" (Malachi 2:17). The answer takes their own words: "And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming" (3:1). Then: "But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire" (3:2). Their seeking and their delight are taken at their word, and the question turns back on them. I read a delight in what is asked for that has not yet faced what it asks. The comparison with Isaiah 58:2 is mine; each passage says its own part. His coming as refiner is in 13.1 (*Delight*).  **Rule offered, refused, and sought.** "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon refused: "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the Lord will rule over you" (Judges 8:22–23). Daniel, offered a place as third ruler for reading the writing, refused the reward and did the task: "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king and make known to him the interpretation" (Daniel 5:17). Gideon's son sought what his father refused, and won it by kinship. "Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you? Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." And "their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'" (Judges 9:2–3). He then killed his seventy brothers (9:5). The verses set refusing and seeking side by side in one family, and say no more about why. 
  - note: in part: an inner act weighed by what God chooses
- **C-341** telling added · 13.1 *Choosing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Choosing  The verses on a person's choosing keep speaking of God. They speak of him in his own right, not only as the one a person chooses.  **He chooses.** The verb used of a person's choosing is also used of his: - **a place:** "the place that the Lord your God will choose out of all your tribes to put his name and make his habitation there" (Deuteronomy 12:5) - **people, for a purpose:** "God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe" (Acts 15:7) - **an answer to people's choosing:** "I also will choose harsh treatment for them and bring their fears upon them, because when I called, no one answered, when I spoke, they did not listen" (Isaiah 66:4). The verse gives the reason for his choice.  **He chooses before anything is in the one chosen.** "he chose us in him before the foundation of the world" (Ephesians 1:4). He chooses those whom others pass over: "has not God chosen those who are poor in the world to be rich in faith" (James 2:5). He chooses witnesses who are "blind, yet have eyes" (Isaiah 43:8), "that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he" (43:10). His choosing is spoken of with his own love and pleasure: - "In love he predestined us for adoption to himself as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will" (Ephesians 1:4–5) - "among my father's sons he took pleasure in me to make me king over all Israel" (1 Chronicles 28:4) - "who chose me above your father and above all his house" (2 Samuel 6:21) - Not for what they were: *"It was not because you were more in number than any other people that the Lord set his love on you and chose you, for you were the fewest of all peoples, but it is because the Lord loves you"* (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). *"Yet the Lord set his heart in love on your fathers and chose their offspring after them … Circumcise therefore the foreskin of your heart"* (10:15–16). His set heart is answered by a call on theirs.  **He chooses his servant with delight, and puts his Spirit on him.** Matthew applies Isaiah's words to Jesus: "Behold, my servant whom I have chosen, my beloved with whom my soul is well pleased. I will put my Spirit upon him, and he will proclaim justice to the Gentiles" (Matthew 12:18, quoting Isaiah 42:1). The one verse holds the one who chooses, whose soul is well pleased; the servant he has chosen, whom Matthew sees fulfilled in Jesus; and his Spirit, put upon him. Matthew gives the setting. The Pharisees "conspired against him, how to destroy him" (Matthew 12:14). Jesus, "aware of this, withdrew", healed them all, and "ordered them not to make him known" (12:15–16). "This was to fulfill what was spoken by the prophet Isaiah" (12:17), and the words go on: "He will not quarrel or cry aloud … a bruised reed he will not break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory" (12:19–20).  **He has eyes and delight, and they are the measure of a choice.** The same verse goes on: "but they did what was evil in my eyes and chose that in which I did not delight" (Isaiah 66:4). Its opposite is those "who choose the things that please me" (56:4).  **He acts first.** At Shechem he speaks of what he has done before anyone chooses: "I took your father Abraham from beyond the River" (Joshua 24:3); "I gave you a land on which you had not labored" (24:13). In Isaiah he offers himself to people who did not look for him: - "I was ready to be sought by those who did not ask for me" (Isaiah 65:1) - "I said, 'Here I am, here I am,' to a nation that was not called by my name" (65:1) - "I spread out my hands all the day to a rebellious people" (65:2)  **He is good, upright and holy.** His instructing comes from his goodness: "Good and upright is the Lord; therefore he instructs sinners in the way" (Psalm 25:8). "The friendship of the Lord is for those who fear him" (25:14). Joshua tells the people who have just chosen him what he is: "he is a holy God. He is a jealous God" (Joshua 24:19).  His goodness is named toward those who wait: *"The Lord is good to those who wait for him, to the soul who seeks him"* (Lamentations 3:25). It is said straight after the soul's own word, *"'The Lord is my portion,' says my soul, 'therefore I will hope in him'"* (3:24). And it is asked for the upright under pressure: *"Do good, O Lord, to those who are good, and to those who are upright in their hearts!"* (Psalm 125:4; 10.8).  **He knows the heart, and gives.** - "God, who knows the heart, bore witness to them, by giving them the Holy Spirit just as he did to us" (Acts 15:8). - "thanks be to God, who put into the heart of Titus the same earnest care I have for you" (2 Corinthians 8:16). - The church's decision is spoken as one with the Spirit's: "it has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us" (Acts 15:28).  **He searches hearts, and acts on them.** "the Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9). He acts on the hearts of people who are not his chosen, and the verses give his purpose: - of those who "refused to love the truth": "Therefore God sends them a strong delusion, so that they may believe what is false" (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11) - of the kings who give their power to the beast: "for God has put it into their hearts to carry out his purpose by being of one mind" (Revelation 17:17) - of the rest of Israel, who sought and did not obtain: "God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear" (Romans 11:8). Paul at once refuses to make it the end: "did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!" (11:11). The remnant is "chosen by grace" (11:5). - of those who do not believe: "They stumble because they disobey the word, as they were destined to do" (1 Peter 2:8). The verse gives the disobedience as the cause, and does not explain the rest.  Solomon prays to him as the one who alone knows hearts: "for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1 Kings 8:39). He also asks him to do the turning: "that he may incline our hearts to him" (8:58).  **He answers those who set themselves against his choosing.** The verses show others resenting the one he chose, and they show him answering. - **He counts it as against himself, and makes his choice plain.** "What is Aaron that you grumble against him?" (Numbers 16:11). "And the staff of the man whom I choose shall sprout. Thus I will make to cease from me the grumblings of the people of Israel, which they grumble against you" (17:5). The staff is kept "that you may make an end of their grumblings against me, lest they die" (17:10). - **He turns contempt round by his faithfulness.** To the one "deeply despised, abhorred by the nation": "Kings shall see and arise; princes, and they shall prostrate themselves; because of the Lord, who is faithful, the Holy One of Israel, who has chosen you" (Isaiah 49:7). - **He sets his choosing beside the fixed order of creation.** When people say "The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose" (Jeremiah 33:24), he answers: "If I have not established my covenant with day and night and the fixed order of heaven and earth, then I will reject the offspring of Jacob and David my servant … For I will restore their fortunes and will have mercy on them" (33:25–26). - **He is hated first.** "If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before it hated you" (John 15:18). "I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you" (15:19).  **He calls those who do not know him, for the sake of his chosen.** "For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me. … I equip you, though you do not know me, that people may know, from the rising of the sun and from the west, that there is none besides me" (Isaiah 45:4–6).  **He blesses at the place he chose, so that his people rejoice.** "because the Lord your God will bless you in all your produce and in all the work of your hands, so that you will be altogether joyful" (Deuteronomy 16:15). Those who return to him he gathers there: "I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen, to make my name dwell there" (Nehemiah 1:9).  **His eyes and his heart are at the place he chose.** At night he says to Solomon: "I have heard your prayer and have chosen this place for myself as a house of sacrifice" (2 Chronicles 7:12). "Now my eyes will be open and my ears attentive to the prayer that is made in this place. For now I have chosen and consecrated this house that my name may be there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (7:15–16). His choosing of the place goes with his hearing of the prayer made there. In the same speech he says what he will do if he is forsaken: "this house that I have consecrated for my name, I will cast out of my sight" (7:20).  **What he chooses is turned toward others.** "Is not this the fast that I choose: to loose the bonds of wickedness, to undo the straps of the yoke, to let the oppressed go free, and to break every yoke?" (Isaiah 58:6). The self-humbling offered beside oppression is not what he chooses (58:3–5).  **His wrath is turned away when his chosen one stands before him.** "Therefore he said he would destroy them—had not Moses, his chosen one, stood in the breach before him, to turn away his wrath from destroying them" (Psalm 106:23). His anger is taken up in 10.13.  **He remembers, and he does not remember.** "He remembers his covenant forever, the word that he commanded, for a thousand generations" (Psalm 105:8). "For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham, his servant" (105:42). When his chosen people had forgotten him, "For their sake he remembered his covenant, and relented according to the abundance of his steadfast love" (106:45). Of their sins he says the opposite: "I, I am he who blots out your transgressions for my own sake, and I will not remember your sins" (Isaiah 43:25). To the one he has chosen: "you will not be forgotten by me" (44:21).  **He reasons, answers and judges.** - He invites a people to reason with him: "Come now, let us reason together, says the Lord" (Isaiah 1:18). - He answers a person's verdict on himself. The eunuch said "Behold, I am a dry tree" (56:3), and the Lord says "I will give them an everlasting name that shall not be cut off" (56:5). - He gives the last word on those who weighed Job's choices: "you have not spoken of me what is right, as my servant Job has" (Job 42:7).  "he went up on the mountain and called to him those whom he desired, and they came to him. And he appointed twelve … so that they might be with him" (Mark 3:13–14). The calling follows his desire, and the purpose is that they be with him. 
  - note: in part: his eyes and heart at the place; the soul well pleased in the servant

"Turn" and "repent" are the one verb. Solomon prays it to the one who alone knows hearts (8:39), and he asks God himself to *"incline our hearts to him"* (8:58). Nehemiah prays from exile in the same verb, holding God to his word: *"if you return to me and keep my commandments and do them, … I will gather them and bring them to the place that I have chosen"* (Nehemiah 1:9). The return is to God, and the place is where he brings those who return.  **Set against the one chosen.** Several passages show others turning on someone chosen, and each names what moves them. - **Grumbling, and seeking more.** When God's choice of Aaron was challenged, Moses named what lay under it: *"would you seek the priesthood also? … What is Aaron that you grumble against him?"* (Numbers 16:10–11). Psalm 106 calls it jealousy (106:16). God counts the grumbling as against himself, and makes his choice plain *"to cease from me the grumblings"* (Numbers 17:5). Once it was plain, the grumbling turned to terror: *"Are we all to perish?"* (17:13). - **Anger at what a choice costs.** Saul's anger is kindled against Jonathan: *"do I not know that you have chosen the son of Jesse to your own shame"* (1 Samuel 20:30). He gives his reason: *"neither you nor your kingdom shall be established"* (20:31). The anger is for his house, and it ends in a spear thrown at his own son (20:33). Jonathan chose in love, *"for he loved him as he loved his own soul"* (20:17). His anger in reply is grief for the one he chose: *"he was grieved for David, because his father had disgraced him"* (20:34). He keeps the choice, and seals it with an oath in the name of the Lord (20:42). - **Contempt in the heart.** Michal *"saw King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and she despised him in her heart"* (2 Samuel 6:16). It was inward before it was spoken, and when it came out its measure was the servants' eyes (6:20). - **Despised and abhorred.** The servant is addressed as *"one deeply despised, abhorred by the nation"* (Isaiah 49:7), in the same verb as Michal's. The same verse turns it round, not by anything the servant does: *"Kings shall see and arise … because of the Lord, who is faithful, … who has chosen you"*. - **A verdict drawn from ruin.** People looked at the chosen in their ruin and said *"The Lord has rejected the two clans that he chose"*, and so *"despised my people so that they are no longer a nation in their sight"* (Jeremiah 33:24). - **Hatred.** *"because you are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you"* (John 15:19). The world loves *"its own"*. The verse names the choosing as the cause. The passage says the hatred fell first on Jesus (15:18), and puts under it *"because they do not know him who sent me"* (15:21). - **Rejection after testing.** *"a living stone rejected by men but in the sight of God chosen and precious"* (1 Peter 2:4).  **With the chosen, and for them.** Others stand with the chosen too. The psalmist asks to be let in: *"Remember me, O Lord, … that I may rejoice in the gladness of your nation"* (Psalm 106:4–5). He asks God, not the chosen, and he asks it confessing his sin (106:6). Paul writes in chains: *"I endure everything for the sake of the elect, that they also may obtain the salvation"* (2 Timothy 2:10). The elder loves the elect lady *"in truth"*, *"because of the truth that abides in us"* (2 John 1–2): the love rests on the truth, not on her being chosen. And whoever believes in the stone God chose *"will not be put to shame"* (1 Peter 2:6). For those who do not believe, the same stone is *"a stone of stumbling"* (2:8).  **Knowing that a choice was made, and not knowing.** Knowing of a choice can settle a quarrel. In the dispute at Jerusalem, Peter appeals to what they all know: *"you know that in the early days God made a choice among you, that by my mouth the Gentiles should hear the word of the gospel and believe"* (Acts 15:7). The purpose of God's choosing one man lay in others, that they would hear and believe, and their hearts were *"cleansed … by faith"* (15:9). The debate falls silent (15:12). Paul knows that the Thessalonians are chosen from what he saw happen: *"because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction"* (1 Thessalonians 1:4–5).  Not knowing does not stop God from using a man for the sake of the chosen. To Cyrus: *"For the sake of my servant Jacob, and Israel my chosen, I call you by your name, I name you, though you do not know me"* (Isaiah 45:4). Knowing is still held out to him: *"that you may know that it is I"* (45:3). Of those outside the chosen, Paul says *"Israel failed to obtain what it was seeking. The elect obtained it, but the rest were hardened"* (Romans 11:7). They were seeking, and did not see. He refuses at once to make it the end: *"did they stumble in order that they might fall? By no means!"* (11:11).  **An inner act weighed by what God chooses.** In one passage what the others offer from within is set against God's own choosing. The people fast and complain, *"Why have we humbled ourselves, and you take no knowledge of it?"*, while *"in the day of your fast you seek your own pleasure, and oppress all your workers"* (Isaiah 58:3). God answers, *"Is such the fast that I choose, a day for a person to humble himself?"* (58:5). What he chooses is turned outward: *"to let the oppressed go free"*, *"to share your bread with the hungry"*, *"not to hide yourself from your own flesh"* (58:6–7). The humbling stood beside oppression in the same people, and it was not what he chooses. The same people *"delight to know my ways"* (58:2), in the same delight word as Isaiah 66:4 in *Whose measure*.  The same passage opens on what they appear to be doing: "Yet they seek me daily and delight to know my ways, as if they were a nation that did righteousness and did not forsake the judgment of their God; they ask of me righteous judgments; they delight to draw near to God" (Isaiah 58:2). The act is seeking and drawing near. Their delight measures how eager it is, and "as if" says what it lacks. I read that eagerness to draw near can sit beside oppressing workers (58:3) without the person seeing the two together.  Malachi has the same pairing of seeking and delight, and God answers it. The people had said, "Everyone who does evil is good in the sight of the Lord, and he delights in them", and asked, "Where is the God of justice?" (Malachi 2:17). The answer takes their own words: "And the Lord whom you seek will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant in whom you delight, behold, he is coming" (3:1). Then: "But who can endure the day of his coming, and who can stand when he appears? For he is like a refiner's fire" (3:2). Their seeking and their delight are taken at their word, and the question turns back on them. I read a delight in what is asked for that has not yet faced what it asks. The comparison with Isaiah 58:2 is mine; each passage says its own part. His coming as refiner is in 13.1 (*Delight*).  **Rule offered, refused, and sought.** "Rule over us, you and your son and your grandson also, for you have saved us from the hand of Midian." Gideon refused: "I will not rule over you, and my son will not rule over you; the Lord will rule over you" (Judges 8:22–23). Daniel, offered a place as third ruler for reading the writing, refused the reward and did the task: "Let your gifts be for yourself, and give your rewards to another. Nevertheless, I will read the writing to the king and make known to him the interpretation" (Daniel 5:17). Gideon's son sought what his father refused, and won it by kinship. "Which is better for you, that all seventy of the sons of Jerubbaal rule over you, or that one rule over you? Remember also that I am your bone and your flesh." And "their hearts inclined to follow Abimelech, for they said, 'He is our brother'" (Judges 9:2–3). He then killed his seventy brothers (9:5). The verses set refusing and seeking side by side in one family, and say no more about why. 
  - note: in part: desire near and far; heart and soul turned toward the chosen city
- **C-341** telling added · 10.7 *What draws it* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## What draws it  What a person wants is named beside what they choose. The account of wanting is in 10.6. Here the verses set it next to the choice. - **Desire.** *"For they shall be ashamed of the oaks that you desired; and you shall blush for the gardens that you have chosen"* (Isaiah 1:29). - **The soul's delight.** *"These have chosen their own ways, and their soul delights in their abominations"* (Isaiah 66:3). - **Envy.** The pull is named before the choice, and the command reaches it: *"Do not envy a man of violence and do not choose any of his ways"* (Proverbs 3:31). - **Being pleased.** *"what they said pleased the whole gathering, and they chose Stephen"* (Acts 6:5). - **Earnestness.** Titus, *"being himself very earnest he is going to you of his own accord"* (2 Corinthians 8:17). - **Preferring.** To choose can be to weigh one good above another: *"How much better to get wisdom than gold! To get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver"* (Proverbs 16:16). Proverbs 3 sets wisdom above all desire: *"nothing you desire can compare with her"* (3:15).  What is seen as pleasant can draw a person under a yoke. "Issachar is a strong donkey, crouching between the sheepfolds. He saw that a resting place was good, and that the land was pleasant, so he bowed his shoulder to bear, and became a servant at forced labor" (Genesis 49:14–15). The act is bowing the shoulder. What draws it is the rest and the land, seen as good and pleasant. I read a strong animal choosing to lie down, and the rest costing it its freedom.  Folly draws by what is hidden. "The woman Folly is loud; she is seductive and knows nothing", and she calls, "Whoever is simple, let him turn in here!" and "Stolen water is sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant." "But he does not know that the dead are there, that her guests are in the depths of Sheol" (Proverbs 9:13, 16–18). The act is her call and the turning in. The sweetness is what she claims for stolen water. The one who turns in knows the claim and not the end. 
  - note: in part: the soul's delight beside the choice
- **C-342** telling added · 10.7 *Life and death set before a person* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Life and death set before a person  Scripture sets life itself before the inner being as a choice. *"I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse. Therefore choose life, that you and your offspring may live"* (Deuteronomy 30:19). The passage says what choosing life is: *"loving the Lord your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life and length of days"* (30:20). It describes the other way from inside: *"if your heart turns away, and you will not hear, but are drawn away to worship other gods and serve them"* (30:17). Before the choice is set out, it says the choice can be made: *"the word is very near you. It is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you can do it"* (30:14). Turning that chooses life is a considered act: *"Because he considered and turned away from all the transgressions that he had committed, he shall surely live; he shall not die"* (Ezekiel 18:28). Chapter 2 gives the account.  Death is set before the inner being in the same words: *"Behold, I set before you the way of life and the way of death"* (Jeremiah 21:8). - **A way can seem right and still end there.** *"There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death"* (Proverbs 14:12). - **A choice can be made with death in view.** Esau: *"I am about to die; of what use is a birthright to me?"* (Genesis 25:32). - **A death can set the direction of a life.** *"he died for all, that those who live might no longer live for themselves but for him who for their sake died and was raised"* (2 Corinthians 5:15). - **A choice between two goods can stay open.** *"Yet which I shall choose I cannot tell. I am hard pressed between the two. My desire is to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better. But to remain in the flesh is more necessary on your account"* (Philippians 1:22–24). Paul does not settle it by choosing. He goes on: *"Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and continue with you all"* (1:25).  Plans are made inside a life that is brief. *"What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, 'If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.'"* (James 4:14–15). Some choices are about life itself: - *"Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life"* (John 6:27) - *"For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few"* (Matthew 7:14)  Chapter 2 ("Breath lent", "Life set before a person") gives the setting. 
  - note: in full
- **2-12** telling added · 11 *8. God has a heart and a soul* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## 8. God has a heart and a soul  The inner words are not only for humans. Scripture gives God a heart and a soul, and lets them act.  - "It grieved him to his heart" (Genesis 6:6). - "My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender" (Hosea 11:8). - "I will rejoice in doing them good … with all my heart and all my soul" (Jeremiah 32:41). - "My soul delights" in his chosen servant (Isaiah 42:1). "My soul hates" empty feasts held with bloodied hands (Isaiah 1:14–15). - He swears "by himself" (Amos 6:8), literally by his soul. - He "does not afflict from his heart" (Lamentations 3:33). - He holds back his anger for reasons of his own: "I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man" (Hosea 11:9). - And the one place where his inner self turns away from a people is not hardness: "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people" (Jeremiah 15:1).  Leviticus 26 shows God's soul and the people's soul in a movement back and forth. God promises: "my soul shall not abhor you" (26:11). The people's "soul abhors my rules" (26:15). God answers in kind: "my soul will abhor you" (26:30). Then, at the end, God breaks the exchange: "Yet for all that … I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them" (26:44). The same verb passes between two souls, and God refuses to return it a final time.  God also thinks and plans. "The counsel of the Lord stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations" (Psalm 33:11). "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isaiah 55:8). Where human plans and his cross, his stand: "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Even a cold calculation can be taken up into his purpose. Caiaphas reckoned "that it is better for you that one man should die for the people" (John 11:50). John adds: "He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation" (11:51).  And God speaks in his heart. After the flood, "the Lord said in his heart, 'I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth'" (Genesis 8:21). Before the flood he saw "that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (6:5), and "the Lord regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart" (6:6). Now he names it again, and it is the reason he gives for holding back.  God names his heart with a place. "I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (1 Kings 9:3; 13.1, *Choosing*).  
  - note: in full

- **C-346** telling added · 10.7 *Willing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Willing  Planning reaches ahead from the person. The will, in these verses, mostly answers what comes to the person. In the Hebrew narratives the word for being willing, *ʾāḇâ*, almost always stands just after someone has asked, urged, commanded, enticed, pleaded, warned or offered. And it is almost always a "no": *"would not"*, *"was not willing"*, *"would have none"*. In the Greek, the words for wanting and intending (*boulomai*, *boulēma*) belong to the same family as the words for planning and counsel. One of them, *boulēma*, is translated "plan" in one verse (Acts 27:43) and "will" in another (Romans 9:19). So the verses keep the will and the plan close, without making them one act.  **The will asked for.** Jesus asks people what they want. - To blind men who had cried out against the crowd's rebuke: "What do you want me to do for you?" "Lord, let our eyes be opened." And "Jesus in pity touched their eyes" (Matthew 20:32–34). To Bartimaeus, the same question, and "your faith has made you well" (Mark 10:51–52). - To a man ill for thirty-eight years: "Do you want to be healed?" He answers with what he lacks: "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool" (John 5:6–7). He is healed without the pool (5:8). - To James and John, who came saying "we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you": "What do you want me to do for you?" They asked for the places of honour, and he answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?" (Mark 10:35–38; Matthew 20:21–22). - To the twelve, when many turned back: "Do you want to go away as well?" "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6:67–68). The same question is answered with sight, with a lack, with ambition and with staying. I read the question as drawing the will out into words, where it can be met.  **A will redirected.** Jesus takes the will to be first and the will to follow, and turns them. - The disciples "had argued with one another about who was the greatest". "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all" (Mark 9:34–35). "whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve" (Mark 10:44–45; Matthew 20:27–28). - After Peter was told "you are not setting your mind on the things of God": "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it" (Matthew 16:23–25; Mark 8:34–35; Luke 9:23–24, "daily"). The will is not removed. Its aim is named, wanting to be first, wanting to save one's life, and it is given another way to that end.  **The will meets something put before it.** What is put forward varies: - a request: *"Please let us pass through your land," but the king of Edom would not listen* (Judges 11:17) - pressing, day after day, until *"the man would not spend the night"* (Judges 19:7–10) - a command: Saul's guard *"would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the Lord"* (1 Samuel 22:17) - an enticement, even from the nearest: *"your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly … you shall not yield to him"* (Deuteronomy 13:6–8); *"My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent"* (Proverbs 1:10) - a demand, answered with a line drawn: *"All that you first demanded of your servant I will do, but this thing I cannot do"* (1 Kings 20:9), after the elders said *"Do not listen or consent"* (20:8) - a plea, and the stronger one shutting it out: Tamar said *"No, my brother, do not violate me"*, *"But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her"* (2 Samuel 13:12, 14) - a warning: Abner told Asahel twice to turn aside, *"But he refused to turn aside"*, and he died (2 Samuel 2:21–23) - a feast: the older brother *"was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him"* (Luke 15:28). His anger took the form of a will that would not go in, and the father did not wait inside for it to change (10.13). - a wedding feast: "they would not come", and again, "they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business" (Matthew 22:3, 5) - a plea for patience: "Have patience with me, and I will pay you." "He refused and went and put him in prison" (Matthew 18:29–30), he who had been forgiven all his debt (18:32) - a reign: "his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, 'We do not want this man to reign over us'" (Luke 19:14) - a threat: "He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him" (John 7:1), and his brothers urged him to go (7:3) - an urging between friends: "I strongly urged him to visit you … but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity" (1 Corinthians 16:12)  **The "no" can keep faith, and it can do violence.** The verb does not tell you which; the passage does, and it gives the reason every time. - The king's servants would not kill the priests, and Doeg did (1 Samuel 22:17–18). - David would not *"put out my hand against the Lord's anointed"*. He prayed that, as Saul's life had been precious in his sight, his own would be precious in the Lord's (26:23–24). - The water from Bethlehem shows it most fully. David *"said longingly, 'Oh, that someone would give me water to drink'"* (2 Samuel 23:15). Three men broke through the Philistine camp to bring it. *"But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the Lord and said, 'Far be it from me, O Lord, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?'"* (23:16–17). His own longing was met, and he refused it for their sake, aloud and before the Lord (10.6 follows wanting). - Against that stands Amnon's "would not" (2 Samuel 13:14), and the men of Gibeah who *"would not listen"* (Judges 19:25). - Those who lay burdens on others "are not willing to move them with their finger" (Matthew 23:4), for "they preach, but do not practice" (23:3). - At the cross Jesus was offered "wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it" (Matthew 27:34).  The same verb is used for a refusal that honours other people and for a refusal that tramples them.  **A refusal can be selective.** Saul and the people *"spared Agag and the best of the sheep … and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction"* (1 Samuel 15:9). They refused only where they valued what they kept. God's word on it was *"he has turned back from following me"*, and *"Samuel was angry, and he cried to the Lord all night"* (15:11).  **Wanting to go back.** "But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?" (Galatians 4:9). "Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law?" (4:21). Paul is "afraid I may have labored over you in vain" (4:11). After the defeat at Ai, when "the hearts of the people melted", Joshua said, "Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!" (Joshua 7:5, 7). In a figure: "no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, 'The old is good'" (Luke 5:39).
