Both verses follow a king who *"did what was evil in the sight of the Lord"*. - In grace: *"the Lord was gracious to them and had compassion on them, and he turned toward them, because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and would not destroy them"* (2 Kings 13:23). - Out of love, against a curse that was paid for: *"the Lord your God would not listen to Balaam; instead the Lord your God turned the curse into a blessing for you, because the Lord your God loved you"* (Deuteronomy 23:5; Joshua 24:10).  **He is not willing to forgive, and the verses say why.** - One man *"blesses himself in his heart, saying, 'I shall be safe, though I walk in the stubbornness of my heart'"* (Deuteronomy 29:19). Of him: *"The Lord will not be willing to forgive him"* (29:20). The verse names what the man said to himself. - Manasseh *"filled Jerusalem with innocent blood, and the Lord would not pardon"* (2 Kings 24:4).  His "not willing" runs both ways. In each case the verses name what it rests on: intercession, promise, covenant, grace, love, a heart that blesses itself, or innocent blood.  **He does as he wills.** Nebuchadnezzar learned it by being humbled: *"till you know that the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will"* (Daniel 4:25; 4:17, 32; 5:21). When his reason returned, he said, *"he does according to his will among the host of heaven and among the inhabitants of the earth; and none can stay his hand or say to him, 'What have you done?'"* (4:35). He set it beside *"those who walk in pride he is able to humble"* (4:37).  Paul writes: *"So then he has mercy on whomever he wills, and he hardens whomever he wills"* (Romans 9:18). He gives the objection in full, *"Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?"* (9:19), and answers it with the potter: *"Will what is molded say to its molder, 'Why have you made me like this?'"* (9:20). Jeremiah also uses the potter, for plans that God may relent of (*Purposing*). The two passages use the same picture for different points. I do not join them.  Three verses on, his will and his patience stand in one question: *"What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy"* (Romans 9:22–23). It is a question, "What if", and I leave it as one.  **His will brings to life, and waits.** - *"Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures"* (James 1:18). The verses before set it against human desire, which *"when it has conceived gives birth to sin"* (1:15), and they name the Father *"with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change"* (1:17). - *"The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance"* (2 Peter 3:9). - His will and his purpose stand together: *"when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath"* (Hebrews 6:17).  **The Father's will, the Son's choosing, the Spirit's willing.** - *"yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father … and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Matthew 11:26–27). Luke adds that Jesus said it as *"he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit"* (Luke 10:21–22). The word for the Son's choosing is the will word. - The Spirit gives gifts *"to each one individually as he wills"* (1 Corinthians 12:11). - The Son gives life: *"For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will"* (John 5:21). - Over a disciple's life: *"If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"* (John 21:22). The saying was misread at once: *"So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die"* (21:23). What it meant for Peter is in 10.7 (*Willing*).  **The Son's will, in its own words.** - **"I will; be clean."** To the leper who said "If you will, you can make me clean", Jesus, "moved with pity, … stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, 'I will; be clean'" (Mark 1:40–41; Matthew 8:2–3; Luke 5:12–13). His will and his pity are named together, and his hand touches before he speaks. - **A gathering refused.** "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37; Luke 13:34). Then: "your house is left to you desolate", and the door left open, "until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord'" (Matthew 23:38–39). - **A longing joined with distress.** "I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!" (Luke 12:49–50). - **For those given him.** "Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24). - **In a parable, the owner's will against the begrudging eye.** "I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?" (Matthew 20:14–15). *Do you begrudge* is literally *is your eye evil*, the opposite of the good eye that shares its bread (Proverbs 22:9; 10.6).  **The Father's will, said of creation and of people.** "for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created" (Revelation 4:11). "God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose" (1 Corinthians 12:18). "God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:27). Christ "gave himself for our sins … according to the will of our God and Father" (Galatians 1:4). God "desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4). And after the shepherd who rejoices over the one found: "So it is not the will of my Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish" (Matthew 18:14).  **At Gethsemane the Son's will is given up to the Father's.** *"Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done." And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in agony he prayed more earnestly* (Luke 22:42–44). Two wills are named side by side here, and one is given up to the other. John has the Son say it beforehand, as the reason he came: *"For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me. And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day. For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life"* (John 6:38–40). The Father's will there has content: that none be lost. What it means for a person's own will is in 10.7 (*Willing*).  **Nature.** *"Is the wild ox willing to serve you? Will he spend the night at your manger?"* (Job 39:9). It is one of the creatures God names as beyond a man's control. 13.4 takes up nature. 
  - note: in part: he does as he wills

Three verses on, his will and his patience stand in one question: *"What if God, desiring to show his wrath and to make known his power, has endured with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy"* (Romans 9:22–23). It is a question, "What if", and I leave it as one.  **His will brings to life, and waits.** - *"Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of firstfruits of his creatures"* (James 1:18). The verses before set it against human desire, which *"when it has conceived gives birth to sin"* (1:15), and they name the Father *"with whom there is no variation or shadow due to change"* (1:17). - *"The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance"* (2 Peter 3:9). - His will and his purpose stand together: *"when God desired to show more convincingly to the heirs of the promise the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath"* (Hebrews 6:17).  **The Father's will, the Son's choosing, the Spirit's willing.** - *"yes, Father, for such was your gracious will. All things have been handed over to me by my Father … and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him"* (Matthew 11:26–27). Luke adds that Jesus said it as *"he rejoiced in the Holy Spirit"* (Luke 10:21–22). The word for the Son's choosing is the will word. - The Spirit gives gifts *"to each one individually as he wills"* (1 Corinthians 12:11). - The Son gives life: *"For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he will"* (John 5:21). - Over a disciple's life: *"If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"* (John 21:22). The saying was misread at once: *"So the saying spread abroad among the brothers that this disciple was not to die"* (21:23). What it meant for Peter is in 10.7 (*Willing*).  **The Son's will, in its own words.** - **"I will; be clean."** To the leper who said "If you will, you can make me clean", Jesus, "moved with pity, … stretched out his hand and touched him and said to him, 'I will; be clean'" (Mark 1:40–41; Matthew 8:2–3; Luke 5:12–13). His will and his pity are named together, and his hand touches before he speaks. - **A gathering refused.** "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, the city that kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to it! How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37; Luke 13:34). Then: "your house is left to you desolate", and the door left open, "until you say, 'Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord'" (Matthew 23:38–39). - **A longing joined with distress.** "I came to cast fire on the earth, and would that it were already kindled! I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how great is my distress until it is accomplished!" (Luke 12:49–50). - **For those given him.** "Father, I desire that they also, whom you have given me, may be with me where I am, to see my glory that you have given me because you loved me before the foundation of the world" (John 17:24). - **In a parable, the owner's will against the begrudging eye.** "I choose to give to this last worker as I give to you. Am I not allowed to do what I choose with what belongs to me? Or do you begrudge my generosity?" (Matthew 20:14–15). *Do you begrudge* is literally *is your eye evil*, the opposite of the good eye that shares its bread (Proverbs 22:9; 10.6).  **The Father's will, said of creation and of people.** "for you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created" (Revelation 4:11). "God arranged the members in the body, each one of them, as he chose" (1 Corinthians 12:18). "God chose to make known how great among the Gentiles are the riches of the glory of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory" (Colossians 1:27). Christ "gave himself for our sins … according to the will of our God and Father" (Galatians 1:4). God "desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4). And after the shepherd who rejoices over the one found: "So it is not the will of my Father who is in heaven that one of these little ones should perish" (Matthew 18:14).  **At Gethsemane the Son's will is given up to the Father's.** *"Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done." And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in agony he prayed more earnestly* (Luke 22:42–44). Two wills are named side by side here, and one is given up to the other. John has the Son say it beforehand, as the reason he came: *"For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me. And this is the will of him who sent me, that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me, but raise it up on the last day. For this is the will of my Father, that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life"* (John 6:38–40). The Father's will there has content: that none be lost. What it means for a person's own will is in 10.7 (*Willing*).  **Nature.** *"Is the wild ox willing to serve you? Will he spend the night at your manger?"* (Job 39:9). It is one of the creatures God names as beyond a man's control. 13.4 takes up nature. 
  - note: in part: nature: the wild ox
- **C-355** telling added · 13.4 *(opening)* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: # 13.4 Nature  Nature here means the creatures and the world in their own right, as the verses speak of them before God.  **God's look on what he made.** The first seeing in Scripture is God's. After each work, "God saw that it was good": the sea creatures and the birds (Genesis 1:21), the beasts of the earth (1:25). At the end, "God saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good" (1:31). His look approves what he made before anything in it has done anything. The next look in the story, the woman's at the tree, uses the same words and goes another way (10.6, *Through the eye*).  **The creatures' thirst and hunger met.** "You make springs gush forth in the valleys; they flow between the hills; they give drink to every beast of the field; the wild donkeys quench their thirst" (Psalm 104:10–11). The same list runs on without a break to people: "wine to gladden the heart of man, oil to make his face shine and bread to strengthen man's heart" (104:15). Then it gathers them together: "These all look to you, to give them their food in due season. When you give it to them, they gather it up; when you open your hand, they are filled with good things" (104:27–28). The creatures' need and a man's heart are met by one open hand. Psalm 145:16 says the same: "you satisfy the desire of every living thing" (10.6).  When the water fails, the creatures are pictured turning to God: *"Even the beasts of the field pant for you because the water brooks are dried up"* (Joel 1:20). The same verb is used of the sun: it *"hastens to the place where it rises"* (Ecclesiastes 1:5), and of a person panting for God's commandments (Psalm 119:131; 10.6).  The psalmist also takes the creature's thirst as the picture of his own: "As a deer pants for flowing streams, so pants my soul for you, O God" (Psalm 42:1; Chapter 5). The difference is in what is thirsted for. The donkey's thirst is met by water. The psalmist's thirst is for God himself.  **A creature without understanding.** God shows Job the ostrich: "For she leaves her eggs to the earth and lets them be warmed on the ground, forgetting that a foot may crush them … She deals cruelly with her young, as if they were not hers … because God has made her forget wisdom and given her no share in understanding" (Job 39:14–17). Wisdom and understanding, which are inner words when they are used of people, are named here as things God gave or withheld in a creature.  **Willing.** "Is the wild ox willing to serve you?" (Job 39:9; 13.1, *Willing*).  **Harm ended.** "The wolf shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the young goat" (Isaiah 11:6). "The nursing child shall play over the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child shall put his hand on the adder's den. They shall not hurt or destroy in all my holy mountain; for the earth shall be full of the knowledge of the Lord as the waters cover the sea" (11:8–9). The act is creation at peace. The child's play over the cobra's hole shows it: where there is no harm, a child plays without fear. The verse gives the ground, the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord.  **Lights that rule.** "And God made the two great lights — the greater light to rule the day and the lesser light to rule the night — and the stars" (Genesis 1:16). The psalm gives the same with its refrain: "the sun to rule over the day, for his steadfast love endures forever; the moon and stars to rule over the night, for his steadfast love endures forever" (Psalm 136:8–9).  **Creatures under man's dominion.** "And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the heavens and over the livestock and over all the earth" (Genesis 1:26). "You have given him dominion over the works of your hands; you have put all things under his feet, all sheep and oxen, and also the beasts of the field" (Psalm 8:6–7). The creatures are given under man by the one who made them both (Chapter 11, section 7).  *Verses are gathered here as each part of the study is taken up again (see 13 "Other beings").* 
  - note: in part: willing: the wild ox

- **C-356** telling added · 10.10 *Plotting against another* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Plotting against another  The power to look ahead (10.7, *Planning*) is turned most often, in these verses, against another person. The words are the planning words: to devise, to purpose, to plan. They are used here of harm worked out in advance. What thinking does in plotting is in 10.4, and what the tongue does in 10.5. This section is about what passes between the one who plots and the one plotted against.  **It is planned in the heart.** *"who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually"* (Psalm 140:2). The prophets name the heart as the place where it has to be stopped: *"let none of you devise evil against another in your heart"* (Zechariah 7:10). Zechariah says it again among the things God hates: *"do not devise evil in your hearts against one another, and love no false oath, for all these things I hate"* (8:17).  **It is often done together, and it invites others in.** A son is told what to do when the invitation comes: "My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, 'Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood; let us ambush the innocent without reason'" (Proverbs 1:10–11). The will's "no" is set right against the group's plan (10.7, *Willing*). - *"I hear the whispering of many—terror on every side!—as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life"* (Psalm 31:13) - *"In Heshbon they planned disaster against her: 'Come, let us cut her off from being a nation!'"* (Jeremiah 48:2) - The council, after Caiaphas spoke: *"So from that day on they made plans to put him to death"* (John 11:53). Then the plan widened: *"the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus"* (12:10–11). The plan grew to take in a man whose life was itself the reason people believed. - Ezekiel is shown *"the men who devise iniquity and who give wicked counsel in this city"* (Ezekiel 11:2). - Kings at one table: *"their hearts shall be bent on doing evil. They shall speak lies at the same table"* (Daniel 11:27), and *"plots shall be devised against him"* (11:25). A conqueror's plan is told to those it is aimed at, so that they can flee: "Flee, wander far away … For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you and formed a purpose against you" (Jeremiah 49:30).  **It is aimed at the quiet and the weak.** The verses name who it is aimed at: - *"In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor"* (Psalm 10:2) - *"against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit"* (Psalm 35:20) - *"The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him"* (Psalm 37:12) - Gog: *"thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme and say, 'I will go up against the land of unwalled villages. I will fall upon the quiet people who dwell securely'"* (Ezekiel 38:10–11)  **It hides behind something friendly.** *"Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, 'Come and let us meet together at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono.' But they intended to do me harm"* (Nehemiah 6:2). They sent four times. Nehemiah's answer was not to argue about their intent but to keep to his own work: *"I am doing a great work and I cannot come down"* (6:3). Saul's offer of his daughter was the same: *"Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines"* (1 Samuel 18:25). 10.11 gives the hidden trap.  **It presses another's will.** Absalom invited the king to his sheepshearing. The king "would not go", but "Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him" (2 Samuel 13:25, 27). Then he ordered Amnon's death (13:28). When Joab "would not come", twice, Absalom had his field set on fire, and Joab came (14:29–31). Pilate had said of Jesus, "I find no guilt in him" (John 18:38). Yet, "wishing to satisfy the crowd," he "released for them Barabbas" (Mark 15:15). A will can be pushed until it gives way, and in these passages that is how the plan was carried out.  **It accuses the other of a plan.** Sanballat's fifth letter turned the charge round: *"you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are building the wall"* (Nehemiah 6:6). The council said the same to the apostles: *"you intend to bring this man's blood upon us"* (Acts 5:28). Peter answered, *"We must obey God rather than men"* (5:29). Nehemiah named it as made up: *"you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Nehemiah 6:8). The next verse gives their aim: *"they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, 'Their hands will drop from the work'"* (6:9). I read this as a plan to harm that works by pinning a plan on the other person.  **The one plotted against.** The verses also give the inner life of the person a plot is aimed at. - **He may not know.** *"But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes"* (Jeremiah 11:19). He hands the matter to the one who sees inside: *"O Lord of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind … to you have I committed my cause"* (11:20). - **He prays to be guarded, and that the plan will not go forward.** *"Guard me, O Lord, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from violent men, who have planned to trip up my feet"* (Psalm 140:4). *"Grant not, O Lord, the desires of the wicked; do not further their evil plot"* (140:8). *"Let them be turned back and disappointed who devise evil against me!"* (Psalm 35:4). - **He trusts while it goes on.** After the whispering and the scheming, *"But I trust in you, O Lord; I say, 'You are my God.' My times are in your hand"* (Psalm 31:14–15). The plotters plan his time, and he puts his times in God's hand. - **Someone else may plead.** Esther *"fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews"* (Esther 8:3). Haman had *"plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur"* (9:24). - **Someone else may stop it.** In the shipwreck, *"The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan"* (Acts 27:42–43). One man's wish for one prisoner stopped a plan against all of them.  **It is named, and checked.** - *"Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer"* (Proverbs 24:8), and the next verse says what it is: *"The devising of folly is sin"* (24:9). - *"If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth"* (Proverbs 30:32). The check is to stop before the plan reaches the mouth. The verse after it names where pressing leads: *"pressing anger produces strife"* (30:33). - In the law, the false witness who planned another's ruin receives his own plan: *"you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother"* (Deuteronomy 19:19), *"And the rest shall hear and fear"* (19:20). 10.4 follows what is devised coming back.  Plotting is also turned against God (10.9).  A plot can be dressed as delight. Saul thought, "Let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him" (1 Samuel 18:21), and told his servants to say to David in private, "Behold, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you" (18:22). The act is the snare. The delight is the bait, and it is spoken in private.  The plot can come back on the one who made it. Harbona told the king of "the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, whose word saved the king", and the king said, "Hang him on that." "So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated" (Esther 7:9–10).  Absalom gave the reason for the burned field when Joab came: "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still. Now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death" (2 Samuel 14:32). I read the fire as a demand to be seen by his father. "So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom" (14:33).  
  - note: in part: planned in the heart; done together; aimed at the quiet and the weak; hidden behind something friendly; accusing the other; the one plotted against
- **C-356** telling added · 10.11 *The hidden trap* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ### The hidden trap  In the Psalms a purpose is hidden in order to catch someone. "They hold fast to their evil purpose; they talk of laying snares secretly, thinking, 'Who can see them?'" (Psalm 64:5). The next verse says where the purpose was hidden first: "For the inward mind and heart of a man are deep" (64:6).  A friendly word can be the cover. *"Come and let us meet together"*, Sanballat wrote, *"But they intended to do me harm"* (Nehemiah 6:2). Jeremiah did not see it at all: *"I did not know it was against me they devised schemes"* (Jeremiah 11:19). The psalmist names the arrogant who *"have hidden a trap for me"* (Psalm 140:5). 10.10 (*Plotting against another*) follows what passes between them.  The one it is set for prays out of his weakness. "When my spirit faints within me, you know my way! In the path where I walk they have hidden a trap for me" (Psalm 142:3). "No one cares for my soul" (142:4). It is worse when it comes from those he had prayed for: "Yet they have dug a pit for my life. Remember how I stood before you to speak good for them" (Jeremiah 18:20).  And the trap turns. "In the net that they hid, their own foot has been caught" (Psalm 9:15). The soul the pit was dug for (Psalm 35:7) is the soul that rejoices: "Then my soul will rejoice in the Lord" (35:9). The one taken "out of the net they have hidden for me" says, "Into your hand I commit my spirit" (Psalm 31:4–5). 
  - note: in part: a friendly word as the cover
- **C-357** telling added · 10.9 *(opening)* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: # 10.9 Relating to God  Relating to God engages the whole inner being, and Scripture says so by formula: "with all your heart and with all your soul". That formula governs loving God (Deuteronomy 6:5), serving him (Deuteronomy 10:12), seeking him (Deuteronomy 4:29), returning to him (Deuteronomy 30:10) and keeping covenant (2 Kings 23:3). Jesus adds the mind to it: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind" (Matthew 22:37). The thinking self is named as part of what is given to God in love.  - **Prayer lives in the heart.** It can be complete there without a voice (1 Samuel 1:13). "Pour out your heart like water before the presence of the Lord" (Lamentations 2:19). "With my whole heart I cry; answer me, O Lord!" (Psalm 119:145). - **God speaks to the heart.** To comfort someone, in Hebrew, is to *speak to their heart*. Joseph "comforted them and spoke kindly to them" (Genesis 50:21), literally to their hearts. God says of his people, "I will allure her, and bring her into the wilderness, and speak tenderly to her" (Hosea 2:14), again to her heart. "Speak tenderly to Jerusalem" (Isaiah 40:2). - **Comforted as by a mother.** "As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted in Jerusalem" (Isaiah 66:13). Before it the people are pictured as infants: "that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breast; that you may drink deeply with delight from her glorious abundance" (66:11), "carried upon her hip, and bounced upon her knees" (66:12). The act is being comforted. The delight is the infant's, in being fed, and the one who comforts is God (13.1). - **God tests the heart.** "The Lord tests hearts" (Proverbs 17:3). And he forgives according to what he knows there: "render to each whose heart you know, according to all his ways, for you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind" (1 Kings 8:39). - **The soul is the self in address.** It is told to bless, to hope and to rest (Chapter 5). - **Life is asked of him.** "Give me life" runs through Psalm 119, and each time it rests on something in God: "give me life according to your word!" (Psalm 119:25); "In your steadfast love give me life" (119:88). The life asked for is for keeping his word, praising him and calling on him: "Let my soul live and praise you" (119:175); "give us life, and we will call upon your name!" (Psalm 80:18). Chapter 2 gives the account. - **He holds the breath.** Daniel to a king who had praised idols: "the God in whose hand is your breath, and whose are all your ways, you have not honored" (Daniel 5:23). - **Seeing and hearing him, and living.** "You cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live" (Exodus 33:20). Israel marvelled: "This day we have seen God speak with man, and man still live" (Deuteronomy 5:24). Manoah feared the same: "We shall surely die, for we have seen God" (Judges 13:22). To Gideon God said, "Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die" (Judges 6:23). - **Relied on in the face of death.** "we felt that we had received the sentence of death. But that was to make us rely not on ourselves but on God who raises the dead" (2 Corinthians 1:9). Chapter 2 ("Facing death") gives the account. - **Asked for a brother.** "If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he shall ask, and God will give him life" (1 John 5:16). - **Inquired of, not the dead.** "should not a people inquire of their God? Should they inquire of the dead on behalf of the living?" (Isaiah 8:19). - **Told to depart.** Those who "spend their days in prosperity, and in peace they go down to Sheol" (Job 21:13) "say to God, 'Depart from us! We do not desire the knowledge of your ways. What is the Almighty, that we should serve him? And what profit do we get if we pray to him?'" (21:14–15). The act is a sending away. It is argued as a sum: serving and praying are weighed for profit and found not worth it. Job answers, "The counsel of the wicked is far from me" (21:16). - **Returned to.** Eliphaz counsels Job: "Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you. Receive instruction from his mouth, and lay up his words in your heart. If you return to the Almighty you will be built up" (Job 22:21–23). Then "the Almighty will be your gold and your precious silver" (22:25), and "you will delight yourself in the Almighty and lift up your face to God. You will make your prayer to him, and he will hear you" (22:26–27). The act is returning. Delight comes after it, and prayer after the delight. It is a friend's counsel, given as a condition. - **The human spirit worships.** "God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth" (John 4:24). "My spirit rejoices in God my Savior" (Luke 1:47). Paul serves God "with my spirit" (Romans 1:9). At death the spirit is what is committed into God's hands. - **God's Spirit prays within.** "God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!'" (Galatians 4:6). The Spirit "intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit" (Romans 8:26–27). The cry to God rises from inside the heart, and it is God's own Spirit crying. - **God knows the leaning before the deed.** "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). "The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9). - **God reveals in the night.** "There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries … Your dream and the visions of your head as you lay in bed are these" (Daniel 2:28). - **God reckons, and faith reckons.** God counted Abraham's faith "to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). "Blessed is the man against whom the Lord will not count his sin" (Romans 4:8). Abraham, for his part, "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19). - **His plans against are open to turning.** "It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them because of their evil deeds" (Jeremiah 26:3). How his own plans work is in 13.1 (*Purposing*). - **Plotting is turned against him.** "Although I trained and strengthened their arms, yet they devise evil against me" (Hosea 7:15). The verse before shows the same people: "They do not cry to me from the heart, but they wail upon their beds" (7:14). Nahum asks, "What do you plot against the Lord?" (Nahum 1:9), and names "one who plotted evil against the Lord, a worthless counselor" (1:11). Plotting against people is in 10.10. - **His word can be reckoned strange, and his name esteemed.** "Were I to write for him my laws by the ten thousands, they would be regarded as a strange thing" (Hosea 8:12). Against that stand "those who feared the Lord and esteemed his name" (Malachi 3:16), whom "the Lord paid attention and heard". - **Thinking done in his presence sees differently.** "When I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:16–17). What he had been thinking about was envy: "For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked" (73:3). In the sanctuary he sees it as "a dream when one awakes" (73:20; 10.6, *Jealousy and envy*). - **God cannot be likened.** "To whom then will you liken God, or what likeness compare with him?" (Isaiah 40:18). And God rebukes those who thought him "one like yourself" (Psalm 50:21). - **The heart meditates on him.** "On his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6). - **And he thinks of me.** "What is man that you regard him, or the son of man that you think of him?" (Psalm 144:3). "I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). And his thoughts are precious to the one he knows: "How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!" (Psalm 139:17). - **Sought, and not far.** Paul tells the Athenians that God set the times and places of the nations *"that they should seek God, and perhaps feel their way toward him and find him. Yet he is actually not far from each one of us"* (Acts 17:27). The seeking is a groping in the dark; the one sought is close by. The next verse is *"In him we live and move and have our being"* (17:28; Chapter 2). - **Recognised, and gone to.** At the lake, *"That disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, 'It is the Lord!' When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he put on his outer garment, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea. The other disciples came in the boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from the land"* (John 21:7–8). One sees and says it; one hears and leaps; the others come in with the catch. I read the same recognition met in three ways, none of them rebuked. 
  - note: in part: plotting is turned against him
- **C-358** telling added · 10.4 *What is devised comes back* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## What is devised comes back  What a person devises does not stay where it was sent. It returns to the one who devised it. - Haman's "evil plan that he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head" (Esther 9:25). - "Let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised" (Psalm 10:2). - "He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head" (Psalm 7:15–16). - "I am bringing disaster upon this people, the fruit of their devices" (Jeremiah 6:19). - The law makes it so for the false witness: "you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother" (Deuteronomy 19:19). - "He catches the wise in their own craftiness, and the schemes of the wily are brought to a quick end" (Job 5:13).  Micah shows it in the words themselves. "Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds!" (Micah 2:1). Two verses later, "Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, against this family I am devising disaster" (2:3). The same verb comes back to them, now with God as its subject.  It comes back for good as well. "The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance" (Proverbs 21:5). The wicked who forsakes "his thoughts" finds that God "will abundantly pardon" (Isaiah 55:7). 
  - note: in full
- **C-358** telling added · 10.0 *The path runs back* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## The path runs back  The path does not end at the deed. What was devised comes back to the one who devised it. - Haman's "evil plan that he had devised against the Jews should return on his own head" (Esther 9:25). - "He makes a pit, digging it out, and falls into the hole that he has made. His mischief returns upon his own head" (Psalm 7:15–16). - "Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds!" (Micah 2:1). And two verses later, "behold, against this family I am devising disaster" (2:3). The deviser meets the same verb coming back, with God as its subject. - Anger poured out comes back. "Woe to him who makes his neighbors drink — you pour out your wrath and make them drunk … The cup in the Lord's right hand will come around to you" (Habakkuk 2:15–16). Provoking God harms the provoker: "Is it not themselves, to their own shame?" (Jeremiah 7:19). - It comes back for good too: "The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance" (Proverbs 21:5). "Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established" (Proverbs 16:3). 
  - note: in full
- **C-358** telling added · 10.10 *Plotting against another* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Plotting against another  The power to look ahead (10.7, *Planning*) is turned most often, in these verses, against another person. The words are the planning words: to devise, to purpose, to plan. They are used here of harm worked out in advance. What thinking does in plotting is in 10.4, and what the tongue does in 10.5. This section is about what passes between the one who plots and the one plotted against.  **It is planned in the heart.** *"who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually"* (Psalm 140:2). The prophets name the heart as the place where it has to be stopped: *"let none of you devise evil against another in your heart"* (Zechariah 7:10). Zechariah says it again among the things God hates: *"do not devise evil in your hearts against one another, and love no false oath, for all these things I hate"* (8:17).  **It is often done together, and it invites others in.** A son is told what to do when the invitation comes: "My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, 'Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood; let us ambush the innocent without reason'" (Proverbs 1:10–11). The will's "no" is set right against the group's plan (10.7, *Willing*). - *"I hear the whispering of many—terror on every side!—as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life"* (Psalm 31:13) - *"In Heshbon they planned disaster against her: 'Come, let us cut her off from being a nation!'"* (Jeremiah 48:2) - The council, after Caiaphas spoke: *"So from that day on they made plans to put him to death"* (John 11:53). Then the plan widened: *"the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus"* (12:10–11). The plan grew to take in a man whose life was itself the reason people believed. - Ezekiel is shown *"the men who devise iniquity and who give wicked counsel in this city"* (Ezekiel 11:2). - Kings at one table: *"their hearts shall be bent on doing evil. They shall speak lies at the same table"* (Daniel 11:27), and *"plots shall be devised against him"* (11:25). A conqueror's plan is told to those it is aimed at, so that they can flee: "Flee, wander far away … For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you and formed a purpose against you" (Jeremiah 49:30).  **It is aimed at the quiet and the weak.** The verses name who it is aimed at: - *"In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor"* (Psalm 10:2) - *"against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit"* (Psalm 35:20) - *"The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him"* (Psalm 37:12) - Gog: *"thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme and say, 'I will go up against the land of unwalled villages. I will fall upon the quiet people who dwell securely'"* (Ezekiel 38:10–11)  **It hides behind something friendly.** *"Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, 'Come and let us meet together at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono.' But they intended to do me harm"* (Nehemiah 6:2). They sent four times. Nehemiah's answer was not to argue about their intent but to keep to his own work: *"I am doing a great work and I cannot come down"* (6:3). Saul's offer of his daughter was the same: *"Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines"* (1 Samuel 18:25). 10.11 gives the hidden trap.  **It presses another's will.** Absalom invited the king to his sheepshearing. The king "would not go", but "Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him" (2 Samuel 13:25, 27). Then he ordered Amnon's death (13:28). When Joab "would not come", twice, Absalom had his field set on fire, and Joab came (14:29–31). Pilate had said of Jesus, "I find no guilt in him" (John 18:38). Yet, "wishing to satisfy the crowd," he "released for them Barabbas" (Mark 15:15). A will can be pushed until it gives way, and in these passages that is how the plan was carried out.  **It accuses the other of a plan.** Sanballat's fifth letter turned the charge round: *"you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are building the wall"* (Nehemiah 6:6). The council said the same to the apostles: *"you intend to bring this man's blood upon us"* (Acts 5:28). Peter answered, *"We must obey God rather than men"* (5:29). Nehemiah named it as made up: *"you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Nehemiah 6:8). The next verse gives their aim: *"they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, 'Their hands will drop from the work'"* (6:9). I read this as a plan to harm that works by pinning a plan on the other person.  **The one plotted against.** The verses also give the inner life of the person a plot is aimed at. - **He may not know.** *"But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes"* (Jeremiah 11:19). He hands the matter to the one who sees inside: *"O Lord of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind … to you have I committed my cause"* (11:20). - **He prays to be guarded, and that the plan will not go forward.** *"Guard me, O Lord, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from violent men, who have planned to trip up my feet"* (Psalm 140:4). *"Grant not, O Lord, the desires of the wicked; do not further their evil plot"* (140:8). *"Let them be turned back and disappointed who devise evil against me!"* (Psalm 35:4). - **He trusts while it goes on.** After the whispering and the scheming, *"But I trust in you, O Lord; I say, 'You are my God.' My times are in your hand"* (Psalm 31:14–15). The plotters plan his time, and he puts his times in God's hand. - **Someone else may plead.** Esther *"fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews"* (Esther 8:3). Haman had *"plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur"* (9:24). - **Someone else may stop it.** In the shipwreck, *"The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan"* (Acts 27:42–43). One man's wish for one prisoner stopped a plan against all of them.  **It is named, and checked.** - *"Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer"* (Proverbs 24:8), and the next verse says what it is: *"The devising of folly is sin"* (24:9). - *"If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth"* (Proverbs 30:32). The check is to stop before the plan reaches the mouth. The verse after it names where pressing leads: *"pressing anger produces strife"* (30:33). - In the law, the false witness who planned another's ruin receives his own plan: *"you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother"* (Deuteronomy 19:19), *"And the rest shall hear and fear"* (19:20). 10.4 follows what is devised coming back.  Plotting is also turned against God (10.9).  A plot can be dressed as delight. Saul thought, "Let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him" (1 Samuel 18:21), and told his servants to say to David in private, "Behold, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you" (18:22). The act is the snare. The delight is the bait, and it is spoken in private.  The plot can come back on the one who made it. Harbona told the king of "the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, whose word saved the king", and the king said, "Hang him on that." "So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated" (Esther 7:9–10).  Absalom gave the reason for the burned field when Joab came: "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still. Now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death" (2 Samuel 14:32). I read the fire as a demand to be seen by his father. "So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom" (14:33).  
  - note: in part: it is named, and checked
- **C-359** telling added · 10.7 *Planning* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Planning  A choice settles a direction. A plan carries it ahead, into a time that has not yet come. Scripture gives the inner being this power plainly. Of the builders at Babel God says, *"this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them"* (Genesis 11:6). The words for it are the words for thinking: to devise, to reckon, to purpose (10.4). They are used for a woman buying a field, a king counting his soldiers, a sailor looking for a beach, and a man plotting on his bed. This section is about the looking ahead itself. Plans made against another person are in 10.10. The next section, *Willing*, is about how a person answers what others put forward. The two often appear in the same passage.  The place of it is the heart: *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). In that one verse the plan is the person's own, and the steps are not. I read the rest of what the verses say about planning inside that verse.  **Weighing first.** Jesus asks his hearers to look ahead before they begin. "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28). A builder who lays a foundation and cannot finish is mocked: *"This man began to build and was not able to finish"* (Luke 14:30). *"Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?"* (14:31). If the answer is no, he sends for terms *"while the other is yet a great way off"* (14:32). The looking ahead here is honest about strength, and it acts early, while there is still time. Jesus uses it for following him: *"So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple"* (14:33).  The same weighing is praised in an ordinary life. The woman of Proverbs 31 *"rises while it is yet night"* (31:15). *"She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard"* (31:16). The verb for considering is a planning verb. She weighs it, and then she acts.  When something has happened that no one has seen before, the first call is to weigh it before acting. After the outrage at Gibeah, *"all who saw it said, 'Such a thing has never happened or been seen … consider it, take counsel, and speak'"* (Judges 19:30).  **Planning without knowing.** The fullest picture of planning ahead in these verses is a voyage. Paul warned the crew: *"I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss"* (Acts 27:10). They listened to the pilot and the owner instead (27:11). The plan that followed is worded with all its uncertainty: - *"the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix"* (27:12) - *"Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor"* (27:13) - after the storm, *"they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore"* (27:39)  *"on the chance that somehow"*, *"supposing"*, *"if possible"*: Luke records the planners' own sense that they could not see far. The first plan was undone by the wind (Acts 27:14). The last was undone by a reef they had not seen (27:41).  Paul plans the same way, and says so. *"I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented)"* (Romans 1:13). His intending was real and often repeated, and something outside him held it back. James says what such planning should sound like: *"If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that"* (James 4:15; see *Life and death set before a person*).  Paul's own plans are said under God's will, again and again, and his wanting stays strong inside them. - At parting: "I will return to you if God wills" (Acts 18:21), after he "declined" to stay longer (18:20). - With purpose: "I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power" (1 Corinthians 4:19). He then asks their will: "What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love?" (4:21). - With his own wish: "I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits" (16:7). - In prayer: "asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you. For I long to see you" (Romans 1:10–11); "so that by God's will I may come to you with joy" (15:32). - Hindered: "we wanted to come to you, I, Paul, again and again, but Satan hindered us" (1 Thessalonians 2:18), after "with great desire to see you face to face" (2:17). - Yielded by others: "since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, 'Let the will of the Lord be done'" (Acts 21:14), after "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?" (21:13). - A wish set beside a gift: "I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God" (1 Corinthians 7:7). The verses keep apart Paul's wanting, God's will, and what hinders, named once as Satan. I read the plan as held open toward God without the wanting being given up.  **A plan carries a person's word.** When Paul changed his travel plans, he was charged with being unreliable, and he answers with the inner question: *"Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say 'Yes, yes' and 'No, no' at the same time?"* (2 Corinthians 1:17). He rests his answer on God: *"As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No"* (1:18). In this passage, a plan is something said to others. When it changes, the change can be read as a divided heart.  **Planning together, and parting.** Plans are often made with others, and others may not agree. - Paul and Barnabas planned to revisit the churches. *"Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them"* (Acts 15:37–38). Each weighed the same past differently, and *"there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other"* (15:39). - Joseph of Arimathea sat in the council that sent Jesus to death, but he *"had not consented to their decision and action"* (Luke 23:51). He did not share their plan, and the next verse shows him acting on his own: *"This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus"* (23:52).  **Planning for another's good.** Darius *"planned to set him over the whole kingdom"* (Daniel 6:3), and the verse gives the reason: *"because an excellent spirit was in him"*. The plan for Daniel at once stirred others to look for a fault in him (6:4).  A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).  **A purpose held.** Some plans are aimed at one's own life. *"You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress"* (Psalm 17:3). The psalmist has set a course for his own speech ahead of time, and he states it under God's testing. He goes on: *"My steps have held fast to your paths"* (17:5). - Barnabas, at Antioch, *"exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose"* (Acts 11:23). The verse says what moved him: he *"saw the grace of God"* and *"was glad"*. - Paul lists his *"aim in life"* among what Timothy had followed, beside *"my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness"* (2 Timothy 3:10). - David prays that God will keep what the people have set: *"keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you"* (1 Chronicles 29:18). He asks God to hold the purpose in place. - Paul uses a purpose word for where the mind is set: *"to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace"* (Romans 8:6). *"For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"* (8:7). Chapter 7 gives the flesh. - The verb of the same word names a mind set downward: *"their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things"* (Philippians 3:19). The next verse turns it: *"But our citizenship is in heaven"* (3:20). And the call uses the same verb: *"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth"* (Colossians 3:2). - *"You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you"* (Isaiah 26:3).  **Devised from one's own heart.** A plan can begin in the self and stay there. Jeroboam set up his own feast *"in the month that he had devised from his own heart"* (1 Kings 12:33). The month was his own invention, set against the feast in Judah (12:32). Nehemiah said to the plotters, *"No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Nehemiah 6:8). The same capacity that looks ahead can make up what is not there (10.4, *Imagination that makes gods*).  **The plan and its outcome.** The verses do not let a plan secure its own end. - *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). - *"Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us"* (Isaiah 8:10). - Gamaliel, of the apostles: *"if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them"* (Acts 5:38–39). - Of those who plot against the king: *"Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed"* (Psalm 21:11). Of a king's plans against strongholds: *"but only for a time"* (Daniel 11:24). The next verse says what he roused for it: *"he shall stir up his power and his heart"* (11:25). The heart is stirred up as a resource for war. - Counsel that cannot save: *"You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you … No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!"* (Isaiah 47:13–14). Many counsels weary the one who keeps them, and they give no warmth. - Joseph, of his brothers: *"you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"* (Genesis 50:20). The same verb is used of both.  The verses also show that what a person intends is seen before it is done and will be shown in full. *"The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (1 Chronicles 28:9). The Lord *"will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart"* (1 Corinthians 4:5). Paul draws a warning from it for himself: *"do not pronounce judgment before the time"* (4:5). He has just said, *"I do not even judge myself"* (4:3).  Joseph's counsel to Pharaoh plans against a famine he has been shown. "Let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man", gather the food of the good years "under the authority of Pharaoh", and keep it as "a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine", "so that the land may not perish" (Genesis 41:33–36). "This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants" (41:37).  
  - note: in part: weighing first; planning without knowing; a plan carries a word; planning together and parting; planning for another's good
- **C-360** telling added · 10.7 *Planning* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Planning  A choice settles a direction. A plan carries it ahead, into a time that has not yet come. Scripture gives the inner being this power plainly. Of the builders at Babel God says, *"this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them"* (Genesis 11:6). The words for it are the words for thinking: to devise, to reckon, to purpose (10.4). They are used for a woman buying a field, a king counting his soldiers, a sailor looking for a beach, and a man plotting on his bed. This section is about the looking ahead itself. Plans made against another person are in 10.10. The next section, *Willing*, is about how a person answers what others put forward. The two often appear in the same passage.  The place of it is the heart: *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). In that one verse the plan is the person's own, and the steps are not. I read the rest of what the verses say about planning inside that verse.  **Weighing first.** Jesus asks his hearers to look ahead before they begin. "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28). A builder who lays a foundation and cannot finish is mocked: *"This man began to build and was not able to finish"* (Luke 14:30). *"Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?"* (14:31). If the answer is no, he sends for terms *"while the other is yet a great way off"* (14:32). The looking ahead here is honest about strength, and it acts early, while there is still time. Jesus uses it for following him: *"So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple"* (14:33).  The same weighing is praised in an ordinary life. The woman of Proverbs 31 *"rises while it is yet night"* (31:15). *"She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard"* (31:16). The verb for considering is a planning verb. She weighs it, and then she acts.  When something has happened that no one has seen before, the first call is to weigh it before acting. After the outrage at Gibeah, *"all who saw it said, 'Such a thing has never happened or been seen … consider it, take counsel, and speak'"* (Judges 19:30).  **Planning without knowing.** The fullest picture of planning ahead in these verses is a voyage. Paul warned the crew: *"I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss"* (Acts 27:10). They listened to the pilot and the owner instead (27:11). The plan that followed is worded with all its uncertainty: - *"the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix"* (27:12) - *"Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor"* (27:13) - after the storm, *"they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore"* (27:39)  *"on the chance that somehow"*, *"supposing"*, *"if possible"*: Luke records the planners' own sense that they could not see far. The first plan was undone by the wind (Acts 27:14). The last was undone by a reef they had not seen (27:41).  Paul plans the same way, and says so. *"I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented)"* (Romans 1:13). His intending was real and often repeated, and something outside him held it back. James says what such planning should sound like: *"If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that"* (James 4:15; see *Life and death set before a person*).  Paul's own plans are said under God's will, again and again, and his wanting stays strong inside them. - At parting: "I will return to you if God wills" (Acts 18:21), after he "declined" to stay longer (18:20). - With purpose: "I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power" (1 Corinthians 4:19). He then asks their will: "What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love?" (4:21). - With his own wish: "I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits" (16:7). - In prayer: "asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you. For I long to see you" (Romans 1:10–11); "so that by God's will I may come to you with joy" (15:32). - Hindered: "we wanted to come to you, I, Paul, again and again, but Satan hindered us" (1 Thessalonians 2:18), after "with great desire to see you face to face" (2:17). - Yielded by others: "since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, 'Let the will of the Lord be done'" (Acts 21:14), after "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?" (21:13). - A wish set beside a gift: "I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God" (1 Corinthians 7:7). The verses keep apart Paul's wanting, God's will, and what hinders, named once as Satan. I read the plan as held open toward God without the wanting being given up.  **A plan carries a person's word.** When Paul changed his travel plans, he was charged with being unreliable, and he answers with the inner question: *"Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say 'Yes, yes' and 'No, no' at the same time?"* (2 Corinthians 1:17). He rests his answer on God: *"As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No"* (1:18). In this passage, a plan is something said to others. When it changes, the change can be read as a divided heart.  **Planning together, and parting.** Plans are often made with others, and others may not agree. - Paul and Barnabas planned to revisit the churches. *"Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them"* (Acts 15:37–38). Each weighed the same past differently, and *"there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other"* (15:39). - Joseph of Arimathea sat in the council that sent Jesus to death, but he *"had not consented to their decision and action"* (Luke 23:51). He did not share their plan, and the next verse shows him acting on his own: *"This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus"* (23:52).  **Planning for another's good.** Darius *"planned to set him over the whole kingdom"* (Daniel 6:3), and the verse gives the reason: *"because an excellent spirit was in him"*. The plan for Daniel at once stirred others to look for a fault in him (6:4).  A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).  **A purpose held.** Some plans are aimed at one's own life. *"You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress"* (Psalm 17:3). The psalmist has set a course for his own speech ahead of time, and he states it under God's testing. He goes on: *"My steps have held fast to your paths"* (17:5). - Barnabas, at Antioch, *"exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose"* (Acts 11:23). The verse says what moved him: he *"saw the grace of God"* and *"was glad"*. - Paul lists his *"aim in life"* among what Timothy had followed, beside *"my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness"* (2 Timothy 3:10). - David prays that God will keep what the people have set: *"keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you"* (1 Chronicles 29:18). He asks God to hold the purpose in place. - Paul uses a purpose word for where the mind is set: *"to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace"* (Romans 8:6). *"For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"* (8:7). Chapter 7 gives the flesh. - The verb of the same word names a mind set downward: *"their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things"* (Philippians 3:19). The next verse turns it: *"But our citizenship is in heaven"* (3:20). And the call uses the same verb: *"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth"* (Colossians 3:2). - *"You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you"* (Isaiah 26:3).  **Devised from one's own heart.** A plan can begin in the self and stay there. Jeroboam set up his own feast *"in the month that he had devised from his own heart"* (1 Kings 12:33). The month was his own invention, set against the feast in Judah (12:32). Nehemiah said to the plotters, *"No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Nehemiah 6:8). The same capacity that looks ahead can make up what is not there (10.4, *Imagination that makes gods*).  **The plan and its outcome.** The verses do not let a plan secure its own end. - *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). - *"Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us"* (Isaiah 8:10). - Gamaliel, of the apostles: *"if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them"* (Acts 5:38–39). - Of those who plot against the king: *"Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed"* (Psalm 21:11). Of a king's plans against strongholds: *"but only for a time"* (Daniel 11:24). The next verse says what he roused for it: *"he shall stir up his power and his heart"* (11:25). The heart is stirred up as a resource for war. - Counsel that cannot save: *"You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you … No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!"* (Isaiah 47:13–14). Many counsels weary the one who keeps them, and they give no warmth. - Joseph, of his brothers: *"you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"* (Genesis 50:20). The same verb is used of both.  The verses also show that what a person intends is seen before it is done and will be shown in full. *"The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (1 Chronicles 28:9). The Lord *"will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart"* (1 Corinthians 4:5). Paul draws a warning from it for himself: *"do not pronounce judgment before the time"* (4:5). He has just said, *"I do not even judge myself"* (4:3).  Joseph's counsel to Pharaoh plans against a famine he has been shown. "Let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man", gather the food of the good years "under the authority of Pharaoh", and keep it as "a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine", "so that the land may not perish" (Genesis 41:33–36). "This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants" (41:37).  
  - note: in part: the place of it is the heart; the plan and its outcome
- **C-361** telling added · 11 *8. God has a heart and a soul* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## 8. God has a heart and a soul  The inner words are not only for humans. Scripture gives God a heart and a soul, and lets them act.  - "It grieved him to his heart" (Genesis 6:6). - "My heart recoils within me; my compassion grows warm and tender" (Hosea 11:8). - "I will rejoice in doing them good … with all my heart and all my soul" (Jeremiah 32:41). - "My soul delights" in his chosen servant (Isaiah 42:1). "My soul hates" empty feasts held with bloodied hands (Isaiah 1:14–15). - He swears "by himself" (Amos 6:8), literally by his soul. - He "does not afflict from his heart" (Lamentations 3:33). - He holds back his anger for reasons of his own: "I will not execute my burning anger … for I am God and not a man" (Hosea 11:9). - And the one place where his inner self turns away from a people is not hardness: "Though Moses and Samuel stood before me, yet my heart would not turn toward this people" (Jeremiah 15:1).  Leviticus 26 shows God's soul and the people's soul in a movement back and forth. God promises: "my soul shall not abhor you" (26:11). The people's "soul abhors my rules" (26:15). God answers in kind: "my soul will abhor you" (26:30). Then, at the end, God breaks the exchange: "Yet for all that … I will not spurn them, neither will I abhor them so as to destroy them utterly and break my covenant with them" (26:44). The same verb passes between two souls, and God refuses to return it a final time.  God also thinks and plans. "The counsel of the Lord stands forever, the plans of his heart to all generations" (Psalm 33:11). "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isaiah 55:8). Where human plans and his cross, his stand: "As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). Even a cold calculation can be taken up into his purpose. Caiaphas reckoned "that it is better for you that one man should die for the people" (John 11:50). John adds: "He did not say this of his own accord, but being high priest that year he prophesied that Jesus would die for the nation" (11:51).  And God speaks in his heart. After the flood, "the Lord said in his heart, 'I will never again curse the ground because of man, for the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth'" (Genesis 8:21). Before the flood he saw "that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (6:5), and "the Lord regretted that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him to his heart" (6:6). Now he names it again, and it is the reason he gives for holding back.  God names his heart with a place. "I have consecrated this house that you have built, by putting my name there forever. My eyes and my heart will be there for all time" (1 Kings 9:3; 13.1, *Choosing*).  
  - note: in part: God also thinks and plans, and speaks in his heart
- **C-361** telling added · 10.4 *Small, passing, and wholly seen* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Small, passing, and wholly seen  Human thought is real, and it is also small. "The Lord — knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath" (Psalm 94:11).  And none of it is hidden. - "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2). - "The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9). - He knows the inclination before it is acted on: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). - Jesus "perceived their thoughts" (Luke 5:22). - What is hidden will be brought out. Simeon says the child is set for a sign "so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed" (Luke 2:34–35).  The same psalm that says God knows my thoughts uses the same word for his thoughts: "How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!" (Psalm 139:17).  God thinks too, and his thinking is not like mine. "The Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). In the plea that Joab put in a woman's mouth to move David (2 Samuel 14:3), she says of God that "he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14). "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isaiah 55:8). Chapter 11 returns to this. 
  - note: in part: God thinks too
- **C-361** telling added · 13.1 *Purposing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Purposing  The words used for a person who plans, devises or purposes are also used of God. The verses do not give his plans as a hidden decree working out of sight. They show him forming a plan and saying it aloud, setting it against what people devise, holding it open to their turning, carrying it out, and keeping it fixed where he has sworn.  **He forms a plan and makes it known.** "Therefore hear the plan that the Lord has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman" (Jeremiah 49:20). The same words are spoken against Babylon (50:45). In both places the plan follows his question, "For who is like me? Who will summon me?" (49:19; 50:44). Of Babylon it is said that "the Lord has both planned and done what he spoke" (51:12). The verse before shows how it went forward, through other people's spirits: "The Lord has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it" (51:11). His counsel is something to be told in full. Paul counts his own innocence in not holding it back: "I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God" (Acts 20:27).  **His devising answers what people devise.** Micah speaks first of those "who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds" (Micah 2:1), who "covet fields and seize them" (2:2). Then: "Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, against this family I am devising disaster" (2:3). The verb is the same for both, and the "therefore" ties his devising to theirs. In Jeremiah his plan and theirs stand in one exchange: - He says: "Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way" (Jeremiah 18:11). - They answer: "That is in vain! We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12).  **He says what he intends so that people may turn, and he relents.** At the potter's house he says, "like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand" (Jeremiah 18:6). He sets out both directions: - "if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it" (18:8) - "if it does evil in my sight, not listening to my voice, then I will relent of the good that I had intended to do to it" (18:10)  His intention is spoken so that it can be heard. "It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them" (Jeremiah 26:3). It is written in a scroll for the same reason: "that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin" (36:3). I read these verses as saying that the hearing and turning of the people belong to what happens to the plan. The verses themselves say "it may be", and leave the outcome open.  **He also purposes and does not turn back.** "I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back" (Jeremiah 4:28). The verse before it sets a limit inside the judgment: "yet I will not make a full end" (4:27). Zechariah sets a fixed purpose for disaster beside a fixed purpose for good: "As I purposed to bring disaster to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath, and I did not relent … so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not" (Zechariah 8:14–15). When he wished to show "the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath" (Hebrews 6:17). The verses say both that he relents and that he does not relent or turn back. None of them explains how the two stand together, and I leave them as they are written.  **What he purposed is carried out, and people see afterward that it was his.** "The Lord has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago" (Lamentations 2:17). "The Lord determined to lay in ruins the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out the measuring line" (2:8).
