In Zechariah the fathers looked back and recognised it: "As the Lord of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us" (Zechariah 1:6).  **He has plans for welfare, and takes thought for the one in need.** - "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). This is said to exiles, of what will come "When seventy years are completed" (29:10). - "As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). - In the plea Joab put in her mouth (2 Samuel 14:3), the wise woman of Tekoa sets God against the fact that "We must all die": "God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14).  **His plan takes in what people do against him, and does not excuse them.** "this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men" (Acts 2:23). The plan and the guilt are in one sentence. The church, praying Psalm 2, says that those who gathered against Jesus did "whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place" (Acts 4:28). They then ask, "grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness" (4:29). Joseph says to his brothers, "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20); the same verb is used for both.  **His purpose stands before the ages and does not rest on works.** - "because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2 Timothy 1:9) - "though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (Romans 9:11) - "according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will" (Ephesians 1:11)  It is made known in Christ: "the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ" (Ephesians 1:9–10). It is "the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord" (3:11). Christ is the one "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood … to show God's righteousness" (Romans 3:25).  **The Spirit intercedes according to the will of God.** Where people do not know how to pray, the Spirit prays, and his praying is matched to God's will: "Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God" (Romans 8:26–27). The one who searches hearts knows the Spirit's mind. Paul does not say here what "mind" is, and I leave the word as he gives it.  **It is turned toward those who love him.** The next verse goes straight on: "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28).  **A person can refuse it, or serve it.** "the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves" (Luke 7:30), while the people and the tax collectors "declared God just" (7:29). "David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep" (Acts 13:36).  What these verses mean for a person is not taken up here. Each touches the inner life in its own way: - the plan spoken so that a person may hear and turn - the purpose sworn as "a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul" (Hebrews 6:19) - "when you seek me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:13) - "we do not know what to pray for as we ought" (Romans 8:26), the weakness the Spirit helps - the heart poured out "like water before the presence of the Lord" after his purpose was carried out (Lamentations 2:19) - "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zechariah 8:17), said straight after his own purposing for good  These belong with a person's own planning, in 10.7 (*Planning*).  **His purpose is spoken, and carried out by another.** The delight word is also used for his purpose. He is the one "who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'" (Isaiah 44:28), at the end of a line of sayings: "who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers" (44:26). Again: "declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it" (46:10–11). It is said to people told to "remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other" (46:9). And: "Who among them has declared these things? The Lord loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon" (48:14). I read "his purpose" there as the Lord's, carried out by the one he loves, as in 44:28; it can also be read as Cyrus's own pleasure. In each place the purpose is said aloud, set against idols that declare nothing, and done through a named man. What pleases him is what he will do.  **His word carries out what he purposes.** "For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth" (Isaiah 55:10), "so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it" (55:11). The act is the word going out and doing its work. "Purpose" is a delight word: what he delights in, his word carries out. 
  - note: in part: plans for welfare, and thought for the one in need
- **C-362** telling added · 10.7 *Planning* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Planning  A choice settles a direction. A plan carries it ahead, into a time that has not yet come. Scripture gives the inner being this power plainly. Of the builders at Babel God says, *"this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them"* (Genesis 11:6). The words for it are the words for thinking: to devise, to reckon, to purpose (10.4). They are used for a woman buying a field, a king counting his soldiers, a sailor looking for a beach, and a man plotting on his bed. This section is about the looking ahead itself. Plans made against another person are in 10.10. The next section, *Willing*, is about how a person answers what others put forward. The two often appear in the same passage.  The place of it is the heart: *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). In that one verse the plan is the person's own, and the steps are not. I read the rest of what the verses say about planning inside that verse.  **Weighing first.** Jesus asks his hearers to look ahead before they begin. "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28). A builder who lays a foundation and cannot finish is mocked: *"This man began to build and was not able to finish"* (Luke 14:30). *"Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?"* (14:31). If the answer is no, he sends for terms *"while the other is yet a great way off"* (14:32). The looking ahead here is honest about strength, and it acts early, while there is still time. Jesus uses it for following him: *"So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple"* (14:33).  The same weighing is praised in an ordinary life. The woman of Proverbs 31 *"rises while it is yet night"* (31:15). *"She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard"* (31:16). The verb for considering is a planning verb. She weighs it, and then she acts.  When something has happened that no one has seen before, the first call is to weigh it before acting. After the outrage at Gibeah, *"all who saw it said, 'Such a thing has never happened or been seen … consider it, take counsel, and speak'"* (Judges 19:30).  **Planning without knowing.** The fullest picture of planning ahead in these verses is a voyage. Paul warned the crew: *"I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss"* (Acts 27:10). They listened to the pilot and the owner instead (27:11). The plan that followed is worded with all its uncertainty: - *"the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix"* (27:12) - *"Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor"* (27:13) - after the storm, *"they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore"* (27:39)  *"on the chance that somehow"*, *"supposing"*, *"if possible"*: Luke records the planners' own sense that they could not see far. The first plan was undone by the wind (Acts 27:14). The last was undone by a reef they had not seen (27:41).  Paul plans the same way, and says so. *"I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented)"* (Romans 1:13). His intending was real and often repeated, and something outside him held it back. James says what such planning should sound like: *"If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that"* (James 4:15; see *Life and death set before a person*).  Paul's own plans are said under God's will, again and again, and his wanting stays strong inside them. - At parting: "I will return to you if God wills" (Acts 18:21), after he "declined" to stay longer (18:20). - With purpose: "I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power" (1 Corinthians 4:19). He then asks their will: "What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love?" (4:21). - With his own wish: "I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits" (16:7). - In prayer: "asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you. For I long to see you" (Romans 1:10–11); "so that by God's will I may come to you with joy" (15:32). - Hindered: "we wanted to come to you, I, Paul, again and again, but Satan hindered us" (1 Thessalonians 2:18), after "with great desire to see you face to face" (2:17). - Yielded by others: "since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, 'Let the will of the Lord be done'" (Acts 21:14), after "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?" (21:13). - A wish set beside a gift: "I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God" (1 Corinthians 7:7). The verses keep apart Paul's wanting, God's will, and what hinders, named once as Satan. I read the plan as held open toward God without the wanting being given up.  **A plan carries a person's word.** When Paul changed his travel plans, he was charged with being unreliable, and he answers with the inner question: *"Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say 'Yes, yes' and 'No, no' at the same time?"* (2 Corinthians 1:17). He rests his answer on God: *"As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No"* (1:18). In this passage, a plan is something said to others. When it changes, the change can be read as a divided heart.  **Planning together, and parting.** Plans are often made with others, and others may not agree. - Paul and Barnabas planned to revisit the churches. *"Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them"* (Acts 15:37–38). Each weighed the same past differently, and *"there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other"* (15:39). - Joseph of Arimathea sat in the council that sent Jesus to death, but he *"had not consented to their decision and action"* (Luke 23:51). He did not share their plan, and the next verse shows him acting on his own: *"This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus"* (23:52).  **Planning for another's good.** Darius *"planned to set him over the whole kingdom"* (Daniel 6:3), and the verse gives the reason: *"because an excellent spirit was in him"*. The plan for Daniel at once stirred others to look for a fault in him (6:4).  A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).  **A purpose held.** Some plans are aimed at one's own life. *"You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress"* (Psalm 17:3). The psalmist has set a course for his own speech ahead of time, and he states it under God's testing. He goes on: *"My steps have held fast to your paths"* (17:5). - Barnabas, at Antioch, *"exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose"* (Acts 11:23). The verse says what moved him: he *"saw the grace of God"* and *"was glad"*. - Paul lists his *"aim in life"* among what Timothy had followed, beside *"my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness"* (2 Timothy 3:10). - David prays that God will keep what the people have set: *"keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you"* (1 Chronicles 29:18). He asks God to hold the purpose in place. - Paul uses a purpose word for where the mind is set: *"to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace"* (Romans 8:6). *"For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"* (8:7). Chapter 7 gives the flesh. - The verb of the same word names a mind set downward: *"their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things"* (Philippians 3:19). The next verse turns it: *"But our citizenship is in heaven"* (3:20). And the call uses the same verb: *"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth"* (Colossians 3:2). - *"You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you"* (Isaiah 26:3).  **Devised from one's own heart.** A plan can begin in the self and stay there. Jeroboam set up his own feast *"in the month that he had devised from his own heart"* (1 Kings 12:33). The month was his own invention, set against the feast in Judah (12:32). Nehemiah said to the plotters, *"No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Nehemiah 6:8). The same capacity that looks ahead can make up what is not there (10.4, *Imagination that makes gods*).  **The plan and its outcome.** The verses do not let a plan secure its own end. - *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). - *"Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us"* (Isaiah 8:10). - Gamaliel, of the apostles: *"if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them"* (Acts 5:38–39). - Of those who plot against the king: *"Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed"* (Psalm 21:11). Of a king's plans against strongholds: *"but only for a time"* (Daniel 11:24). The next verse says what he roused for it: *"he shall stir up his power and his heart"* (11:25). The heart is stirred up as a resource for war. - Counsel that cannot save: *"You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you … No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!"* (Isaiah 47:13–14). Many counsels weary the one who keeps them, and they give no warmth. - Joseph, of his brothers: *"you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"* (Genesis 50:20). The same verb is used of both.  The verses also show that what a person intends is seen before it is done and will be shown in full. *"The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (1 Chronicles 28:9). The Lord *"will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart"* (1 Corinthians 4:5). Paul draws a warning from it for himself: *"do not pronounce judgment before the time"* (4:5). He has just said, *"I do not even judge myself"* (4:3).  Joseph's counsel to Pharaoh plans against a famine he has been shown. "Let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man", gather the food of the good years "under the authority of Pharaoh", and keep it as "a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine", "so that the land may not perish" (Genesis 41:33–36). "This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants" (41:37).  
  - note: in part: devised from one's own heart
- **C-362** telling added · 12 *Idols taken inside* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Idols taken inside  Idolatry is not only a matter of statues. God says to Ezekiel of Israel's elders, "these men have taken their idols into their hearts" (Ezekiel 14:3). Their hearts "went after their idols" (Ezekiel 20:16). And Hosea: "a spirit of whoredom has led them astray" (Hosea 4:12). "The spirit of whoredom is within them, and they know not the Lord" (Hosea 5:4).  It also starts in the power to imagine and design. Paul says, "we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man" (Acts 17:29). Habakkuk sees the maker turned upside down: "its maker trusts in his own creation when he makes speechless idols!" (Habakkuk 2:18). The word for "creation" there is the word for the heart's inclination (Chapter 10.4).  Isaiah first says what the delight comes to: *"All who fashion idols are nothing, and the things they delight in do not profit. Their witnesses neither see nor know, that they may be put to shame"* (Isaiah 44:9).  Isaiah shows the man who makes one: "He takes a part of it and warms himself; he kindles a fire and bakes bread. Also he makes a god and worships it" (Isaiah 44:15). "Also he warms himself and says, 'Aha, I am warm, I have seen the fire!' And the rest of it he makes into a god, his idol, and falls down to it and worships it" (44:16–17). The same log gives him comfort and a god. The prophet says what is inside: "No one considers, nor is there knowledge or discernment" (44:19); "a deluded heart has led him astray, and he cannot deliver himself or say, 'Is there not a lie in my right hand?'" (44:20). A body satisfied and a heart deceived stand in one man. He is pleased with the warmth and does not see what he has done with the rest. Babylon's counsellors are the same kind of fire: "No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!" (47:14). 
  - note: in part: the power to imagine and design
- **C-362** telling added · 10.4 *When thinking changes character* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## When thinking changes character  Again and again in these words I found the same thought becoming something else.  **One word, three faces: *mᵊzimmāh*.** - In the young it is discretion: "to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the youth" (Proverbs 1:4). It "will watch over you" (2:11). - In the wicked it is an evil device, joined to arrogance: "In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor; let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised" (Psalm 10:2). It sits beside a short temper: "A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated" (Proverbs 14:17). - In God it is purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2). His anger serves it, and it is understood only later: "The anger of the Lord will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jeremiah 23:20).  **One passage, three plans: Jeremiah 18.** - God says, "Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way" (18:11). Even this plan is open: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it" (18:8). - The people answer, "We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12). - Then they turn on the messenger: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18).  God's plan is *against*, and in the same breath he says "Return" (Jeremiah 18:11). The people's plans are, in their own words, "the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12). The word "against" is the same in God's plan and in their plot.  **What it keeps company with.** Plans fail alone and stand with counsel: "Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed" (Proverbs 15:22). "Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established" (16:3). The same togetherness can go the other way: "All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me" (Psalm 41:7).  **The state it rises from.** Paul names the order of cause in so many words: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). A hard heart makes for dark thinking. Ease does it too: "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune; it is ready for those whose feet slip" (Job 12:5). A comfortable mind looks down on those who fall.  **Its pace.** "The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). Haste is named again in Job 20:2 (below).  **Where it is done.** Thinking alone can stall. "When I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:16–17). The bed, as I show below, is a place that holds both ways of thinking.  **Reasoning that becomes a quarrel.** The Greek word for inner reasoning is also the word for a quarrel. The disciples' reasoning about greatness became an argument: "An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child" (Luke 9:46–47). Paul uses the word for dispute: "Do all things without grumbling or disputing" (Philippians 2:14). And he uses it beside anger: men are to pray "lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1 Timothy 2:8).  **Imagination that makes gods.** The power to design can be turned to making a god: "we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man" (Acts 17:29).  None of these is a rule I have laid on the verses. They are what the verses themselves put beside the change. Chapter 11 gathers them across all the activities. 
  - note: in part: imagination that makes gods
- **C-363** telling added · 10.4 *Small, passing, and wholly seen* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Small, passing, and wholly seen  Human thought is real, and it is also small. "The Lord — knows the thoughts of man, that they are but a breath" (Psalm 94:11).  And none of it is hidden. - "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2). - "The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought" (1 Chronicles 28:9). - He knows the inclination before it is acted on: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). - Jesus "perceived their thoughts" (Luke 5:22). - What is hidden will be brought out. Simeon says the child is set for a sign "so that thoughts from many hearts may be revealed" (Luke 2:34–35).  The same psalm that says God knows my thoughts uses the same word for his thoughts: "How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!" (Psalm 139:17).  God thinks too, and his thinking is not like mine. "The Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). In the plea that Joab put in a woman's mouth to move David (2 Samuel 14:3), she says of God that "he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14). "My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways" (Isaiah 55:8). Chapter 11 returns to this. 
  - note: in part: none of it is hidden
- **C-363** telling added · 04 *The heart is hidden, and God sees it* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## The heart is hidden, and God sees it  "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9). "The heart knows its own bitterness, and no stranger shares its joy" (Proverbs 14:10). Other people cannot fully see into it, and often its owner cannot either. But "man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). The word corrects a prophet. Samuel had looked on Eliab and "thought, 'Surely the Lord's anointed is before him'" (16:6). The one sent to choose formed his thought from what he saw. God is the one who "knows the secrets of the heart" (Psalm 44:21). "You discern my thoughts from afar" (Psalm 139:2). He knows the heart's leaning before it acts: "I know what they are inclined to do even today" (Deuteronomy 31:21). He tests it and weighs it: "the Lord weighs the heart" (Proverbs 21:2). People try to hide what the heart holds, and Isaiah answers them: "Ah, you who hide deep from the Lord your counsel … and who say, 'Who sees us? Who knows us?' You turn things upside down!" (Isaiah 29:15–16). Section 10.11 follows hiding and disclosing.  The heart can lead a person away from life itself. "Take care, brothers, lest there be in any of you an evil, unbelieving heart, leading you to fall away from the living God" (Hebrews 3:12). Paul traces being "alienated from the life of God" to "the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). Chapter 2 ("Living before God", "Death in the living") gives the setting.  The heart is tied to life and death in plain words. "The lips of the righteous feed many, but fools die for lack of sense" (Proverbs 10:21). The word for "sense" there is *heart*. "Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit! Why will you die, O house of Israel?" (Ezekiel 18:31). And what is believed in the heart is that God raised Jesus "from the dead" (Romans 10:9). Of the heart after death, I have found nothing (Chapter 2, "Soul, spirit and heart at death"). 
  - note: in part: he knows the heart's leaning before it acts

The verse says what moved him: he *"saw the grace of God"* and *"was glad"*. - Paul lists his *"aim in life"* among what Timothy had followed, beside *"my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness"* (2 Timothy 3:10). - David prays that God will keep what the people have set: *"keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you"* (1 Chronicles 29:18). He asks God to hold the purpose in place. - Paul uses a purpose word for where the mind is set: *"to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace"* (Romans 8:6). *"For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"* (8:7). Chapter 7 gives the flesh. - The verb of the same word names a mind set downward: *"their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things"* (Philippians 3:19). The next verse turns it: *"But our citizenship is in heaven"* (3:20). And the call uses the same verb: *"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth"* (Colossians 3:2). - *"You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you"* (Isaiah 26:3).  **Devised from one's own heart.** A plan can begin in the self and stay there. Jeroboam set up his own feast *"in the month that he had devised from his own heart"* (1 Kings 12:33). The month was his own invention, set against the feast in Judah (12:32). Nehemiah said to the plotters, *"No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Nehemiah 6:8). The same capacity that looks ahead can make up what is not there (10.4, *Imagination that makes gods*).  **The plan and its outcome.** The verses do not let a plan secure its own end. - *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). - *"Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us"* (Isaiah 8:10). - Gamaliel, of the apostles: *"if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them"* (Acts 5:38–39). - Of those who plot against the king: *"Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed"* (Psalm 21:11). Of a king's plans against strongholds: *"but only for a time"* (Daniel 11:24). The next verse says what he roused for it: *"he shall stir up his power and his heart"* (11:25). The heart is stirred up as a resource for war. - Counsel that cannot save: *"You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you … No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!"* (Isaiah 47:13–14). Many counsels weary the one who keeps them, and they give no warmth. - Joseph, of his brothers: *"you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"* (Genesis 50:20). The same verb is used of both.  The verses also show that what a person intends is seen before it is done and will be shown in full. *"The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (1 Chronicles 28:9). The Lord *"will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart"* (1 Corinthians 4:5). Paul draws a warning from it for himself: *"do not pronounce judgment before the time"* (4:5). He has just said, *"I do not even judge myself"* (4:3).  Joseph's counsel to Pharaoh plans against a famine he has been shown. "Let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man", gather the food of the good years "under the authority of Pharaoh", and keep it as "a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine", "so that the land may not perish" (Genesis 41:33–36). "This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants" (41:37).

- **C-364** telling added · 10.7 *Planning* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Planning  A choice settles a direction. A plan carries it ahead, into a time that has not yet come. Scripture gives the inner being this power plainly. Of the builders at Babel God says, *"this is only the beginning of what they will do. And nothing that they propose to do will now be impossible for them"* (Genesis 11:6). The words for it are the words for thinking: to devise, to reckon, to purpose (10.4). They are used for a woman buying a field, a king counting his soldiers, a sailor looking for a beach, and a man plotting on his bed. This section is about the looking ahead itself. Plans made against another person are in 10.10. The next section, *Willing*, is about how a person answers what others put forward. The two often appear in the same passage.  The place of it is the heart: *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). In that one verse the plan is the person's own, and the steps are not. I read the rest of what the verses say about planning inside that verse.  **Weighing first.** Jesus asks his hearers to look ahead before they begin. "For which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?" (Luke 14:28). A builder who lays a foundation and cannot finish is mocked: *"This man began to build and was not able to finish"* (Luke 14:30). *"Or what king, going out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand?"* (14:31). If the answer is no, he sends for terms *"while the other is yet a great way off"* (14:32). The looking ahead here is honest about strength, and it acts early, while there is still time. Jesus uses it for following him: *"So therefore, any one of you who does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple"* (14:33).  The same weighing is praised in an ordinary life. The woman of Proverbs 31 *"rises while it is yet night"* (31:15). *"She considers a field and buys it; with the fruit of her hands she plants a vineyard"* (31:16). The verb for considering is a planning verb. She weighs it, and then she acts.  When something has happened that no one has seen before, the first call is to weigh it before acting. After the outrage at Gibeah, *"all who saw it said, 'Such a thing has never happened or been seen … consider it, take counsel, and speak'"* (Judges 19:30).  **Planning without knowing.** The fullest picture of planning ahead in these verses is a voyage. Paul warned the crew: *"I perceive that the voyage will be with injury and much loss"* (Acts 27:10). They listened to the pilot and the owner instead (27:11). The plan that followed is worded with all its uncertainty: - *"the majority decided to put out to sea from there, on the chance that somehow they could reach Phoenix"* (27:12) - *"Now when the south wind blew gently, supposing that they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor"* (27:13) - after the storm, *"they noticed a bay with a beach, on which they planned if possible to run the ship ashore"* (27:39)  *"on the chance that somehow"*, *"supposing"*, *"if possible"*: Luke records the planners' own sense that they could not see far. The first plan was undone by the wind (Acts 27:14). The last was undone by a reef they had not seen (27:41).  Paul plans the same way, and says so. *"I have often intended to come to you (but thus far have been prevented)"* (Romans 1:13). His intending was real and often repeated, and something outside him held it back. James says what such planning should sound like: *"If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that"* (James 4:15; see *Life and death set before a person*).  Paul's own plans are said under God's will, again and again, and his wanting stays strong inside them. - At parting: "I will return to you if God wills" (Acts 18:21), after he "declined" to stay longer (18:20). - With purpose: "I will come to you soon, if the Lord wills, and I will find out not the talk of these arrogant people but their power" (1 Corinthians 4:19). He then asks their will: "What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or with love?" (4:21). - With his own wish: "I do not want to see you now just in passing. I hope to spend some time with you, if the Lord permits" (16:7). - In prayer: "asking that somehow by God's will I may now at last succeed in coming to you. For I long to see you" (Romans 1:10–11); "so that by God's will I may come to you with joy" (15:32). - Hindered: "we wanted to come to you, I, Paul, again and again, but Satan hindered us" (1 Thessalonians 2:18), after "with great desire to see you face to face" (2:17). - Yielded by others: "since he would not be persuaded, we ceased and said, 'Let the will of the Lord be done'" (Acts 21:14), after "What are you doing, weeping and breaking my heart?" (21:13). - A wish set beside a gift: "I wish that all were as I myself am. But each has his own gift from God" (1 Corinthians 7:7). The verses keep apart Paul's wanting, God's will, and what hinders, named once as Satan. I read the plan as held open toward God without the wanting being given up.  **A plan carries a person's word.** When Paul changed his travel plans, he was charged with being unreliable, and he answers with the inner question: *"Was I vacillating when I wanted to do this? Do I make my plans according to the flesh, ready to say 'Yes, yes' and 'No, no' at the same time?"* (2 Corinthians 1:17). He rests his answer on God: *"As surely as God is faithful, our word to you has not been Yes and No"* (1:18). In this passage, a plan is something said to others. When it changes, the change can be read as a divided heart.  **Planning together, and parting.** Plans are often made with others, and others may not agree. - Paul and Barnabas planned to revisit the churches. *"Barnabas wanted to take with them John called Mark. But Paul thought best not to take with them one who had withdrawn from them"* (Acts 15:37–38). Each weighed the same past differently, and *"there arose a sharp disagreement, so that they separated from each other"* (15:39). - Joseph of Arimathea sat in the council that sent Jesus to death, but he *"had not consented to their decision and action"* (Luke 23:51). He did not share their plan, and the next verse shows him acting on his own: *"This man went to Pilate and asked for the body of Jesus"* (23:52).  **Planning for another's good.** Darius *"planned to set him over the whole kingdom"* (Daniel 6:3), and the verse gives the reason: *"because an excellent spirit was in him"*. The plan for Daniel at once stirred others to look for a fault in him (6:4).  A plan can also be held against someone's good without anyone calling it a plot. Joab knew *"that the king's heart went out to Absalom"* (2 Samuel 14:1). He sent a wise woman of Tekoa with a staged plea, and *"put the words in her mouth"* (14:3). In it she told David that by leaving Absalom in exile he had *"planned such a thing against the people of God"* (14:13). Beside it she set God, who *"devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast"* (14:14). David saw whose plan it was: *"Is the hand of Joab with you in all this?"* (14:19). Three are at work in the one passage: Joab's scheme, the king's planning, and God's devising as she declares it. The king's planning is measured against God's (13.1, *Purposing*).  **A purpose held.** Some plans are aimed at one's own life. *"You have tried my heart, you have visited me by night, you have tested me, and you will find nothing; I have purposed that my mouth will not transgress"* (Psalm 17:3). The psalmist has set a course for his own speech ahead of time, and he states it under God's testing. He goes on: *"My steps have held fast to your paths"* (17:5). - Barnabas, at Antioch, *"exhorted them all to remain faithful to the Lord with steadfast purpose"* (Acts 11:23). The verse says what moved him: he *"saw the grace of God"* and *"was glad"*. - Paul lists his *"aim in life"* among what Timothy had followed, beside *"my faith, my patience, my love, my steadfastness"* (2 Timothy 3:10). - David prays that God will keep what the people have set: *"keep forever such purposes and thoughts in the hearts of your people, and direct their hearts toward you"* (1 Chronicles 29:18). He asks God to hold the purpose in place. - Paul uses a purpose word for where the mind is set: *"to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace"* (Romans 8:6). *"For the mind that is set on the flesh is hostile to God"* (8:7). Chapter 7 gives the flesh. - The verb of the same word names a mind set downward: *"their god is their belly, and they glory in their shame, with minds set on earthly things"* (Philippians 3:19). The next verse turns it: *"But our citizenship is in heaven"* (3:20). And the call uses the same verb: *"Set your minds on things that are above, not on things that are on earth"* (Colossians 3:2). - *"You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you"* (Isaiah 26:3).  **Devised from one's own heart.** A plan can begin in the self and stay there. Jeroboam set up his own feast *"in the month that he had devised from his own heart"* (1 Kings 12:33). The month was his own invention, set against the feast in Judah (12:32). Nehemiah said to the plotters, *"No such things as you say have been done, for you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Nehemiah 6:8). The same capacity that looks ahead can make up what is not there (10.4, *Imagination that makes gods*).  **The plan and its outcome.** The verses do not let a plan secure its own end. - *"The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps"* (Proverbs 16:9). - *"Take counsel together, but it will come to nothing; speak a word, but it will not stand, for God is with us"* (Isaiah 8:10). - Gamaliel, of the apostles: *"if this plan or this undertaking is of man, it will fail; but if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow them"* (Acts 5:38–39). - Of those who plot against the king: *"Though they plan evil against you, though they devise mischief, they will not succeed"* (Psalm 21:11). Of a king's plans against strongholds: *"but only for a time"* (Daniel 11:24). The next verse says what he roused for it: *"he shall stir up his power and his heart"* (11:25). The heart is stirred up as a resource for war. - Counsel that cannot save: *"You are wearied with your many counsels; let them stand forth and save you … No coal for warming oneself is this, no fire to sit before!"* (Isaiah 47:13–14). Many counsels weary the one who keeps them, and they give no warmth. - Joseph, of his brothers: *"you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"* (Genesis 50:20). The same verb is used of both.  The verses also show that what a person intends is seen before it is done and will be shown in full. *"The Lord searches all hearts and understands every plan and thought"* (1 Chronicles 28:9). The Lord *"will bring to light the things now hidden in darkness and will disclose the purposes of the heart"* (1 Corinthians 4:5). Paul draws a warning from it for himself: *"do not pronounce judgment before the time"* (4:5). He has just said, *"I do not even judge myself"* (4:3).  Joseph's counsel to Pharaoh plans against a famine he has been shown. "Let Pharaoh select a discerning and wise man", gather the food of the good years "under the authority of Pharaoh", and keep it as "a reserve for the land against the seven years of famine", "so that the land may not perish" (Genesis 41:33–36). "This proposal pleased Pharaoh and all his servants" (41:37).

- **C-365** telling added · 10.4 *What thinking does* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## What thinking does  **It designs.** The verb for devising is used of the craftsmen who worked the cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1), and of people who plot. One word, *mᵊzimmāh*, covers both: "discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11), and "a man of evil devices he condemns" (Proverbs 12:2).  The same skill is put to different uses: - The tabernacle craftsmen were given it for God's house (Exodus 35:35). Huram-abi, sent to Solomon for the temple, was trained "to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him" (2 Chronicles 2:14). His skill was to carry out a design another gave him. - King Uzziah's engineers turned it to war: "he made machines, invented by skillful men … And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong" (2 Chronicles 26:15). The next verse: "But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (26:16). - Those "at ease in Zion" (Amos 6:1) turned it on themselves: they "like David invent for themselves instruments of music" (6:5).  **It reckons**, giving things their worth. People reckon wrongly. - Judah "thought she was a prostitute" (Genesis 38:15). - Eli watched Hannah praying silently and "took her to be a drunken woman" (1 Samuel 1:13). - A whole people looked at the servant of the Lord and "esteemed him not … we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted" (Isaiah 53:3–4). - A price can be set on a person, and called lordly in irony: "Then the Lord said to me, 'Throw it to the potter'—the lordly price at which I was priced by them" (Zechariah 11:13). It was thirty pieces of silver (11:12). Matthew reads it of the silver Judas brought back when he "changed his mind": "the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel" (Matthew 27:3, 9). - Opponents reckon the worst: "some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh" (2 Corinthians 10:2). - People reckon by the surface: "Even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise" (Proverbs 17:28). Even a good act can be reckoned by its manner: "Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing" (27:14). - A people at ease can be made to reckon itself: "Pass over to Calneh, and see … Are you better than these kingdoms? Or is their territory greater than your territory" (Amos 6:2), said to those "at ease in Zion" (6:1) who "put far away the day of disaster" (6:3). - A father can reckon his own daughters as strangers. Rachel and Leah: "Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us" (Genesis 31:15). - What is precious can be reckoned cheap: "The precious sons of Zion, worth their weight in fine gold, how they are regarded as earthen pots, the work of a potter's hands!" (Lamentations 4:2). - When a land breaks down, regard for people goes with it: "Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man" (Isaiah 33:8). The Medes are named by what they do not value: they "have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold" (13:17), and the next verse says "they will have no mercy" (13:18).  Being reckoned is felt from the inside. - "Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered" (Psalm 44:22). - "I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength" (Psalm 88:4). The verse before says, "my soul is full of troubles" (88:3). - A people can reckon itself apart. Balaam, sent to curse, sees "a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations!" (Numbers 23:9). - Being reckoned trustworthy carries a charge. Nehemiah appointed treasurers "for they were considered reliable, and their duty was to distribute to their brothers" (Nehemiah 13:13). - A man can be reckoned worthy by others and reckon himself not. The elders said of the centurion, "He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation" (Luke 7:4–5). He sent word, "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed" (7:6–7). Jesus "marveled at him" (7:9).  God reckons truly. - Abraham "believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). - The nations "are accounted as the dust on the scales" (Isaiah 40:15). Yet the same God "takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17).  Jesus took the wrong reckoning on himself: "this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: 'And he was numbered with the transgressors'" (Luke 22:37). And reckoning is not mine to turn toward myself: "Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God" (2 Corinthians 3:5).  Reckoning is not only about judging. In the law it serves **release**: the man who sold himself "shall calculate with his buyer from the year when he sold himself to him until the year of jubilee" (Leviticus 25:50), and pay his way free. And there are times when reckoning is laid aside because there is trust: "they did not ask for an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money … for they dealt honestly" (2 Kings 12:15).  The Greek word carries this on. "I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us" (Romans 8:18). And faith is itself a reckoning: Abraham "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19). Paul says the same of Abraham before his own body: "He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb" (Romans 4:19).  Reckoning from what God has done can answer a fear of dying. Manoah said, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God." His wife answered, "If the Lord had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things" (Judges 13:22–23). Chapter 2 follows the fear of dying.  **It likens.** The Hebrew *dāmāh* means both "to be like" and "to think". - Mordecai warns Esther, "Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews" (Esther 4:13). - Worshippers say, "We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple" (Psalm 48:9). - Love likens: "I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots" (Song of Songs 1:9). - Comfort tries to liken, and sometimes cannot: "What can I say for you, to what compare you, O daughter of Jerusalem? What can I liken to you, that I may comfort you …? For your ruin is vast as the sea; who can heal you?" (Lamentations 2:13).  - Lament likens the self truly: "I am like a desert owl of the wilderness" (Psalm 102:6). - God himself teaches by likening: "through the prophets gave parables" (Hosea 12:10).  Likening can go badly wrong. God says, "you thought that I was one like yourself" (Psalm 50:21). Chapter 12 follows this further.  **It murmurs.** *Hāgāh* is the word for meditating, and it is not silent. "On his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6). But the same word devises and plots: "their hearts devise violence" (Proverbs 24:2). And it can "meditate treachery all day long" (Psalm 38:12). Chapter 10.5 picks up its sense of uttering.  **It reasons, inside and between.** The Greek word for reasoning is used for a single heart talking to itself and for people talking together, with no change of word. - Inside: a thought can be a whole sentence. "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 10:4). Jesus perceived "that they thus questioned within themselves" (Mark 2:8). The rich man "thought to himself, 'What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?'" (Luke 12:17). - Between: "What were you discussing on the way?" (Mark 9:33).  **It can be troubled.** Mary "was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be" (Luke 1:29). She is trying to understand. The disciples' worried reasoning about bread is different. "Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened?" (Mark 8:17). Jesus connects it with a hard heart and "little faith" (Matthew 16:8).  Thinking can weigh answers by their cost, not by their truth. Asked by what authority he acted, Jesus asked in return, "The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" "And they discussed it among themselves, saying, 'If we say, From heaven, he will say to us, Why then did you not believe him? But if we say, From man, we are afraid of the crowd'" (Matthew 21:25–26). They answered, "We do not know" (21:27). Both answers were weighed against what each would cost them (10.12, 10.11).  A wrong expectation can be what a teaching answers. Jesus told the parable of the nobleman and the minas "because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately" (Luke 19:11).  
  - note: in part: it designs
- **C-366** telling added · 10.4 *Where thoughts come from* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Where thoughts come from  They come from the heart. "For from within, out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts" (Mark 7:21). "The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9).  They are not always chosen. Often they simply **arise**, and often at night. - "To you, O king, as you lay in bed came thoughts of what would be after this, and he who reveals mysteries made known to you what is to be" (Daniel 2:29). - "Amid thoughts from visions of the night, when deep sleep falls on men" (Job 4:13). - Jesus asks his frightened disciples, "Why are you troubled, and why do doubts arise in your hearts?" (Luke 24:38). - Of Gog: "thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme" (Ezekiel 38:10). The thought arrives first, and the devising follows it. 10.10 follows where that scheme was aimed.  What arises has also been **shaped from outside**. - God fills craftsmen "with skill" (Exodus 35:35) "to devise artistic designs" (35:32). - Instruction forms thinking: "discretion will watch over you, understanding will guard you" (Proverbs 2:11). - Thinking can also be darkened. People who knew God "became futile in their thinking, and their foolish hearts were darkened" (Romans 1:21). "The god of this world has blinded the minds of the unbelievers" (2 Corinthians 4:4). The enemy has thoughts of his own, and the word for them is the word for ours: "we are not ignorant of his designs" (2 Corinthians 2:11). The serpent's cunning can lead thoughts "astray from a sincere and pure devotion to Christ" (2 Corinthians 11:3). Yet the same mind can be guarded: "the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus" (Philippians 4:7).  A thought can be answered by God. To the elders who came "to inquire of the Lord" (Ezekiel 20:1), he names what is in them: "What is in your mind shall never happen—the thought, 'Let us be like the nations, like the tribes of the countries, and worship wood and stone.'" And he answers it with an oath by his own life: "As I live, declares the Lord God, surely with a mighty hand and an outstretched arm and with wrath poured out I will be king over you" (20:32–33; 13.1). 
  - note: in part: they arise; shaped from outside

  - note: in part: they come from the heart
- **C-367** telling added · 04 *The heart thinks, attends and remembers* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## The heart thinks, attends and remembers  Much of what we would call the mind, Scripture calls the heart. Here I am concerned with the heart as the *place* of thinking. What thinking itself does (arising, weighing, devising, meditating) I take up in Chapter 10.4.  - **It plans.** "The heart of man plans his way, but the Lord establishes his steps" (Proverbs 16:9). "Many are the plans in the mind [heart] of a man, but it is the purpose of the Lord that will stand" (Proverbs 19:21). - **It understands.** Solomon asks for "an understanding mind" (1 Kings 3:9). The Hebrew is a *hearing heart*. The prophets speak of people who will not "understand with their hearts" (Isaiah 6:10; Matthew 13:15). - **It pays attention.** To pay attention is literally to *set the heart*. Haggai's "Consider your ways" (Haggai 1:5) is literally *set your heart on your ways*. The Preacher "applied my heart to seek and to search out" (Ecclesiastes 1:13). The failure is its opposite: "it burned him up, but he did not take it to heart" (Isaiah 42:25). - **It remembers and holds.** "I have stored up your word in my heart" (Psalm 119:11). Mary "treasured up all these things, pondering them in her heart" (Luke 2:19). Mary's second treasuring comes straight after a saying she "did not understand" (2:50–51). Earlier, at the angel's greeting, she "was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be" (Luke 1:29). Daniel, alarmed by his vision, "kept the matter in my heart" (Daniel 7:28). - **It watches what people do with power.** "All this I observed while applying my heart to all that is done under the sun, when man had power over man to his hurt" (Ecclesiastes 8:9). 
  - note: in part: it plans
- **C-368** telling added · 10.4 *The night and the bed* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## The night and the bed  The bed is where several kinds of thinking happen. - People plot there: "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). - Unbidden thoughts come there, and God's revealing with them (Daniel 2:29). - The psalmist meditates on God there (Psalm 63:6). - The angry are told: "ponder in your own hearts on your beds, and be silent" (Psalm 4:4).  Night thoughts are not all the same. For Nebuchadnezzar they became revelation, because God made them known and Daniel interpreted them (Daniel 2:29–30). For Belshazzar, with no one to read the writing, they only frightened: "his thoughts alarmed him" (Daniel 5:6), until the queen pointed to the one who could "show the interpretation" (5:12). And a night thought can be claimed as revelation and still be wrong. Eliphaz tells of "thoughts from visions of the night" (Job 4:13). At the end God says to him, "you have not spoken of me what is right" (Job 42:7).  What fills the heart in the night shows by morning. "Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it" (Micah 2:1). 
  - note: in full
- **C-369** telling added · 10.4 *The inclination: a shaped thing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## The inclination: a shaped thing  The word behind "every *intention* of the thoughts of his heart" (Genesis 6:5) is *yēṣer*. It is the same word Isaiah uses for what a potter makes: "the thing formed say of him who formed it, 'He has no understanding'" (Isaiah 29:16). And it is the word in "he knows our *frame*; he remembers that we are dust" (Psalm 103:14).  The inclination in Genesis 6:5 is "only evil continually". The ESV renders the same word "mind" in a promise: "You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you" (Isaiah 26:3).  The word can be turned upside down from either end. In Isaiah, the thing formed says its maker has no understanding. In Habakkuk, the maker trusts the thing he formed: "its maker trusts in his own creation when he makes speechless idols!" (Habakkuk 2:18). And God's knowing of my frame does not end in contempt. The verse before says, "As a father shows compassion to his children, so the Lord shows compassion to those who fear him" (Psalm 103:13). 
  - note: in full
- **C-369** telling added · 12 *The heart as the source* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## The heart as the source  - "The Lord saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5). - "The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately sick; who can understand it?" (Jeremiah 17:9). - "For out of the heart come evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false witness, slander" (Matthew 15:19). What defiles comes "from within, out of the heart of man" (Mark 7:21). - "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron; with a point of diamond it is engraved on the tablet of their heart" (Jeremiah 17:1). - "Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in his heart" (Psalm 36:1).  The word translated "intention" in Genesis 6:5 is *yēṣer*: the inclination or shape of the heart (Chapter 10.4). It returns straight after the flood: "the intention of man's heart is evil from his youth" (Genesis 8:21). But there God says it in his heart as the reason he will not curse the ground again. Scripture sets the evil inclination beside God's forbearance, not only beside his judgement. I do not want to quote Genesis 6:5 without 8:21.  The heart is the place where wrongdoing starts, is stored and is written. It is also where God looks when he judges: "I the Lord search the heart and test the mind" (Jeremiah 17:10).  The psalm names the inner self with a word that elsewhere means desire: *"there is no truth in their mouth; their inmost self is destruction; their throat is an open grave; they flatter with their tongue"* (Psalm 5:9). In Proverbs the same word is the captor: *"the treacherous are taken captive by their lust"* (Proverbs 11:6; 10.6).  The Preacher says the heart's state lasts as long as the life: "the hearts of the children of man are full of evil, and madness is in their hearts while they live, and after that they go to the dead" (Ecclesiastes 9:3). The psalmist asks not to be judged, "for no one living is righteous before you" (Psalm 143:2). Paul traces a life cut off from God to the heart: "alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). Chapter 2 ("Life weighed", "Death in the living") gives the setting. 
  - note: in part: the word translated intention is yetser
- **C-370** telling added · 10.0 *From a thought to a deed* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## From a thought to a deed  Read side by side, the verses trace a path.  1. **Thoughts arise.** "To you, O king, as you lay in bed came thoughts of what would be after this" (Daniel 2:29). "Why do doubts arise in your hearts?" (Luke 24:38). 2. **They lodge.** "How long shall your wicked thoughts lodge within you?" (Jeremiah 4:14). 3. **They weigh and judge.** "We esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted" (Isaiah 53:4). 4. **They take the shape of a plan.** "He plots trouble while on his bed" (Psalm 36:4). 5. **They reach the tongue, the lips and the eyes.** "Your tongue plots destruction" (Psalm 52:2). "Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass" (Proverbs 16:30). 6. **They reach the hand and the feet.** "Woe to those who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds! When the morning dawns, they perform it, because it is in the power of their hand" (Micah 2:1). "A heart that devises wicked plans, feet that make haste to run to evil" (Proverbs 6:18). "Their feet run to evil … their thoughts are thoughts of iniquity" (Isaiah 59:7).  No single verse lists these six steps. The order is my reading of many verses together. But the stories show the path being walked. - David "said in his heart, 'Now I shall perish one day by the hand of Saul. There is nothing better for me than that I should escape to the land of the Philistines'" (1 Samuel 27:1). And he went. - Jeroboam "said in his heart, 'Now the kingdom will turn back to the house of David'" (1 Kings 12:26). Two verses later, "the king took counsel and made two calves of gold" (12:28). A private sentence became a nation's idolatry. - The tenants in the parable reason it through together: "they said to themselves, 'This is the heir. Let us kill him, so that the inheritance may be ours'" (Luke 20:14).  The same path runs toward good. - "When I think on my ways, I turn my feet to your testimonies" (Psalm 119:59). The thinking reaches the feet. - Joshua is told to meditate on the law day and night "so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it" (Joshua 1:8).  There can be a pause on the path, and the pause matters: "The heart of the righteous ponders how to answer, but the mouth of the wicked pours out evil things" (Proverbs 15:28).  **What lodges is not always a plan.** Thoughts that lodge can also act back on the person who holds them. "My thoughts answer me, because of my haste within me" (Job 20:2). "My thoughts greatly alarmed me, and my color changed, but I kept the matter in my heart" (Daniel 7:28). Daniel's thoughts stayed with him, but they did not move on toward a deed. He kept them. So the second step can be a lodging that plots, or a keeping that waits. 
  - note: in full
- **C-370** telling added · 10.5 *The tongue, the lips and the eyes devise* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## The tongue, the lips and the eyes devise  Several verses give the tongue, the lips and the eyes the verbs of planning. - "Your tongue plots destruction, like a sharp razor, you worker of deceit" (Psalm 52:2). - "They do not speak peace, but against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit" (Psalm 35:20). - "Whoever winks his eyes plans dishonest things; he who purses his lips brings evil to pass" (Proverbs 16:30). - "All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me" (Psalm 41:7). - Jeremiah's enemies: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah … let us strike him with the tongue" (Jeremiah 18:18). 
  - note: in full
- **C-371** telling added · 10.0 *Where I am answerable* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Where I am answerable  The commands meet this path from the second step onward. - "Let the wicked forsake his way, and the unrighteous man his thoughts" (Isaiah 55:7). - "Let none of you devise evil against another in your heart" (Zechariah 7:10). - "Do not say in your heart … 'It is because of my righteousness'" (Deuteronomy 9:4). - "Take every thought captive to obey Christ" (2 Corinthians 10:5). - "Wash your heart from evil" (Jeremiah 4:14).  I have found no command about what first arises. But what arises is not neutral. "Every intention of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually" (Genesis 6:5). "Out of the heart of man, come evil thoughts" (Mark 7:21). The commands address what lodges, what is planned, what is said and what is done.  Scripture does more than command. It also answers the sentence the heart speaks. "If you say in your heart, 'These nations are greater than I. How can I dispossess them?' you shall not be afraid of them but you shall remember what the Lord your God did to Pharaoh and to all Egypt" (Deuteronomy 7:17–18). The answer to a fearful inner sentence is a remembered act of God. 
  - note: in full
- **C-372** telling added · 10.4 *What thinking does* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## What thinking does  **It designs.** The verb for devising is used of the craftsmen who worked the cherubim "skillfully" into the tabernacle curtains (Exodus 26:1), and of people who plot. One word, *mᵊzimmāh*, covers both: "discretion will watch over you" (Proverbs 2:11), and "a man of evil devices he condemns" (Proverbs 12:2).  The same skill is put to different uses: - The tabernacle craftsmen were given it for God's house (Exodus 35:35). Huram-abi, sent to Solomon for the temple, was trained "to do all sorts of engraving and execute any design that may be assigned him" (2 Chronicles 2:14). His skill was to carry out a design another gave him. - King Uzziah's engineers turned it to war: "he made machines, invented by skillful men … And his fame spread far, for he was marvelously helped, till he was strong" (2 Chronicles 26:15). The next verse: "But when he was strong, he grew proud, to his destruction" (26:16). - Those "at ease in Zion" (Amos 6:1) turned it on themselves: they "like David invent for themselves instruments of music" (6:5).  **It reckons**, giving things their worth. People reckon wrongly. - Judah "thought she was a prostitute" (Genesis 38:15). - Eli watched Hannah praying silently and "took her to be a drunken woman" (1 Samuel 1:13). - A whole people looked at the servant of the Lord and "esteemed him not … we esteemed him stricken, smitten by God, and afflicted" (Isaiah 53:3–4). - A price can be set on a person, and called lordly in irony: "Then the Lord said to me, 'Throw it to the potter'—the lordly price at which I was priced by them" (Zechariah 11:13). It was thirty pieces of silver (11:12). Matthew reads it of the silver Judas brought back when he "changed his mind": "the price of him on whom a price had been set by some of the sons of Israel" (Matthew 27:3, 9). - Opponents reckon the worst: "some who suspect us of walking according to the flesh" (2 Corinthians 10:2). - People reckon by the surface: "Even a fool who keeps silent is considered wise" (Proverbs 17:28). Even a good act can be reckoned by its manner: "Whoever blesses his neighbor with a loud voice, rising early in the morning, will be counted as cursing" (27:14). - A people at ease can be made to reckon itself: "Pass over to Calneh, and see … Are you better than these kingdoms? Or is their territory greater than your territory" (Amos 6:2), said to those "at ease in Zion" (6:1) who "put far away the day of disaster" (6:3). - A father can reckon his own daughters as strangers. Rachel and Leah: "Are we not regarded by him as foreigners? For he has sold us" (Genesis 31:15). - What is precious can be reckoned cheap: "The precious sons of Zion, worth their weight in fine gold, how they are regarded as earthen pots, the work of a potter's hands!" (Lamentations 4:2). - When a land breaks down, regard for people goes with it: "Covenants are broken; cities are despised; there is no regard for man" (Isaiah 33:8). The Medes are named by what they do not value: they "have no regard for silver and do not delight in gold" (13:17), and the next verse says "they will have no mercy" (13:18).  Being reckoned is felt from the inside. - "Yet for your sake we are killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered" (Psalm 44:22). - "I am counted among those who go down to the pit; I am a man who has no strength" (Psalm 88:4). The verse before says, "my soul is full of troubles" (88:3). - A people can reckon itself apart. Balaam, sent to curse, sees "a people dwelling alone, and not counting itself among the nations!" (Numbers 23:9). - Being reckoned trustworthy carries a charge. Nehemiah appointed treasurers "for they were considered reliable, and their duty was to distribute to their brothers" (Nehemiah 13:13). - A man can be reckoned worthy by others and reckon himself not. The elders said of the centurion, "He is worthy to have you do this for him, for he loves our nation" (Luke 7:4–5). He sent word, "Lord, do not trouble yourself, for I am not worthy to have you come under my roof. Therefore I did not presume to come to you. But say the word, and let my servant be healed" (7:6–7). Jesus "marveled at him" (7:9).  God reckons truly. - Abraham "believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6). - The nations "are accounted as the dust on the scales" (Isaiah 40:15). Yet the same God "takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17).  Jesus took the wrong reckoning on himself: "this Scripture must be fulfilled in me: 'And he was numbered with the transgressors'" (Luke 22:37). And reckoning is not mine to turn toward myself: "Not that we are sufficient in ourselves to claim anything as coming from us, but our sufficiency is from God" (2 Corinthians 3:5).  Reckoning is not only about judging. In the law it serves **release**: the man who sold himself "shall calculate with his buyer from the year when he sold himself to him until the year of jubilee" (Leviticus 25:50), and pay his way free. And there are times when reckoning is laid aside because there is trust: "they did not ask for an accounting from the men into whose hand they delivered the money … for they dealt honestly" (2 Kings 12:15).  The Greek word carries this on. "I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us" (Romans 8:18). And faith is itself a reckoning: Abraham "considered that God was able even to raise him from the dead" (Hebrews 11:19). Paul says the same of Abraham before his own body: "He did not weaken in faith when he considered his own body, which was as good as dead (since he was about a hundred years old), or when he considered the barrenness of Sarah's womb" (Romans 4:19).  Reckoning from what God has done can answer a fear of dying. Manoah said, "We shall surely die, for we have seen God." His wife answered, "If the Lord had meant to kill us, he would not have accepted a burnt offering and a grain offering at our hands, or shown us all these things" (Judges 13:22–23). Chapter 2 follows the fear of dying.  **It likens.** The Hebrew *dāmāh* means both "to be like" and "to think". - Mordecai warns Esther, "Do not think to yourself that in the king's palace you will escape any more than all the other Jews" (Esther 4:13). - Worshippers say, "We have thought on your steadfast love, O God, in the midst of your temple" (Psalm 48:9). - Love likens: "I compare you, my love, to a mare among Pharaoh's chariots" (Song of Songs 1:9). - Comfort tries to liken, and sometimes cannot: "What can I say for you, to what compare you, O daughter of Jerusalem? What can I liken to you, that I may comfort you …? For your ruin is vast as the sea; who can heal you?" (Lamentations 2:13).  - Lament likens the self truly: "I am like a desert owl of the wilderness" (Psalm 102:6). - God himself teaches by likening: "through the prophets gave parables" (Hosea 12:10).  Likening can go badly wrong. God says, "you thought that I was one like yourself" (Psalm 50:21). Chapter 12 follows this further.  **It murmurs.** *Hāgāh* is the word for meditating, and it is not silent. "On his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). "I remember you upon my bed, and meditate on you in the watches of the night" (Psalm 63:6). But the same word devises and plots: "their hearts devise violence" (Proverbs 24:2). And it can "meditate treachery all day long" (Psalm 38:12). Chapter 10.5 picks up its sense of uttering.  **It reasons, inside and between.** The Greek word for reasoning is used for a single heart talking to itself and for people talking together, with no change of word. - Inside: a thought can be a whole sentence. "In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 10:4). Jesus perceived "that they thus questioned within themselves" (Mark 2:8). The rich man "thought to himself, 'What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?'" (Luke 12:17). - Between: "What were you discussing on the way?" (Mark 9:33).  **It can be troubled.** Mary "was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be" (Luke 1:29). She is trying to understand. The disciples' worried reasoning about bread is different. "Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened?" (Mark 8:17). Jesus connects it with a hard heart and "little faith" (Matthew 16:8).  Thinking can weigh answers by their cost, not by their truth. Asked by what authority he acted, Jesus asked in return, "The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" "And they discussed it among themselves, saying, 'If we say, From heaven, he will say to us, Why then did you not believe him? But if we say, From man, we are afraid of the crowd'" (Matthew 21:25–26). They answered, "We do not know" (21:27). Both answers were weighed against what each would cost them (10.12, 10.11).  A wrong expectation can be what a teaching answers. Jesus told the parable of the nobleman and the minas "because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately" (Luke 19:11).  
  - note: in part: it reckons
