"In the pride of his face the wicked does not seek him; all his thoughts are, 'There is no God'" (Psalm 10:4). Jesus perceived "that they thus questioned within themselves" (Mark 2:8). The rich man "thought to himself, 'What shall I do, for I have nowhere to store my crops?'" (Luke 12:17). - Between: "What were you discussing on the way?" (Mark 9:33).  **It can be troubled.** Mary "was greatly troubled at the saying, and tried to discern what sort of greeting this might be" (Luke 1:29). She is trying to understand. The disciples' worried reasoning about bread is different. "Why are you discussing the fact that you have no bread? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Are your hearts hardened?" (Mark 8:17). Jesus connects it with a hard heart and "little faith" (Matthew 16:8).  Thinking can weigh answers by their cost, not by their truth. Asked by what authority he acted, Jesus asked in return, "The baptism of John, from where did it come? From heaven or from man?" "And they discussed it among themselves, saying, 'If we say, From heaven, he will say to us, Why then did you not believe him? But if we say, From man, we are afraid of the crowd'" (Matthew 21:25–26). They answered, "We do not know" (21:27). Both answers were weighed against what each would cost them (10.12, 10.11).  A wrong expectation can be what a teaching answers. Jesus told the parable of the nobleman and the minas "because he was near to Jerusalem, and because they supposed that the kingdom of God was to appear immediately" (Luke 19:11).  
  - note: in part: it likens
- **C-374** telling added · 10.4 *When thinking changes character* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## When thinking changes character  Again and again in these words I found the same thought becoming something else.  **One word, three faces: *mᵊzimmāh*.** - In the young it is discretion: "to give prudence to the simple, knowledge and discretion to the youth" (Proverbs 1:4). It "will watch over you" (2:11). - In the wicked it is an evil device, joined to arrogance: "In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor; let them be caught in the schemes that they have devised" (Psalm 10:2). It sits beside a short temper: "A man of quick temper acts foolishly, and a man of evil devices is hated" (Proverbs 14:17). - In God it is purpose: "no purpose of yours can be thwarted" (Job 42:2). His anger serves it, and it is understood only later: "The anger of the Lord will not turn back until he has executed and accomplished the intents of his heart. In the latter days you will understand it clearly" (Jeremiah 23:20).  **One passage, three plans: Jeremiah 18.** - God says, "Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way" (18:11). Even this plan is open: "if that nation … turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it" (18:8). - The people answer, "We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12). - Then they turn on the messenger: "Come, let us make plots against Jeremiah" (18:18).  God's plan is *against*, and in the same breath he says "Return" (Jeremiah 18:11). The people's plans are, in their own words, "the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12). The word "against" is the same in God's plan and in their plot.  **What it keeps company with.** Plans fail alone and stand with counsel: "Without counsel plans fail, but with many advisers they succeed" (Proverbs 15:22). "Commit your work to the Lord, and your plans will be established" (16:3). The same togetherness can go the other way: "All who hate me whisper together about me; they imagine the worst for me" (Psalm 41:7).  **The state it rises from.** Paul names the order of cause in so many words: people are "darkened in their understanding … due to their hardness of heart" (Ephesians 4:18). A hard heart makes for dark thinking. Ease does it too: "In the thought of one who is at ease there is contempt for misfortune; it is ready for those whose feet slip" (Job 12:5). A comfortable mind looks down on those who fall.  **Its pace.** "The plans of the diligent lead surely to abundance, but everyone who is hasty comes only to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). Haste is named again in Job 20:2 (below).  **Where it is done.** Thinking alone can stall. "When I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task, until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end" (Psalm 73:16–17). The bed, as I show below, is a place that holds both ways of thinking.  **Reasoning that becomes a quarrel.** The Greek word for inner reasoning is also the word for a quarrel. The disciples' reasoning about greatness became an argument: "An argument arose among them as to which of them was the greatest. But Jesus, knowing the reasoning of their hearts, took a child" (Luke 9:46–47). Paul uses the word for dispute: "Do all things without grumbling or disputing" (Philippians 2:14). And he uses it beside anger: men are to pray "lifting holy hands without anger or quarreling" (1 Timothy 2:8).  **Imagination that makes gods.** The power to design can be turned to making a god: "we ought not to think that the divine being is like gold or silver or stone, an image formed by the art and imagination of man" (Acts 17:29).  None of these is a rule I have laid on the verses. They are what the verses themselves put beside the change. Chapter 11 gathers them across all the activities. 
  - note: in part: reasoning that becomes a quarrel
- **C-375** telling added · 13.1 *Purposing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Purposing  The words used for a person who plans, devises or purposes are also used of God. The verses do not give his plans as a hidden decree working out of sight. They show him forming a plan and saying it aloud, setting it against what people devise, holding it open to their turning, carrying it out, and keeping it fixed where he has sworn.  **He forms a plan and makes it known.** "Therefore hear the plan that the Lord has made against Edom and the purposes that he has formed against the inhabitants of Teman" (Jeremiah 49:20). The same words are spoken against Babylon (50:45). In both places the plan follows his question, "For who is like me? Who will summon me?" (49:19; 50:44). Of Babylon it is said that "the Lord has both planned and done what he spoke" (51:12). The verse before shows how it went forward, through other people's spirits: "The Lord has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it" (51:11). His counsel is something to be told in full. Paul counts his own innocence in not holding it back: "I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God" (Acts 20:27).  **His devising answers what people devise.** Micah speaks first of those "who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds" (Micah 2:1), who "covet fields and seize them" (2:2). Then: "Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, against this family I am devising disaster" (2:3). The verb is the same for both, and the "therefore" ties his devising to theirs. In Jeremiah his plan and theirs stand in one exchange: - He says: "Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way" (Jeremiah 18:11). - They answer: "That is in vain! We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12).  **He says what he intends so that people may turn, and he relents.** At the potter's house he says, "like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand" (Jeremiah 18:6). He sets out both directions: - "if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it" (18:8) - "if it does evil in my sight, not listening to my voice, then I will relent of the good that I had intended to do to it" (18:10)  His intention is spoken so that it can be heard. "It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them" (Jeremiah 26:3). It is written in a scroll for the same reason: "that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin" (36:3). I read these verses as saying that the hearing and turning of the people belong to what happens to the plan. The verses themselves say "it may be", and leave the outcome open.  **He also purposes and does not turn back.** "I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back" (Jeremiah 4:28). The verse before it sets a limit inside the judgment: "yet I will not make a full end" (4:27). Zechariah sets a fixed purpose for disaster beside a fixed purpose for good: "As I purposed to bring disaster to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath, and I did not relent … so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not" (Zechariah 8:14–15). When he wished to show "the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath" (Hebrews 6:17). The verses say both that he relents and that he does not relent or turn back. None of them explains how the two stand together, and I leave them as they are written.  **What he purposed is carried out, and people see afterward that it was his.** "The Lord has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago" (Lamentations 2:17). "The Lord determined to lay in ruins the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out the measuring line" (2:8). In Zechariah the fathers looked back and recognised it: "As the Lord of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us" (Zechariah 1:6).  **He has plans for welfare, and takes thought for the one in need.** - "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). This is said to exiles, of what will come "When seventy years are completed" (29:10). - "As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). - In the plea Joab put in her mouth (2 Samuel 14:3), the wise woman of Tekoa sets God against the fact that "We must all die": "God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14).  **His plan takes in what people do against him, and does not excuse them.** "this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men" (Acts 2:23). The plan and the guilt are in one sentence. The church, praying Psalm 2, says that those who gathered against Jesus did "whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place" (Acts 4:28). They then ask, "grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness" (4:29). Joseph says to his brothers, "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20); the same verb is used for both.  **His purpose stands before the ages and does not rest on works.** - "because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2 Timothy 1:9) - "though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (Romans 9:11) - "according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will" (Ephesians 1:11)  It is made known in Christ: "the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ" (Ephesians 1:9–10). It is "the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord" (3:11). Christ is the one "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood … to show God's righteousness" (Romans 3:25).  **The Spirit intercedes according to the will of God.** Where people do not know how to pray, the Spirit prays, and his praying is matched to God's will: "Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God" (Romans 8:26–27). The one who searches hearts knows the Spirit's mind. Paul does not say here what "mind" is, and I leave the word as he gives it.  **It is turned toward those who love him.** The next verse goes straight on: "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28).  **A person can refuse it, or serve it.** "the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves" (Luke 7:30), while the people and the tax collectors "declared God just" (7:29). "David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep" (Acts 13:36).  What these verses mean for a person is not taken up here. Each touches the inner life in its own way: - the plan spoken so that a person may hear and turn - the purpose sworn as "a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul" (Hebrews 6:19) - "when you seek me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:13) - "we do not know what to pray for as we ought" (Romans 8:26), the weakness the Spirit helps - the heart poured out "like water before the presence of the Lord" after his purpose was carried out (Lamentations 2:19) - "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zechariah 8:17), said straight after his own purposing for good  These belong with a person's own planning, in 10.7 (*Planning*).  **His purpose is spoken, and carried out by another.** The delight word is also used for his purpose. He is the one "who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'" (Isaiah 44:28), at the end of a line of sayings: "who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers" (44:26). Again: "declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it" (46:10–11). It is said to people told to "remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other" (46:9). And: "Who among them has declared these things? The Lord loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon" (48:14). I read "his purpose" there as the Lord's, carried out by the one he loves, as in 44:28; it can also be read as Cyrus's own pleasure. In each place the purpose is said aloud, set against idols that declare nothing, and done through a named man. What pleases him is what he will do.  **His word carries out what he purposes.** "For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth" (Isaiah 55:10), "so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it" (55:11). The act is the word going out and doing its work. "Purpose" is a delight word: what he delights in, his word carries out. 
  - note: in part: his devising answers what people devise; he says what he intends so that people may turn

The verse before shows how it went forward, through other people's spirits: "The Lord has stirred up the spirit of the kings of the Medes, because his purpose concerning Babylon is to destroy it" (51:11). His counsel is something to be told in full. Paul counts his own innocence in not holding it back: "I did not shrink from declaring to you the whole counsel of God" (Acts 20:27).  **His devising answers what people devise.** Micah speaks first of those "who devise wickedness and work evil on their beds" (Micah 2:1), who "covet fields and seize them" (2:2). Then: "Therefore thus says the Lord: behold, against this family I am devising disaster" (2:3). The verb is the same for both, and the "therefore" ties his devising to theirs. In Jeremiah his plan and theirs stand in one exchange: - He says: "Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way" (Jeremiah 18:11). - They answer: "That is in vain! We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12).  **He says what he intends so that people may turn, and he relents.** At the potter's house he says, "like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand" (Jeremiah 18:6). He sets out both directions: - "if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it" (18:8) - "if it does evil in my sight, not listening to my voice, then I will relent of the good that I had intended to do to it" (18:10)  His intention is spoken so that it can be heard. "It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them" (Jeremiah 26:3). It is written in a scroll for the same reason: "that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin" (36:3). I read these verses as saying that the hearing and turning of the people belong to what happens to the plan. The verses themselves say "it may be", and leave the outcome open.  **He also purposes and does not turn back.** "I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back" (Jeremiah 4:28). The verse before it sets a limit inside the judgment: "yet I will not make a full end" (4:27). Zechariah sets a fixed purpose for disaster beside a fixed purpose for good: "As I purposed to bring disaster to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath, and I did not relent … so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not" (Zechariah 8:14–15). When he wished to show "the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath" (Hebrews 6:17). The verses say both that he relents and that he does not relent or turn back. None of them explains how the two stand together, and I leave them as they are written.  **What he purposed is carried out, and people see afterward that it was his.** "The Lord has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago" (Lamentations 2:17). "The Lord determined to lay in ruins the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out the measuring line" (2:8). In Zechariah the fathers looked back and recognised it: "As the Lord of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us" (Zechariah 1:6).  **He has plans for welfare, and takes thought for the one in need.** - "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). This is said to exiles, of what will come "When seventy years are completed" (29:10). - "As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). - In the plea Joab put in her mouth (2 Samuel 14:3), the wise woman of Tekoa sets God against the fact that "We must all die": "God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14).  **His plan takes in what people do against him, and does not excuse them.** "this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men" (Acts 2:23). The plan and the guilt are in one sentence. The church, praying Psalm 2, says that those who gathered against Jesus did "whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place" (Acts 4:28). They then ask, "grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness" (4:29). Joseph says to his brothers, "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20); the same verb is used for both.  **His purpose stands before the ages and does not rest on works.** - "because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2 Timothy 1:9) - "though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (Romans 9:11) - "according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will" (Ephesians 1:11)  It is made known in Christ: "the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ" (Ephesians 1:9–10). It is "the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord" (3:11). Christ is the one "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood … to show God's righteousness" (Romans 3:25).  **The Spirit intercedes according to the will of God.** Where people do not know how to pray, the Spirit prays, and his praying is matched to God's will: "Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God" (Romans 8:26–27). The one who searches hearts knows the Spirit's mind. Paul does not say here what "mind" is, and I leave the word as he gives it.  **It is turned toward those who love him.** The next verse goes straight on: "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28).  **A person can refuse it, or serve it.** "the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves" (Luke 7:30), while the people and the tax collectors "declared God just" (7:29). "David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep" (Acts 13:36).  What these verses mean for a person is not taken up here. Each touches the inner life in its own way: - the plan spoken so that a person may hear and turn - the purpose sworn as "a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul" (Hebrews 6:19) - "when you seek me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:13) - "we do not know what to pray for as we ought" (Romans 8:26), the weakness the Spirit helps - the heart poured out "like water before the presence of the Lord" after his purpose was carried out (Lamentations 2:19) - "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zechariah 8:17), said straight after his own purposing for good  These belong with a person's own planning, in 10.7 (*Planning*).  **His purpose is spoken, and carried out by another.** The delight word is also used for his purpose. He is the one "who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'" (Isaiah 44:28), at the end of a line of sayings: "who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers" (44:26). Again: "declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it" (46:10–11). It is said to people told to "remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other" (46:9). And: "Who among them has declared these things? The Lord loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon" (48:14). I read "his purpose" there as the Lord's, carried out by the one he loves, as in 44:28; it can also be read as Cyrus's own pleasure. In each place the purpose is said aloud, set against idols that declare nothing, and done through a named man. What pleases him is what he will do.  **His word carries out what he purposes.** "For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth" (Isaiah 55:10), "so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it" (55:11). The act is the word going out and doing its work. "Purpose" is a delight word: what he delights in, his word carries out. 
  - note: in part: he also purposes and does not turn back

In Jeremiah his plan and theirs stand in one exchange: - He says: "Behold, I am shaping disaster against you and devising a plan against you. Return, every one from his evil way" (Jeremiah 18:11). - They answer: "That is in vain! We will follow our own plans, and will every one act according to the stubbornness of his evil heart" (18:12).  **He says what he intends so that people may turn, and he relents.** At the potter's house he says, "like the clay in the potter's hand, so are you in my hand" (Jeremiah 18:6). He sets out both directions: - "if that nation, concerning which I have spoken, turns from its evil, I will relent of the disaster that I intended to do to it" (18:8) - "if it does evil in my sight, not listening to my voice, then I will relent of the good that I had intended to do to it" (18:10)  His intention is spoken so that it can be heard. "It may be they will listen, and every one turn from his evil way, that I may relent of the disaster that I intend to do to them" (Jeremiah 26:3). It is written in a scroll for the same reason: "that every one may turn from his evil way, and that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin" (36:3). I read these verses as saying that the hearing and turning of the people belong to what happens to the plan. The verses themselves say "it may be", and leave the outcome open.  **He also purposes and does not turn back.** "I have spoken; I have purposed; I have not relented, nor will I turn back" (Jeremiah 4:28). The verse before it sets a limit inside the judgment: "yet I will not make a full end" (4:27). Zechariah sets a fixed purpose for disaster beside a fixed purpose for good: "As I purposed to bring disaster to you when your fathers provoked me to wrath, and I did not relent … so again have I purposed in these days to bring good to Jerusalem and to the house of Judah; fear not" (Zechariah 8:14–15). When he wished to show "the unchangeable character of his purpose, he guaranteed it with an oath" (Hebrews 6:17). The verses say both that he relents and that he does not relent or turn back. None of them explains how the two stand together, and I leave them as they are written.  **What he purposed is carried out, and people see afterward that it was his.** "The Lord has done what he purposed; he has carried out his word, which he commanded long ago" (Lamentations 2:17). "The Lord determined to lay in ruins the wall of the daughter of Zion; he stretched out the measuring line" (2:8). In Zechariah the fathers looked back and recognised it: "As the Lord of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us" (Zechariah 1:6).  **He has plans for welfare, and takes thought for the one in need.** - "For I know the plans I have for you, declares the Lord, plans for welfare and not for evil, to give you a future and a hope" (Jeremiah 29:11). This is said to exiles, of what will come "When seventy years are completed" (29:10). - "As for me, I am poor and needy, but the Lord takes thought for me" (Psalm 40:17). - In the plea Joab put in her mouth (2 Samuel 14:3), the wise woman of Tekoa sets God against the fact that "We must all die": "God will not take away life, and he devises means so that the banished one will not remain an outcast" (14:14).  **His plan takes in what people do against him, and does not excuse them.** "this Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men" (Acts 2:23). The plan and the guilt are in one sentence. The church, praying Psalm 2, says that those who gathered against Jesus did "whatever your hand and your plan had predestined to take place" (Acts 4:28). They then ask, "grant to your servants to continue to speak your word with all boldness" (4:29). Joseph says to his brothers, "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20); the same verb is used for both.  **His purpose stands before the ages and does not rest on works.** - "because of his own purpose and grace, which he gave us in Christ Jesus before the ages began" (2 Timothy 1:9) - "though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad—in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (Romans 9:11) - "according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will" (Ephesians 1:11)  It is made known in Christ: "the mystery of his will, according to his purpose, which he set forth in Christ as a plan for the fullness of time, to unite all things in Christ" (Ephesians 1:9–10). It is "the eternal purpose that he has realized in Christ Jesus our Lord" (3:11). Christ is the one "whom God put forward as a propitiation by his blood … to show God's righteousness" (Romans 3:25).  **The Spirit intercedes according to the will of God.** Where people do not know how to pray, the Spirit prays, and his praying is matched to God's will: "Likewise the Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words. And he who searches hearts knows what is the mind of the Spirit, because the Spirit intercedes for the saints according to the will of God" (Romans 8:26–27). The one who searches hearts knows the Spirit's mind. Paul does not say here what "mind" is, and I leave the word as he gives it.  **It is turned toward those who love him.** The next verse goes straight on: "And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose" (Romans 8:28).  **A person can refuse it, or serve it.** "the Pharisees and the lawyers rejected the purpose of God for themselves" (Luke 7:30), while the people and the tax collectors "declared God just" (7:29). "David, after he had served the purpose of God in his own generation, fell asleep" (Acts 13:36).  What these verses mean for a person is not taken up here. Each touches the inner life in its own way: - the plan spoken so that a person may hear and turn - the purpose sworn as "a sure and steadfast anchor of the soul" (Hebrews 6:19) - "when you seek me with all your heart" (Jeremiah 29:13) - "we do not know what to pray for as we ought" (Romans 8:26), the weakness the Spirit helps - the heart poured out "like water before the presence of the Lord" after his purpose was carried out (Lamentations 2:19) - "do not devise evil in your hearts against one another" (Zechariah 8:17), said straight after his own purposing for good  These belong with a person's own planning, in 10.7 (*Planning*).  **His purpose is spoken, and carried out by another.** The delight word is also used for his purpose. He is the one "who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd, and he shall fulfill all my purpose'" (Isaiah 44:28), at the end of a line of sayings: "who confirms the word of his servant and fulfills the counsel of his messengers" (44:26). Again: "declaring the end from the beginning and from ancient times things not yet done, saying, 'My counsel shall stand, and I will accomplish all my purpose,' calling a bird of prey from the east, the man of my counsel from a far country. I have spoken, and I will bring it to pass; I have purposed, and I will do it" (46:10–11). It is said to people told to "remember the former things of old; for I am God, and there is no other" (46:9). And: "Who among them has declared these things? The Lord loves him; he shall perform his purpose on Babylon" (48:14). I read "his purpose" there as the Lord's, carried out by the one he loves, as in 44:28; it can also be read as Cyrus's own pleasure. In each place the purpose is said aloud, set against idols that declare nothing, and done through a named man. What pleases him is what he will do.  **His word carries out what he purposes.** "For as the rain and the snow come down from heaven and do not return there but water the earth" (Isaiah 55:10), "so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for which I sent it" (55:11). The act is the word going out and doing its work. "Purpose" is a delight word: what he delights in, his word carries out. 
  - note: in part: the Spirit intercedes; turned toward those who love him; refused or served
- **C-381** telling added · 10.7 *Willing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Willing  Planning reaches ahead from the person. The will, in these verses, mostly answers what comes to the person. In the Hebrew narratives the word for being willing, *ʾāḇâ*, almost always stands just after someone has asked, urged, commanded, enticed, pleaded, warned or offered. And it is almost always a "no": *"would not"*, *"was not willing"*, *"would have none"*. In the Greek, the words for wanting and intending (*boulomai*, *boulēma*) belong to the same family as the words for planning and counsel. One of them, *boulēma*, is translated "plan" in one verse (Acts 27:43) and "will" in another (Romans 9:19). So the verses keep the will and the plan close, without making them one act.  **The will asked for.** Jesus asks people what they want. - To blind men who had cried out against the crowd's rebuke: "What do you want me to do for you?" "Lord, let our eyes be opened." And "Jesus in pity touched their eyes" (Matthew 20:32–34). To Bartimaeus, the same question, and "your faith has made you well" (Mark 10:51–52). - To a man ill for thirty-eight years: "Do you want to be healed?" He answers with what he lacks: "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool" (John 5:6–7). He is healed without the pool (5:8). - To James and John, who came saying "we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you": "What do you want me to do for you?" They asked for the places of honour, and he answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?" (Mark 10:35–38; Matthew 20:21–22). - To the twelve, when many turned back: "Do you want to go away as well?" "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6:67–68). The same question is answered with sight, with a lack, with ambition and with staying. I read the question as drawing the will out into words, where it can be met.  **A will redirected.** Jesus takes the will to be first and the will to follow, and turns them. - The disciples "had argued with one another about who was the greatest". "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all" (Mark 9:34–35). "whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve" (Mark 10:44–45; Matthew 20:27–28). - After Peter was told "you are not setting your mind on the things of God": "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it" (Matthew 16:23–25; Mark 8:34–35; Luke 9:23–24, "daily"). The will is not removed. Its aim is named, wanting to be first, wanting to save one's life, and it is given another way to that end.  **The will meets something put before it.** What is put forward varies: - a request: *"Please let us pass through your land," but the king of Edom would not listen* (Judges 11:17) - pressing, day after day, until *"the man would not spend the night"* (Judges 19:7–10) - a command: Saul's guard *"would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the Lord"* (1 Samuel 22:17) - an enticement, even from the nearest: *"your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly … you shall not yield to him"* (Deuteronomy 13:6–8); *"My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent"* (Proverbs 1:10) - a demand, answered with a line drawn: *"All that you first demanded of your servant I will do, but this thing I cannot do"* (1 Kings 20:9), after the elders said *"Do not listen or consent"* (20:8) - a plea, and the stronger one shutting it out: Tamar said *"No, my brother, do not violate me"*, *"But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her"* (2 Samuel 13:12, 14) - a warning: Abner told Asahel twice to turn aside, *"But he refused to turn aside"*, and he died (2 Samuel 2:21–23) - a feast: the older brother *"was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him"* (Luke 15:28). His anger took the form of a will that would not go in, and the father did not wait inside for it to change (10.13). - a wedding feast: "they would not come", and again, "they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business" (Matthew 22:3, 5) - a plea for patience: "Have patience with me, and I will pay you." "He refused and went and put him in prison" (Matthew 18:29–30), he who had been forgiven all his debt (18:32) - a reign: "his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, 'We do not want this man to reign over us'" (Luke 19:14) - a threat: "He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him" (John 7:1), and his brothers urged him to go (7:3) - an urging between friends: "I strongly urged him to visit you … but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity" (1 Corinthians 16:12)  **The "no" can keep faith, and it can do violence.** The verb does not tell you which; the passage does, and it gives the reason every time. - The king's servants would not kill the priests, and Doeg did (1 Samuel 22:17–18). - David would not *"put out my hand against the Lord's anointed"*. He prayed that, as Saul's life had been precious in his sight, his own would be precious in the Lord's (26:23–24). - The water from Bethlehem shows it most fully. David *"said longingly, 'Oh, that someone would give me water to drink'"* (2 Samuel 23:15). Three men broke through the Philistine camp to bring it. *"But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the Lord and said, 'Far be it from me, O Lord, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?'"* (23:16–17). His own longing was met, and he refused it for their sake, aloud and before the Lord (10.6 follows wanting). - Against that stands Amnon's "would not" (2 Samuel 13:14), and the men of Gibeah who *"would not listen"* (Judges 19:25). - Those who lay burdens on others "are not willing to move them with their finger" (Matthew 23:4), for "they preach, but do not practice" (23:3). - At the cross Jesus was offered "wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it" (Matthew 27:34).  The same verb is used for a refusal that honours other people and for a refusal that tramples them.  **A refusal can be selective.** Saul and the people *"spared Agag and the best of the sheep … and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction"* (1 Samuel 15:9). They refused only where they valued what they kept. God's word on it was *"he has turned back from following me"*, and *"Samuel was angry, and he cried to the Lord all night"* (15:11).  **Wanting to go back.** "But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?" (Galatians 4:9). "Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law?" (4:21). Paul is "afraid I may have labored over you in vain" (4:11). After the defeat at Ai, when "the hearts of the people melted", Joshua said, "Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!" (Joshua 7:5, 7). In a figure: "no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, 'The old is good'" (Luke 5:39). I read the will turning back toward what it knew, even toward slavery, when the new has cost something.  **Content to stay.** "Moses was content to dwell with the man" (Exodus 2:21), and he named his son for being "a sojourner in a foreign land" (2:22). "the Levite was content to dwell with the man", and Micah said, "Now I know that the Lord will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest" (Judges 17:11, 13). The same willingness to stay sits in two very different settings, and the verses say what each led to.  **Feeling holds the will.** - Fear stops it. The armor-bearer *"would not, for he feared greatly"* (1 Samuel 31:4). David *"was afraid of the Lord that day … So David was not willing to take the ark"* (2 Samuel 6:9–10). Three months later *"it was told King David, 'The Lord has blessed the household of Obed-edom'"*, and he *"went and brought up the ark of God … with rejoicing"* (6:12). What he heard moved his will. - Melted hearts stop it: *"Yet you would not go up"* (Deuteronomy 1:26), and *"Our brothers have made our hearts melt"* (1:28). - Grief holds it. David, fasting for the child, *"would not"* rise or eat (2 Samuel 12:17). - Jealousy fixes it: *"He will accept no compensation; he will refuse though you multiply gifts"* (Proverbs 6:35).  10.12 and 10.1 take these feelings up.  **Refusing God refuses something good.** The passages say what was offered: - the land: *"It is a good land"* (Deuteronomy 1:25), and *"Yet you would not go up"* (1:26) - rest: *"This is rest; give rest to the weary; and this is repose"; yet they would not hear* (Isaiah 28:12); and *"ask for the ancient paths, where the good way is; and walk in it, and find rest for your souls. But they said, 'We will not walk in it'"* (Jeremiah 6:16) - the one who brought God's word: *"He received living oracles to give to us. Our fathers refused to obey him, but thrust him aside, and in their hearts they turned to Egypt"* (Acts 7:38–39) - being filled: *"Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it." But … Israel would not submit to me* (Psalm 81:10–11) - his Spirit and his words: *"If you turn at my reproof, behold, I will pour out my spirit to you"* (Proverbs 1:23) - life itself, from the one who gives it: *"yet you refuse to come to me that you may have life"* (John 5:40). Here the passage says what lies behind the refusal. They had searched the Scriptures (5:39), so it was not that they did not know. *"But I know that you do not have the love of God within you … How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from the only God?"* (5:42, 44). The will refused because the desire was set on glory from people. - being gathered: "How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!" (Matthew 23:37; Luke 13:34). His will and theirs stand in one verb (13.1). - a light received only for a while: "He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for a while in his light" (John 5:35)  - cleansing, after reasoning: *"Come now, let us reason together … though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow … If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land; but if you refuse and rebel, you shall be eaten by the sword"* (Isaiah 1:18–20)  Isaiah 1 invites the will with an "if", and both ways are set before it, as life and death are in the next section. Jesus does the same. A young man asked about doing: *"Teacher, what good deed must I do to have eternal life?"* He was answered with the will: *"If you would enter life, keep the commandments"* (Matthew 19:16–17). He had kept them, and still asked, *"What do I still lack?"* He was answered with the will again: *"If you would be perfect, go, sell what you possess and give to the poor … and come, follow me"* (19:20–21). *"When the young man heard this he went away sorrowful, for he had great possessions"* (19:22). He knew what he lacked. Asked for the thing he held, his will would not, and the sorrow is what that felt like. The disciples ask, *"Who then can be saved?"*, and are told, *"With man this is impossible, but with God all things are possible"* (19:25–26). *A will under another*, below, ends in the same place.  **Where willing and planning are named together.** In three passages the refusal of God stands with the person's own counsel, devices or plan: - *"Because they hated knowledge and did not choose the fear of the Lord, would have none of my counsel and despised all my reproof, therefore they shall eat the fruit of their way, and have their fill of their own devices"* (Proverbs 1:29–31). Not choosing, not willing, and one's own devices stand in one sentence. - *"Israel would not submit to me. So I gave them over to their stubborn hearts, to follow their own counsels"* (Psalm 81:11–12). - Isaiah 30 opens with *"stubborn children … who carry out a plan, but not mine"* (30:1). It ends: *"In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength." But you were unwilling, and you said, "No! We will flee upon horses"* (30:15–16). The refusal and their own plan come out of their mouth together.  I read these three as Scripture's own picture of the acts working together when they go wrong: the "no" to God, and a plan of one's own in its place. The verses say what follows: being given over, and being filled with one's own devices. They do not lay out a sequence that every person goes through.  The same pairing is shown going right. David gives Solomon the plan for the temple, *"all the work to be done according to the plan"* (1 Chronicles 28:19), and then says, *"with you in all the work will be every willing man who has skill"* (28:21). A plan comes from God, and the willing carry it out.  **A plan meets another person's will.** - It can allow for it. Abraham's servant looks ahead: *"Perhaps the woman may not be willing to follow me"* (Genesis 24:5). Abraham answers with what God will do, *"he will send his angel before you"*, and with a way out, *"if the woman is not willing … you will be free from this oath"* (24:7–8). - It can turn when its own cost appears, and another can bind himself instead. The nearer redeemer first says of Naomi's land, *"I will redeem it"* (Ruth 4:4). Told that Ruth comes with it, he says, *"I cannot redeem it for myself, lest I impair my own inheritance"* (4:6). It is the same man in the same scene, and his will turns when his own inheritance is touched. Boaz had left room for that will and had bound his own: *"if he is not willing to redeem you, then, as the Lord lives, I will redeem you"* (3:13). Ruth's choice frames it: *"you have not gone after young men"* (3:10). One will is bound to self-interest, one by an oath, and one, Ruth's, is given in kindness. - It can press it until it gives way. Absalom invited the king, who *"would not go"*. Then *"Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him"* (2 Samuel 13:25, 27). The plan ended in Amnon's death (13:28). When Joab *"would not come"* twice, Absalom set his field on fire (14:29–30). - It can bend to a crowd. Pilate had said, *"I find no guilt in him"* (John 18:38). Then, *"wishing to satisfy the crowd"*, he *"released for them Barabbas"* (Mark 15:15). - It can try, and give way. Pilate asked, "Whom do you want me to release for you: Barabbas, or Jesus who is called Christ? For he knew that it was out of envy that they had delivered him up" (Matthew 27:17–18). He spoke again, "desiring to release Jesus" (Luke 23:20), and asked, "Why? What evil has he done?" (Matthew 27:23). "And their voices prevailed" (Luke 23:23). "he delivered Jesus over to their will" (23:25). - It can bend to please. Felix, "desiring to do the Jews a favor, … left Paul in prison" (Acts 24:27), after hoping "that money would be given him by Paul" (24:26). Festus, "wishing to do the Jews a favor", asked Paul to be tried in Jerusalem, and Paul appealed to Caesar (25:9–11). - It can stand against a plan. The centurion, *"wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan"* (Acts 27:43). - Others can hold it back or help it on. *"when Paul wished to go in among the crowd, the disciples would not let him"* (Acts 19:30). *"when he wished to cross to Achaia, the brothers encouraged him"* (18:27). - It can be held back by the owner of the field. "Then do you want us to go and gather them?" "No, lest in gathering the weeds you root up the wheat along with them" (Matthew 13:28–29).  **A will bound by an oath before guests.** Herod "feared John, knowing that he was a righteous and holy man … When he heard him, he was greatly perplexed, and yet he heard him gladly" (Mark 6:20). At his banquet he said to the girl, "Ask me for whatever you wish, and I will give it to you" (6:22). Her mother chose for her, and she asked "with haste": "I want you to give me at once the head of John the Baptist on a platter" (6:24–25). "And the king was exceedingly sorry, but because of his oaths and his guests he did not want to break his word to her" (6:26). His grief and his will pulled two ways, and the oath and the watching guests decided it.  **A resolve is still being weighed.** Joseph, *"being a just man and unwilling to put her to shame, resolved to divorce her quietly. But as he considered these things, behold, an angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream"* (Matthew 1:19–20). He was unwilling to shame her, then he resolved, then he went on considering, and God spoke into the considering. Herod's intending went the other way. He was *"intending after the Passover to bring him out to the people. So Peter was kept in prison, but earnest prayer for him was made to God by the church"* (Acts 12:4–5). The intention was not carried out.  **The will steers.** *"Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs"* (James 3:4). James uses the picture for the tongue (3:5; 10.5). In the picture, the will is what sets a whole ship's course.  **The will turned toward harm.** *"those who desire to be rich fall into temptation, into a snare"* (1 Timothy 6:9). Against this Paul sets *"godliness with contentment is great gain"* (6:6). *"whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God"* (James 4:4), said after *"your passions are at war within you"* (4:1).  The will to harm can be stopped short. "Get away from here, for Herod wants to kill you." Jesus answered, "Go and tell that fox … I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day following" (Luke 13:31–33). "Some of them wanted to arrest him, but no one laid hands on him", and the officers said, "No one ever spoke like this man!" (John 7:44–46). A man wronging his neighbour turned the will on Moses: "Do you want to kill me as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?" (Acts 7:28), and Moses fled (7:29). A people can be set on what ruins it: "Ephraim is oppressed, crushed in judgment, because he was determined to go after filth" (Hosea 5:11).  **The will set on godliness.** *"Indeed, all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus will be persecuted"* (2 Timothy 3:12). It is the same verb as *"those who desire to be rich"*. The desire for riches falls into a snare. The desire for godliness walks into persecution. Paul does not promise that the godly will has an easy road. He sets it beside his own sufferings: *"yet from them all the Lord rescued me"* (3:11).  **The willing heart.** The will can also be given freely, and the verses say where that comes from. - At the tabernacle, *"they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him"* (Exodus 35:21; see *Setting the heart*). *"All who were of a willing heart brought"* (35:22). - Of the craftsmen, the skill given and the heart that moves are named together: *"every craftsman in whose mind the Lord had put skill, everyone whose heart stirred him up to come to do the work"* (Exodus 36:2). - After consecration, *"all who were of a willing heart brought burnt offerings"* (2 Chronicles 29:31). - At the gifts for the temple, *"the people rejoiced because they had given willingly, for with a whole heart they had offered freely to the Lord. David the king also rejoiced greatly"* (1 Chronicles 29:9). David says of his own gift, *"In the uprightness of my heart I have freely offered all these things, and now I have seen your people, who are present here, offering freely and joyously to you"* (29:17). - In battle: *"My heart goes out to the commanders of Israel who offered themselves willingly among the people. Bless the Lord"* (Judges 5:9). - Of the churches' gift for Jerusalem: *"For they were pleased to do it, and indeed they owe it to them"* (Romans 15:27). - It is also asked of God: *"Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me … uphold me with a willing spirit"* (Psalm 51:10, 12). The next verse goes on: *"Then I will teach transgressors your ways, and sinners will return to you"* (51:13).  So the willing heart is said both to rise in the person and to be upheld by God. Paul guards the freedom of another's will. He would have liked to keep Onesimus, *"but I preferred to do nothing without your consent in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord"* (Philemon 13–14).  The verses on freely offering say more about where it comes from. - **Asked for, then given.** "Who then will offer willingly, consecrating himself today to the Lord?" (1 Chronicles 29:5). "Then the leaders of fathers' houses made their freewill offerings" (29:6). David prays over it: "But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able thus to offer willingly? For all things come from you, and of your own have we given you" (29:14), and "all this abundance … comes from your hand and is all your own" (29:16). - **Stirred, and helped by others.** "everyone whose spirit God had stirred to go up to rebuild", and those about them "aided them … besides all that was freely offered" (Ezra 1:5–6). Some "made freewill offerings for the house of God … according to their ability" (2:68–69). - **Even from a foreign king.** "the silver and gold that the king and his counselors have freely offered to the God of Israel", with "the freewill offerings of the people and the priests, vowed willingly" (Ezra 7:15–16). The same decree lets "anyone … who freely offers to go to Jerusalem" go (7:13). - **Offering oneself.** "That the leaders took the lead in Israel, that the people offered themselves willingly, bless the Lord!" (Judges 5:2). "a volunteer for the service of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 17:16). After lots were cast for who would live in Jerusalem, "the people blessed all the men who willingly offered to live in Jerusalem" (Nehemiah 11:1–2). - **Readiness, and what it is measured by.** "a year ago started not only to do this work but also to desire to do it. So now finish doing it as well, so that your readiness in desiring it may be matched by your completing it out of what you have. For if the readiness is there, it is acceptable according to what a person has, not according to what he does not have" (2 Corinthians 8:10–12). The gift is carried "to show our good will" (8:19). I read the willing offering as answered by gladness and blessing in these verses, and measured by what a person has, not by its size.  **The will made absolute.** Of Nebuchadnezzar: *"Whom he would, he killed, and whom he would, he kept alive; whom he would, he raised up, and whom he would, he humbled"* (Daniel 5:19). The next verse says what happened inside him: *"But when his heart was lifted up and his spirit was hardened so that he dealt proudly, he was brought down"* (5:20). He had been offered counsel (4:27). He was driven out *"until he knew that the Most High God rules the kingdom of mankind and sets over it whom he will"* (5:21). His reason returned when he lifted his eyes to heaven (4:34). His son knew all this, and Daniel says to him, *"you his son, Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, though you knew all this"* (5:22). Knowing did not move his will.  Daniel sees it again in a later king: *"And the king shall do as he wills. He shall exalt himself and magnify himself above every god … He shall prosper till the indignation is accomplished; for what is decreed shall be done"* (Daniel 11:36). The absolute will runs, and runs only until a time already set.  The will made absolute is seen from below as well. "a mighty king shall arise, who shall rule with great dominion and do as he wills. And as soon as he has arisen, his kingdom shall be broken" (Daniel 11:3–4). Another "shall do as he wills, and none shall stand before him" (11:16), until "a commander shall put an end to his insolence" (11:18). Under such rulers a people says, "They rule over our bodies and over our livestock as they please, and we are in great distress" (Nehemiah 9:37), and says it of kings set over them "because of our sins" (Nehemiah 9:37). The same prayer remembers the land given "that they might do with them as they would" (9:24), and what followed: "they ate and were filled … Nevertheless, they were disobedient" (9:25–26). Of Elijah: "they did not recognize him, but did to him whatever they pleased. So also the Son of Man will certainly suffer at their hands" (Matthew 17:12).  **A will that cannot carry itself out.** Paul speaks of a will that is real and wants the good, and does not carry itself out. "For I do not understand my own actions. For I do not do what I want, but I do the very thing I hate. Now if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law, that it is good. So now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells within me" (Romans 7:15–17). "For I have the desire to do what is right, but not the ability to carry it out. For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what I keep on doing" (7:18–19). "So I find it to be a law that when I want to do right, evil lies close at hand" (7:21). He does not deny the will. He wants the good, he hates what he does, and his wanting agrees with the law. What does the opposite he calls "no longer I". I read the will here as a true inner act that is not master in its own house. The delight and the war in the members are in 10.1 (7:22–23), the cry in Chapter 2 (7:24), and the divided service in Chapter 7 (7:25).  **A will under another.** *"So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy"* (Romans 9:16). New birth is *"not of blood nor of the will of the flesh nor of the will of man, but of God"* (John 1:13). The will can be taught and filled: *"Teach me to do your will, for you are my God!"* (Psalm 143:10); Paul prays that the Colossians *"may be filled with the knowledge of his will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding"* (Colossians 1:9). Servants work *"as bondservants of Christ, doing the will of God from the heart"* (Ephesians 6:6), where "heart" is the soul word. And at Gethsemane: *"Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done"* (Luke 22:42). God's will is in 13.1 (*Willing*).  Peter was told that his own will would be overruled at the end: *"when you were young, you used to dress yourself and walk wherever you wanted, but when you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and carry you where you do not want to go"* (John 21:18). His next words were about someone else: *"Lord, what about this man?"* (21:21). The answer was *"If it is my will that he remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!"* (21:22). Told that his own will would be overruled, he turned to compare his lot with another's, and Christ's will answered both.  **Doing the will of God.** The verses speak of God's will as something a person prays, knows, does, or fails to do. - **Prayed.** "Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven" (Matthew 6:10). At Gethsemane, the second time: "My Father, if this cannot pass unless I drink it, your will be done" (26:42), after "The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (26:41). The words he taught are the words he prays. - **Asked within.** "if we ask anything according to his will he hears us" (1 John 5:14). And: "If you abide in me, and my words abide in you, ask whatever you wish, and it will be done for you" (John 15:7). I read the two together: the asking is free where the asker's will has been shaped by his words. - **Known by willing it.** "If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God" (John 7:17). The willing comes before the knowing. Paul was "appointed … to know his will" (Acts 22:14), and was asked at once, "And now why do you wait?" (22:16). "Do not be foolish, but understand what the will of the Lord is" (Ephesians 5:17). - **Known and not done.** "you … know his will and approve what is excellent" (Romans 2:18) is said to one who boasts in God and teaches others (2:17, 19–21). "And that servant who knew his master's will but did not get ready or act according to his will, will receive a severe beating" (Luke 12:47), more than the one who did not know (12:48). - **Said, and not done.** "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 7:21). Of two sons, one said "I will not, but afterward he changed his mind and went", the other "I will, sir, but did not go". "Which of the two did the will of his father?" (21:29–31). Jesus turns the changed mind toward belief: "you did not afterward change your minds and believe him" (21:32). - **What it is, where the verses say.** "give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1 Thessalonians 5:18). "For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from sexual immorality" (4:3), "not in the passion of lust like the Gentiles who do not know God" (4:5). "that by doing good you should put to silence the ignorance of foolish people" (1 Peter 2:15). After confession, "do his will. Separate yourselves" (Ezra 10:11). - **With suffering, and with endurance.** "For it is better to suffer for doing good, if that should be God's will, than for doing evil" (1 Peter 3:17), and the next verse, "For Christ also suffered" (3:18). "For you have need of endurance, so that when you have done the will of God you may receive what is promised" (Hebrews 10:36). - **Those who do it.** "For whoever does the will of my Father in heaven is my brother and sister and mother" (Matthew 12:50; Mark 3:35), said with his hand stretched toward his disciples. "if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, God listens to him" (John 9:31), said by the man who had been blind. - **God working it in them.** "equip you with everything good that you may do his will, working in us that which is pleasing in his sight" (Hebrews 13:21). God "works in you, both to will and to work" (Philippians 2:13; 10.12). The renewed mind discerns "what is the will of God" (Romans 12:2; Chapter 14). Angels do it too (13.2).  The visions picture the same will. The ram "did as he pleased and became great" (Daniel 8:4), and the horn after it "became great, even as great as the Prince of the host" (8:11; 10.15).  
  - note: in part: a plan meets another person's will; the willing heart, Paul guards the freedom of another's will
- **C-381** telling added · 10.10 *Plotting against another* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Plotting against another  The power to look ahead (10.7, *Planning*) is turned most often, in these verses, against another person. The words are the planning words: to devise, to purpose, to plan. They are used here of harm worked out in advance. What thinking does in plotting is in 10.4, and what the tongue does in 10.5. This section is about what passes between the one who plots and the one plotted against.  **It is planned in the heart.** *"who plan evil things in their heart and stir up wars continually"* (Psalm 140:2). The prophets name the heart as the place where it has to be stopped: *"let none of you devise evil against another in your heart"* (Zechariah 7:10). Zechariah says it again among the things God hates: *"do not devise evil in your hearts against one another, and love no false oath, for all these things I hate"* (8:17).  **It is often done together, and it invites others in.** A son is told what to do when the invitation comes: "My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent. If they say, 'Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood; let us ambush the innocent without reason'" (Proverbs 1:10–11). The will's "no" is set right against the group's plan (10.7, *Willing*). - *"I hear the whispering of many—terror on every side!—as they scheme together against me, as they plot to take my life"* (Psalm 31:13) - *"In Heshbon they planned disaster against her: 'Come, let us cut her off from being a nation!'"* (Jeremiah 48:2) - The council, after Caiaphas spoke: *"So from that day on they made plans to put him to death"* (John 11:53). Then the plan widened: *"the chief priests made plans to put Lazarus to death as well, because on account of him many of the Jews were going away and believing in Jesus"* (12:10–11). The plan grew to take in a man whose life was itself the reason people believed. - Ezekiel is shown *"the men who devise iniquity and who give wicked counsel in this city"* (Ezekiel 11:2). - Kings at one table: *"their hearts shall be bent on doing evil. They shall speak lies at the same table"* (Daniel 11:27), and *"plots shall be devised against him"* (11:25). A conqueror's plan is told to those it is aimed at, so that they can flee: "Flee, wander far away … For Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon has made a plan against you and formed a purpose against you" (Jeremiah 49:30).  **It is aimed at the quiet and the weak.** The verses name who it is aimed at: - *"In arrogance the wicked hotly pursue the poor"* (Psalm 10:2) - *"against those who are quiet in the land they devise words of deceit"* (Psalm 35:20) - *"The wicked plots against the righteous and gnashes his teeth at him"* (Psalm 37:12) - Gog: *"thoughts will come into your mind, and you will devise an evil scheme and say, 'I will go up against the land of unwalled villages. I will fall upon the quiet people who dwell securely'"* (Ezekiel 38:10–11)  **It hides behind something friendly.** *"Sanballat and Geshem sent to me, saying, 'Come and let us meet together at Hakkephirim in the plain of Ono.' But they intended to do me harm"* (Nehemiah 6:2). They sent four times. Nehemiah's answer was not to argue about their intent but to keep to his own work: *"I am doing a great work and I cannot come down"* (6:3). Saul's offer of his daughter was the same: *"Now Saul thought to make David fall by the hand of the Philistines"* (1 Samuel 18:25). 10.11 gives the hidden trap.  **It presses another's will.** Absalom invited the king to his sheepshearing. The king "would not go", but "Absalom pressed him until he let Amnon and all the king's sons go with him" (2 Samuel 13:25, 27). Then he ordered Amnon's death (13:28). When Joab "would not come", twice, Absalom had his field set on fire, and Joab came (14:29–31). Pilate had said of Jesus, "I find no guilt in him" (John 18:38). Yet, "wishing to satisfy the crowd," he "released for them Barabbas" (Mark 15:15). A will can be pushed until it gives way, and in these passages that is how the plan was carried out.  **It accuses the other of a plan.** Sanballat's fifth letter turned the charge round: *"you and the Jews intend to rebel; that is why you are building the wall"* (Nehemiah 6:6). The council said the same to the apostles: *"you intend to bring this man's blood upon us"* (Acts 5:28). Peter answered, *"We must obey God rather than men"* (5:29). Nehemiah named it as made up: *"you are inventing them out of your own mind"* (Nehemiah 6:8). The next verse gives their aim: *"they all wanted to frighten us, thinking, 'Their hands will drop from the work'"* (6:9). I read this as a plan to harm that works by pinning a plan on the other person.  **The one plotted against.** The verses also give the inner life of the person a plot is aimed at. - **He may not know.** *"But I was like a gentle lamb led to the slaughter. I did not know it was against me they devised schemes"* (Jeremiah 11:19). He hands the matter to the one who sees inside: *"O Lord of hosts, who judges righteously, who tests the heart and the mind … to you have I committed my cause"* (11:20). - **He prays to be guarded, and that the plan will not go forward.** *"Guard me, O Lord, from the hands of the wicked; preserve me from violent men, who have planned to trip up my feet"* (Psalm 140:4). *"Grant not, O Lord, the desires of the wicked; do not further their evil plot"* (140:8). *"Let them be turned back and disappointed who devise evil against me!"* (Psalm 35:4). - **He trusts while it goes on.** After the whispering and the scheming, *"But I trust in you, O Lord; I say, 'You are my God.' My times are in your hand"* (Psalm 31:14–15). The plotters plan his time, and he puts his times in God's hand. - **Someone else may plead.** Esther *"fell at his feet and wept and pleaded with him to avert the evil plan of Haman the Agagite and the plot that he had devised against the Jews"* (Esther 8:3). Haman had *"plotted against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur"* (9:24). - **Someone else may stop it.** In the shipwreck, *"The soldiers' plan was to kill the prisoners, lest any should swim away and escape. But the centurion, wishing to save Paul, kept them from carrying out their plan"* (Acts 27:42–43). One man's wish for one prisoner stopped a plan against all of them.  **It is named, and checked.** - *"Whoever plans to do evil will be called a schemer"* (Proverbs 24:8), and the next verse says what it is: *"The devising of folly is sin"* (24:9). - *"If you have been foolish, exalting yourself, or if you have been devising evil, put your hand on your mouth"* (Proverbs 30:32). The check is to stop before the plan reaches the mouth. The verse after it names where pressing leads: *"pressing anger produces strife"* (30:33). - In the law, the false witness who planned another's ruin receives his own plan: *"you shall do to him as he had meant to do to his brother"* (Deuteronomy 19:19), *"And the rest shall hear and fear"* (19:20). 10.4 follows what is devised coming back.  Plotting is also turned against God (10.9).  A plot can be dressed as delight. Saul thought, "Let me give her to him, that she may be a snare for him" (1 Samuel 18:21), and told his servants to say to David in private, "Behold, the king has delight in you, and all his servants love you" (18:22). The act is the snare. The delight is the bait, and it is spoken in private.  The plot can come back on the one who made it. Harbona told the king of "the gallows that Haman has prepared for Mordecai, whose word saved the king", and the king said, "Hang him on that." "So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then the wrath of the king abated" (Esther 7:9–10).  Absalom gave the reason for the burned field when Joab came: "Why have I come from Geshur? It would be better for me to be there still. Now therefore let me go into the presence of the king, and if there is guilt in me, let him put me to death" (2 Samuel 14:32). I read the fire as a demand to be seen by his father. "So he came to the king and bowed himself on his face to the ground before the king, and the king kissed Absalom" (14:33).  
  - note: in part: it presses another's will
- **C-382** telling added · 10.7 *Willing* (recorded, 2026-10-23)
  - passage before: —
  - passage after: ## Willing  Planning reaches ahead from the person. The will, in these verses, mostly answers what comes to the person. In the Hebrew narratives the word for being willing, *ʾāḇâ*, almost always stands just after someone has asked, urged, commanded, enticed, pleaded, warned or offered. And it is almost always a "no": *"would not"*, *"was not willing"*, *"would have none"*. In the Greek, the words for wanting and intending (*boulomai*, *boulēma*) belong to the same family as the words for planning and counsel. One of them, *boulēma*, is translated "plan" in one verse (Acts 27:43) and "will" in another (Romans 9:19). So the verses keep the will and the plan close, without making them one act.  **The will asked for.** Jesus asks people what they want. - To blind men who had cried out against the crowd's rebuke: "What do you want me to do for you?" "Lord, let our eyes be opened." And "Jesus in pity touched their eyes" (Matthew 20:32–34). To Bartimaeus, the same question, and "your faith has made you well" (Mark 10:51–52). - To a man ill for thirty-eight years: "Do you want to be healed?" He answers with what he lacks: "Sir, I have no one to put me into the pool" (John 5:6–7). He is healed without the pool (5:8). - To James and John, who came saying "we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you": "What do you want me to do for you?" They asked for the places of honour, and he answered, "You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink?" (Mark 10:35–38; Matthew 20:21–22). - To the twelve, when many turned back: "Do you want to go away as well?" "Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life" (John 6:67–68). The same question is answered with sight, with a lack, with ambition and with staying. I read the question as drawing the will out into words, where it can be met.  **A will redirected.** Jesus takes the will to be first and the will to follow, and turns them. - The disciples "had argued with one another about who was the greatest". "If anyone would be first, he must be last of all and servant of all" (Mark 9:34–35). "whoever would be first among you must be slave of all. For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve" (Mark 10:44–45; Matthew 20:27–28). - After Peter was told "you are not setting your mind on the things of God": "If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me. For whoever would save his life will lose it" (Matthew 16:23–25; Mark 8:34–35; Luke 9:23–24, "daily"). The will is not removed. Its aim is named, wanting to be first, wanting to save one's life, and it is given another way to that end.  **The will meets something put before it.** What is put forward varies: - a request: *"Please let us pass through your land," but the king of Edom would not listen* (Judges 11:17) - pressing, day after day, until *"the man would not spend the night"* (Judges 19:7–10) - a command: Saul's guard *"would not put out their hand to strike the priests of the Lord"* (1 Samuel 22:17) - an enticement, even from the nearest: *"your friend who is as your own soul entices you secretly … you shall not yield to him"* (Deuteronomy 13:6–8); *"My son, if sinners entice you, do not consent"* (Proverbs 1:10) - a demand, answered with a line drawn: *"All that you first demanded of your servant I will do, but this thing I cannot do"* (1 Kings 20:9), after the elders said *"Do not listen or consent"* (20:8) - a plea, and the stronger one shutting it out: Tamar said *"No, my brother, do not violate me"*, *"But he would not listen to her, and being stronger than she, he violated her"* (2 Samuel 13:12, 14) - a warning: Abner told Asahel twice to turn aside, *"But he refused to turn aside"*, and he died (2 Samuel 2:21–23) - a feast: the older brother *"was angry and refused to go in. His father came out and entreated him"* (Luke 15:28). His anger took the form of a will that would not go in, and the father did not wait inside for it to change (10.13). - a wedding feast: "they would not come", and again, "they paid no attention and went off, one to his farm, another to his business" (Matthew 22:3, 5) - a plea for patience: "Have patience with me, and I will pay you." "He refused and went and put him in prison" (Matthew 18:29–30), he who had been forgiven all his debt (18:32) - a reign: "his citizens hated him and sent a delegation after him, saying, 'We do not want this man to reign over us'" (Luke 19:14) - a threat: "He would not go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him" (John 7:1), and his brothers urged him to go (7:3) - an urging between friends: "I strongly urged him to visit you … but it was not at all his will to come now. He will come when he has opportunity" (1 Corinthians 16:12)  **The "no" can keep faith, and it can do violence.** The verb does not tell you which; the passage does, and it gives the reason every time. - The king's servants would not kill the priests, and Doeg did (1 Samuel 22:17–18). - David would not *"put out my hand against the Lord's anointed"*. He prayed that, as Saul's life had been precious in his sight, his own would be precious in the Lord's (26:23–24). - The water from Bethlehem shows it most fully. David *"said longingly, 'Oh, that someone would give me water to drink'"* (2 Samuel 23:15). Three men broke through the Philistine camp to bring it. *"But he would not drink of it. He poured it out to the Lord and said, 'Far be it from me, O Lord, that I should do this. Shall I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives?'"* (23:16–17). His own longing was met, and he refused it for their sake, aloud and before the Lord (10.6 follows wanting). - Against that stands Amnon's "would not" (2 Samuel 13:14), and the men of Gibeah who *"would not listen"* (Judges 19:25). - Those who lay burdens on others "are not willing to move them with their finger" (Matthew 23:4), for "they preach, but do not practice" (23:3). - At the cross Jesus was offered "wine to drink, mixed with gall, but when he tasted it, he would not drink it" (Matthew 27:34).  The same verb is used for a refusal that honours other people and for a refusal that tramples them.  **A refusal can be selective.** Saul and the people *"spared Agag and the best of the sheep … and would not utterly destroy them. All that was despised and worthless they devoted to destruction"* (1 Samuel 15:9). They refused only where they valued what they kept. God's word on it was *"he has turned back from following me"*, and *"Samuel was angry, and he cried to the Lord all night"* (15:11).  **Wanting to go back.** "But now that you have come to know God, or rather to be known by God, how can you turn back again to the weak and worthless elementary principles of the world, whose slaves you want to be once more?" (Galatians 4:9). "Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, do you not listen to the law?" (4:21). Paul is "afraid I may have labored over you in vain" (4:11). After the defeat at Ai, when "the hearts of the people melted", Joshua said, "Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!" (Joshua 7:5, 7). In a figure: "no one after drinking old wine desires new, for he says, 'The old is good'" (Luke 5:39). I read the will turning back toward what it knew, even toward slavery, when the new has cost something.  **Content to stay.** "Moses was content to dwell with the man" (Exodus 2:21), and he named his son for being "a sojourner in a foreign land" (2:22). "the Levite was content to dwell with the man", and Micah said, "Now I know that the Lord will prosper me, because I have a Levite as priest" (Judges 17:11, 13).
